title: Add Stops to Your Route
desc: Have a GPX route? We find the bike-friendly stops near your line, in your browser, and hand the route back with your picks built in as waypoints.
body: Home / Plan Your Trip / Add Stops to Your Route Add Stops to Your Route Riding a route you already have? Choose its GPX file and we'll find the stops near your line: cafés, groceries, campgrounds, bike shops, places to sleep. They come from BC Bike Stops , our directory of cyclist-welcoming places across BC. Pick the ones you want, then download your route back with those stops built in, as waypoints your GPS shows along the way. Your file never leaves your computer. This whole page runs in your browser. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is stored, and we never see your route. Choose a GPX file or see how it works with a sample route : a day on the Sea to Sky Trail, Whistler down to Squamish. Getting the directory ready… Distances off your route are as the crow flies, so a stop just across a river can read closer than it really is. How far off your route Which kinds of stop Select all Clear Tier — tick none to include all three · what the badges mean → Most stops in the file More stops than this? We keep the ones closest to your route. Many head units get unhappy past a few hundred. 0 for no limit. Download route + stops (GPX) Stops only (GPX) Stop list (CSV) Some Garmin units ignore waypoints packed inside a course file. If yours does, load the stops-only file alongside your course. The CSV opens in Excel, Numbers, or Google Sheets: your stops in riding order, with addresses and distances. Your stops Select all Clear all

title: Be Prepared
desc: What's worth knowing before a bike trip in BC, most important first: emergencies and cell coverage, road and trail conditions, wildlife, rules of the road, and how to be a good guest.
body: Home / Plan Your Trip / Be Prepared Be prepared BC is big, wild, and gloriously empty in places. That's exactly why you're coming. It also means a little preparation goes a long way. Here's what's worth knowing before you roll out, most important first. Winlaw, BC Weather moves fast in the mountains. Plan for it, then enjoy it. If something goes wrong # The emergency number everywhere in BC is 911 . It's the right first call for medical emergencies and for search and rescue. The catch: much of the province has zero cell service. Outside towns and highway corridors, assume your phone won't work. Download offline maps and a weather forecast whenever you have signal or wifi. For remote routes, consider a satellite layer: a Garmin inReach, an iPhone with satellite SOS, or Rogers Satellite, which works on recent phones from any carrier and covers most of BC south of the 58th parallel, outdoors with a view of the sky. Texting only, but texting 911 from a valley with no bars is the feature that matters. Before a multi-day trip, tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back. AdventureSmart calls this a trip plan, and their free tools make it a two-minute job. Stranded rather than hurt? A broken frame or unfixable flat is a logistics problem, not an emergency. BCAA members get Bike Assist, roadside help that covers bicycles anywhere a service vehicle can reach. Intercity buses and taxis in many towns will carry a bike, and our directory's transport listings tell you who. And hitchhiking is legal in BC as long as you stand on the shoulder, not the travelled roadway, though it's not allowed on freeway sections. AdventureSmart · trip plans, and the know-before-you-go basics for BC's outdoors Rogers Satellite · satellite texting on any carrier, from about $15/month BCAA Bike Assist · roadside assistance for bikes, included with membership Transport stops in BC Bike Stops · buses, ferries, and taxis that take bikes Pack a small first-aid kit and a repair kit (and if remote touring becomes your thing, a wilderness first aid course is a fine investment). A neon vest is your friend on rural highways, and in hunting season. Check conditions, before and during # The biggest variable on a BC bike trip isn't your legs. It's fire, smoke, ice, and weather. Wildfires can close roads and turn the air smoky for weeks, mostly July through September. Fire season also brings campfire prohibitions, often for months at a stretch, so check the current bans before you plan dinner around a fire. Your camping stove is fine: gas and propane stoves are legal during a campfire ban unless a restriction explicitly says otherwise (charcoal briquettes count as campfires, though). Ice and snow close mountain passes well into spring. And trails close too: washouts, river flooding, and tree blow-downs after big wind storms can take out sections of a rail trail for a whole season, so check for advisories on any trail you're counting on. Checking a couple of status reports when planning and each night is a habit worth building. DriveBC · road closures, construction, and 900+ highway cameras. Want to know if there's still snow on the pass? Look at it. BC Parks advisories and Recreation Sites and Trails BC · trail and park closures; for rail trails, the local trail organization's page usually has the freshest word BC Wildfire Service map · active fires and their perimeters, with layers for evacuations and area restrictions (the closures around a fire often reach much further than the fire itself) BC Wildfire Service fire bans & restrictions · current campfire prohibitions by region EmergencyInfoBC · the province's official feed for active evacuation orders and alerts Alertable · free app that pushes evacuation and closure alerts straight to your phone by location, worth having before a multi-day trip Air Quality Health Index (AQHI) for BC · current values and forecasts by community; when it's high, make it a rest day; our guide to planning around wildfire smoke covers how to read it as a rider FireSmoke.ca · animated smoke forecast map, useful for planning a few days ahead in wildfire season Environment Canada forecasts · and remember it gets colder as you climb: expect 6 to 10°C cooler at the top of a 1,000 m pass Avalanche Canada · relevant on interior passes in spring and fall Wildlife # You're a guest in bear country. It's one of the best things about riding here, and it asks a little of you. At camp, never feed animals, and store food, food waste, and anything scented securely and away from your tent. Bears get the headlines, but raccoons and wolverines are just as happy to relieve you of tomorrow's lunch, and they're better at it. On the road, give all animals room, especially anything with young nearby. Bear spray is legal in Canada and available in most outdoor stores and gas stations in bear country. Keep it on your body so it is accessible even when you are off your bike, and learn to use it before you need it. Bikepacking without a bear cache at your site? A traditional bear bag needs to go up high and well out on a branch to work. An Ursack, a reinforced fabric sack, works the opposite way: don't hang it, tie it low around a sturdy tree trunk instead. Check your route's BC Parks page first: some popular backcountry sites, Garibaldi Lake among them, already provide bear caches or hang cables. Ticks are out roughly April through June, and again in drier interior spots come fall. Cover up in tall grass or brush if you can, check yourself after, and if you find one, grab it close to the skin and pull straight out, don't twist. Watch the bite site for a few weeks after. Lyme disease is rare in BC but not unheard of. WildSafeBC · what to do if you meet a bear, cougar, moose, or elk Parks Canada: camping in bear country · food storage done right Ursack · how to use one (tie it, don't hang it) HealthLink BC: ticks · how to avoid and remove ticks And if you can't tell your mountain sheep from your mountain goats, Parks Canada made a song about it . We're not sorry. ( more ) Rules of the road # A lot of BC has great cycling infrastructure, but it pays to know the rules of the road. Helmets are the law in BC at any age. Drivers must give you at least 1 metre when passing, or 1.5 metres where the limit is over 50 km/h, thanks to a law passed in 2024. Ride on the right, and on the shoulder where there is one. On Forest Service Roads, pull over and give logging trucks the right of way: they're heavy, they're working, and they may not expect bikes. A handful of highway sections are closed to bikes, mostly urban freeway stretches and a few tunnels and bridges. Signed detours or shuttles exist for each. The George Massey Tunnel has a free bike shuttle . Some bridges ban bikes from the roadway but allow the sidewalk. Province of BC: cycling regulations and restrictions · official list of bike-restricted roads and rules BCCC BikeSense: Where to Cycle · especially the provincial highways section BCCC: Cycling and the Law · your rights and duties in detail People's Law School: rules of the road for BC cyclists · a plain-language version Be a good guest # Every kilometre you ride in BC crosses the traditional territory of First Nations. Learn whose land you're riding through, and where it's welcome, spend your money with Indigenous-owned businesses and experiences along the way. Some places and sites are culturally significant; if an area is signed as closed or restricted, that's the whole answer. Camp where camping is allowed. Free camping on Crown land is generally allowed for up to 14 days in one spot, but not everywhere: parks, private land, tenured areas, and community watersheds all have their own rules. When in doubt, ask locally. Pack out everything you packed in. One more quiet way to help: clean your bike, tires, and shoes between regions. Bikes spread invasive species surprisingly well. Indigenous Tourism BC · experiences, itineraries, and Indigenous-owned stops worth planning a day around Native Land map · whose territory am I on? Recreation sites and trails: know the rules · camping rules on public land PlayCleanGo BC · 30 seconds scrubbing your tires with a boot brush does it The comforts: water, washrooms, food # The unglamorous trio that actually makes or breaks a touring day. Water. Community centres, libraries, and visitor centres will reliably fill a bottle in BC, and our BC Bike Stops directory tracks water and washrooms at thousands of places. Outdoor drinking fountains in much of BC are seasonal, roughly May to October, though Vancouver and Victoria are installing more year-round models. Most supermarkets and gas stations will help you out too (buy something, be the cyclist they remember fondly). Washrooms. Nearly everywhere that refills a bottle has one. Food. Touring appetite is real. Double portions, lots of carbs, eat often, and yes, that means pancakes at small-town diners. Keep some emergency food in your bags in case a mechanical problem keeps you out of towns longer than you expect. MapComplete drinking water map · every fountain OpenStreetMap knows about Free Taps · community-mapped refill points Project 529 · register your bike free before your trip; it helps recovery if it's stolen Plan ahead # BC's best-loved places are popular for a reason, and summer capacity is real. Sought-after hotels and provincial campgrounds book up months in advance. Buses that carry bikes can fill up too, especially on a beautiful summer Sunday night. Book what matters early, and have a backup plan for the rest. BC Parks camping reservations · popular campgrounds open reservations months out Cycle touring gear favourites · a few quirky favourites from twenty years of touring BC cycling and bikepacking groups on Facebook, Reddit, and Discord are great places to ask for current advice, and cyclists love giving it. Conditions, rules, and services change, and this page links out to the people who know best. Treat everything here as a starting point, check current sources before and during your trip, and make your own calls. You know your ride better than any web page does. How did your trip go? Seriously, we'd love to know. What worked, what didn't, which diner had the best pancakes. Email us and help us keep this site true to what BC riding is actually like.

title: Design Your Own Route
desc: Tools for building your own BC bike route from scratch, plus where to find welcoming stops along the way.
body: Home / Plan Your Trip / Design Your Own Route Design your own route Some of the best BC trips start with a blank map. If you love plotting your own line, you're in good company. Tools like Ride with GPS let you draw a route, add cues, and send it straight to your bike computer or phone. Find places to stop # A line on a map becomes a trip when you know where you'll sleep, eat, and refill. Our BC Bike Stops directory tracks thousands of places to sleep, eat, refill water, and explore, the kind of details that turn a line on a map into a real trip. Already drawn your line? # Once your route is a GPX file, bring it to Add Stops to Your Route . We'll find the welcoming stops near your line and hand the file back with your picks built in. Add stops to your route → Something better is coming # We're building a free, BC-made route designer that knows the rail trails, the backroads, the ferries, and the services. Whether that means a gentle e-bike ride on quiet paths, a long day on pavement, or a week deep in the backcountry, dream it up and we'll help you make it real. Want first crack at it? Leave your email and we'll save you a spot at the front of the line. Save my spot

title: How we describe routes
desc: What every route label on this site means, value by value: difficulty, comfort, surface, ruggedness, climbing, and remoteness, plus where the data comes from and how to tell us when it looks wrong.
body: Home / Get Inspired / How we describe routes How we describe routes Routes on this site come from many different publishers, and each one describes rides in its own words. One publisher’s “intermediate” is another’s “hard”, and many say nothing about traffic or surface at all. We encourage you to read how the publishers describe their own routes. To help you understand routes across publishers, here we describe every route ourselves, the same way, with the same labels. When two routes both say Mostly gravel , they mean the same thing. Here’s what each label means. Difficulty # Our overall read of how demanding a route is. We score surface roughness, climbing, singletrack, and how far it runs from services. The route publisher's own rating, a lot of busy road riding, or sheer scale can push the tier up, never down. Easy Smooth surfaces and gentle climbing. Moderate One step up. Some real climbing, or a rougher surface. Ambitious A real undertaking. Demanding on a couple of fronts, like rough surfaces plus steady climbing, or a long stretch on busier roads. Challenging Demanding on several fronts at once, or a lot of riding on busy roads. Epic Expedition scale. Many demanding factors stacked, or 1,000 km and up, or 10,000 m of climbing. Comfort # How much of the route you spend sharing the road with cars. Bike paths, quiet streets, and car free backcountry roads count as comfortable. Busy or fast roads don't. Low-traffic riding At least 75% of the riding we could measure is on bike paths, quiet streets, or car free backcountry roads. Some traffic sharing 45 to 75% of the riding we could measure is low-traffic. The rest shares busier roads. Shares roads with traffic Less than half of the riding we could measure is low-traffic. Expect regular stretches on busier roads. Fast roads # A heads-up when a route includes riding near fast traffic. Fast means the lowest rungs of our traffic-comfort ladder: roads posted 60 km/h and up with nothing built for bikes, or faster roads where there's only a painted line or shoulder between you and traffic. The label shows the distance so you can decide for yourself. Fast-road sections This route includes stretches on fast roads, often a highway link between quieter riding. The label shows how many kilometres; we flag from as little as 2 km on the fastest roads, because a short highway stretch is worth knowing about before you commit. Mostly fast roads Half or more of the route is on fast roads. This is a highway touring route. No fast-road sections We measured this route and found no meaningful fast-road riding. Under 2 km on the fastest roads and under 20 km on busier ones; routes we couldn't measure aren't in this list. Surface # How much of the route is paved versus gravel or dirt, by distance ridden. Surfaces come from OpenStreetMap. Where nothing is mapped we assume ordinary roads are paved and backcountry tracks are gravel, and leave the rest uncounted. Mostly paved Under 15% of the mapped riding is unpaved. Mixed surface 15 to 49% unpaved. Bring tires that can handle gravel. Mostly gravel 50 to 84% unpaved. Almost all gravel 85% or more unpaved. Ruggedness # Flags for routes where a good share of the riding is rougher than the surface label suggests. No rough sections Nothing we measured on this route is rougher than ordinary maintained gravel. Chunky gravel At least 10% of the riding we could measure crosses loose stones, ruts, or sand. Tires of 33 to 40 mm make it a lot more fun. Rough, near-MTB At least 10% of the riding we could measure crosses genuinely rough ground: rock, ballast, mud. Tires of 40 mm or wider recommended. Lots of singletrack The route's publisher reports 30% or more singletrack. That's their number, not one we measure, and only BIKEPACKING.com provides it. Climbing feel # Average climbing per kilometre over the whole route. It's an average, so a short steep wall can hide inside a gentle looking number. Gentle grades Under 6 m of climbing per km. About as flat as BC gets. Some climbing 6 to 12 m per km. Rolling terrain, or a few real hills. Lots of climbing 12 to 20 m per km. Expect sustained climbs. Max climbing More than 20 m per km. Genuinely mountainous. Remoteness # Remote stretches At least 20% of the route runs far from resupply, roughly 25 km or more in a straight line from the nearest places to buy supplies. Carry what you need, and confirm shops are open. We measure distance to supplies, not water. No remote stretches We measured this route and less than 20% of it runs far from resupply. Routes we couldn't measure aren't in this list. Distance and total climb # Measured from the GPS track the route's publisher provides. Cross border routes show their BC portion only. Where the data comes from # Most of these labels are derived from OpenStreetMap, the open map of the world that volunteers build and keep up to date. That's where surface, road type, and traffic come from. Climbing and distance are measured from the GPS track the route's publisher provides. Steepness comes from satellite elevation data. How far you are from resupply is measured against our own directory of places to buy supplies. We credit the other open data we build on with thanks . For this kind of question OpenStreetMap is the best open data there is, and it's good, but it is not perfect. Most backcountry tracks have never had their surface recorded, so we infer it. Some trails are missing. Some tags are years out of date, and a few are just wrong. We need at least 5 km of a route measured before we'll show a label. When we can't measure it, we leave the label off rather than guess. So we compute what we can, and there are surely some mistakes. If a label on a route looks wrong or misleading to you, tell us . We can correct the data, fix the map, or change how we handle the gap, and every one of those makes the next rider's plan better. If you are curious about more detail than we go into here, please get in touch ! We are happy to nerd out about it in very great depth :)

title: Vancouver, Coast and Mountains
desc: 152 cycling routes in Vancouver, Coast and Mountains, BC, from 17 route publishers — mapped and described by the people who know them best.
body: Photo: The Fraser Valley Group Abbotsford, BC Vancouver, Coast and Mountains Ferries, fjords, and gravel above the inlets. Some of the best riding here starts an hour from downtown Vancouver. Home / Get Inspired / Vancouver, Coast and Mountains 152 rides from 17 publishers — all of them, no shortlist. Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there; the maps, turn-by-turns and full details live on the publishers' sites, one click further. Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Bikepacking the Sea to Sky Trail Highlight Bikepacking the Sea to Sky Trail BIKEPACKING.com · 101 km · Weekend or more Challenging Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 14 km Mixed surface Lots of singletrack Lots of climbing The Sea to Sky Trail runs 101 km from Squamish through Whistler to Pemberton, tracing a corridor the Coast Salish and Interior Salish peoples travelled long before highways. Nearly half is flowy singletrack, and the rest mixes doubletrack, gravel, and pavement past turquoise lakes, swimming holes, suspension bridges, and even an old train wreck. Climbs come short and punchy rather than long. Resupply is easy in all three towns, and public transit can carry you back to the start. Guide by Miles Arbour and Nathan Reimer. Stops, map + getting there → Let's Go Biking guidebook author visit site → Let's Go Biking is a British Columbia cycling guidebook series written by Colleen MacDonald, a champion of slow, scenic, family-friendly riding. Her three guidebooks — Around Vancouver; Okanagan and Beyond; and Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands and Sunshine Coast — come with a companion website of mapped rides, walks, and runs. 179 of their BC rides + their story → Ridge Meadows Dyke 7 km · 7 m up · Afternoon A flat gravel dyke ride between Pitt Meadows and Maple Ridge, 7 km one way, with the river on one side and farmland on the other. Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Gentle grades Photo: Let's Go Biking Pitt Lake (Trails) Around the Mountain 23 km · Afternoon Around Burnaby Mountain: a 27 km climb-and-descend loop linking Port Moody, Coquitlam, and Burnaby with open views up top. Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Photo: Let's Go Biking Around the Mountain Barnston Island (from Tynehead Park) 18 km · 22 m up · Afternoon A tiny free ferry, a flat 10 km island lap: Barnston Island is the Fraser's best-kept cycling secret. Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Chunky gravel Gentle grades Photo: Let's Go Biking Barnston Island (from Tynehead Park) Belcarra Park & Sasamat Lake 40km 21 km · 469 m up · Afternoon Port Moody to Belcarra and Sasamat Lake: a 26 km forest loop with a swimming lake in the middle and sea views at the far end. Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Max climbing Photo: Let's Go Biking Belcarra Park & Sasamat Lake 40km Blue Heron Loop 18 km · 130 m up · Afternoon The Blue Heron Loop: 18 km of quiet gravel through Pitt Meadows farmland and forest, where the herons outnumber the cars. Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Chunky gravel Some climbing Photo: Let's Go Biking Blue Heron Loop BMUT - Burnaby Mountain Urban Trail 17 km · Afternoon The Burnaby Mountain Urban Trail: 8.5 km of flat, forest-lined path, glowing with colour in fall. Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Photo: Let's Go Biking BMUT - Burnaby Mountain Urban Trail BMUT Lougheed to Gastown 42 km · Full day Forest to waterfront to Gastown's brick streets: a 21 km one-way ride across the city, with SkyTrain at both ends. Moderate Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Photo: Let's Go Biking BMUT Lougheed to Gastown Boundary Bay Dyke Trail 25 km · 12 m up · Afternoon The Boundary Bay dyke: dead-flat gravel along Delta's shoreline, 15 to 40 km, and some of Canada's best birdwatching. Easy Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Gentle grades Photo: Let's Go Biking Boundary Bay Dyke Trail Burnaby Lakes & Creeks 28 km · 266 m up · Afternoon Lakes, creeks, and forest paths through Burnaby's green heart, in loops of 11 to 29 km. Moderate Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Some climbing Photo: Let's Go Biking Burnaby Lakes & Creeks Burrard Inlet Trails 7 km · Afternoon Waterfront paths and forest singletrack along Burrard Inlet between Burnaby and Port Moody, 4 to 20 km, easy or rowdy as you choose. Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Photo: Let's Go Biking Burrard Inlet Trails Campbell Valley 26 km · 121 m up · Afternoon Campbell Valley's quiet corner of South Langley: parkland trails, horse country, and wineries, 7 to 27 km. body: Photo: Graeme Owsianski Tofino, BC Vancouver Island Rail trails out of Victoria, logging roads up-island, and a coastline that never quite lets you go. Photo: Let's Go Biking Galloping Goose Highlight Galloping Goose Let's Go Biking · 55 km · Full day Moderate Low-traffic riding Mixed surface The Galloping Goose is one of BC's best-known rail trails, running 55 km from downtown Victoria out through Langford's lakes and forest to Sooke, with the Matheson Lake stretch a favourite finale. Flat, family-friendly, and paved near the city before turning to gravel, it carries commuters, tourers, and first-timers alike. Access points and transit connections along the whole length make any distance possible. Stops, map + getting there → Let's Go Biking guidebook author visit site → Let's Go Biking is a British Columbia cycling guidebook series written by Colleen MacDonald, a champion of slow, scenic, family-friendly riding. Photo: Let's Go Biking Myra Canyon Highlight Myra Canyon Let's Go Biking · 22 km · Afternoon Easy Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel The most famous stretch of the Kettle Valley Rail Trail: Myra Canyon's historic wooden trestles and rock tunnels curve around the canyon rim high above Kelowna, in Myra-Bellevue Provincial Park. It is 11 km one way, 22 km return, on gentle rail grade the whole way, well suited to families. Go early or late in summer; the exposed sections get hot. Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Best of the South Chilcotin Mountains Highlight Best of the South Chilcotin Mountains BIKEPACKING.com · 121 km · Weekend or more Epic Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Lots of singletrack Rough, near-MTB Max climbing Remote stretches Canada's bikepacking hotspot, ridden in a long weekend: a 121 km loop linking the South Chilcotins' most rideable singletrack through mid-elevation meadows, dry forest, and open alpine under high peaks. It is all unpaved, mostly trail, and genuinely remote, with no resupply or cell service, so arrive self-sufficient. Strong fitness and mountain bike skills turn it from an ordeal into the highlight of your year. Wildflowers peak in June and July. The riding threads temperate rainforest and rugged coastline, passing near ancient Haida village sites, with about 5,500 m of climbing along the way. Roughly a third is unpaved, and services are few and far between. The published account of riding it solo is a story of connection as much as cycling: this is a place you visit on its terms. title: The Route Makers
desc: The 16 route publishers behind Get Inspired's BC cycling routes — who they are and their full BC collections.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers The people behind the routes Every ride on Get Inspired was researched, mapped, and written up by one of these 16 route publishers. We point; they know the way. Here's who they are, in full — and their showcased BC rides. Let's Go Biking guidebook author 179 BC rides showcased here Let's Go Biking is a British Columbia cycling guidebook series written by Colleen MacDonald, a champion of slow, scenic, family-friendly riding. Her three guidebooks — Around Vancouver; Okanagan and Beyond; and Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands and Sunshine Coast — come with a companion website of mapped rides, walks, and runs. Their story + 179 BC rides → Visit Let's Go Biking ↗ BIKEPACKING.com bikepacking platform 26 BC rides showcased here Founded in 2012, BIKEPACKING.com is the leading resource for bikepacking routes, in-depth gear reviews, inspiration, planning insight, adventure stories, news, and events. For over a decade, we've been building, establishing, sharing, and maintaining the largest library of high-quality bikepacking routes around the world. We now have over 240,000 kilometers (150,000 miles) worth of routes in over 70 countries. This includes our Bikepacking Collective Route Network, which is our collection of original and exceptional bikepacking routes designed by our team of experienced Route Architects or skilled contributors from the community. New Bikepacking Collective Routes are partially funded and supported by the Bikepacking Collective , our member community. As we update and refine some of our popular published routes, we'll induct them into the network, along with other distinguished rides. We're a fully independent platform with a core team of editors who strive to inspire readers to get out and explore our planet, discover its wild places, and connect with its diverse cultures, all via the bicycle's elegant simplicity. Their story + 26 BC rides → Visit BIKEPACKING.com ↗ Gravel Buddies cycling club 23 BC rides showcased here Gravel Buddies is a Vancouver-based cycling community that organizes group gravel rides for women, gender-diverse, and 2SLGBTQIA+ riders, ranging from short evening rides in Stanley Park to multi-day bikepacking trips. Their story + 23 BC rides → Visit Gravel Buddies ↗ Love Machine individual route creator 16 BC rides showcased here Love Machine is a Vancouver-based gravel cycling project run by two friends, Max and Cam, as a side project — not a brand, shop, or club. It publishes free, downloadable GPX routes across southwestern British Columbia, with a stated goal of keeping gravel cycling welcoming rather than gatekept. Their story + 16 BC rides → Visit Love Machine ↗ Trails BC trail organization 12 BC rides showcased here Trails BC (the Trails Society of BC) is a non-profit charity that advocates for greenway trails for self-propelled recreation and active transportation across the province. Léon Lebrun has been at the heart of that work for nearly three decades, building and championing non-motorized trails across the Lower Mainland and beyond; a bridge in Chilliwack and a trail in Port Moody now carry his name. The rides shown here are a handful of the many he's helped map over the years. Their story + 12 BC rides → Visit Trails BC ↗ Bikepack Canada bikepacking platform 12 BC rides showcased here Bikepack Canada is a bikepacking route-sharing platform founded in 2016 by adventure cyclist Ryan Correy, author of the guidebook 'Bikepacking in the Canadian Rockies' and the memoir 'A Purpose Ridden.' Correy died in 2018; the site continues today, hosting routes contributed by bikepackers from across the country. Their story + 12 BC rides → Visit Bikepack Canada ↗ Bike Gear Database route network 10 BC rides showcased here Bike Gear Database is a Canadian online publication covering gravel and bikepacking gear reviews, rider stories, and community-submitted route guides. Routes are organized by country and region, including a Canada section with several British Columbia rides — and every route in the library has actually been ridden by the community before it's published. Their story + 10 BC rides → Visit Bike Gear Database ↗ BT 700 Bikepacking individual route creator 10 BC rides showcased here BT 700 Bikepacking is a route-publishing site run by Ontario adventure cyclist and writer Matt Kadey, one of Canada's most prolific bikepacking route builders. It grew out of the original BT700 gravel loop in southwestern Ontario and now offers downloadable route files for gravel and bikepacking rides across Canada, including several in British Columbia. Their story + 10 BC rides → Visit BT 700 Bikepacking ↗ Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society touring organization 7 BC rides showcased here The Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society (CCCTS) is a non-profit cycling club founded in 1982, based in British Columbia with a chapter in Ottawa. In its own words, it is a club for active adults of all ages; members are mainly retired people who love recreational cycling. Volunteers organize weekly day rides plus multi-day and cross-Canada tours, some of which have run continuously since the 1980s. Their story + 7 BC rides → Visit Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society ↗ Adventure Cycling Association touring organization 6 BC rides showcased here For over 50 years, Adventure Cycling Association has been mapping the most iconic bike routes in North America, including the TransAmerica Trail and the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route. It hosts over 90,000 kilometres of bikepacking and bike touring routes, leads dozens of guided tours each year, and advocates to protect the routes, access, and infrastructure that make bike travel possible. Supported by members and donors, Adventure Cycling's nonprofit mission is to inspire, empower, and connect people to travel by bike. Their story + 6 BC rides → Visit Adventure Cycling Association ↗ Elbow Valley Cycle Club cycling club 6 BC rides showcased here Elbow Valley Cycle Club is a Calgary-based recreational cycling club, one of the largest in Western Canada with roughly 700 members. It organizes about 250 events a year, including road, gravel, and multi-day touring rides, several of which cross into British Columbia. Their story + 6 BC rides → Visit Elbow Valley Cycle Club ↗ British Columbia Randonneurs cycling club 3 BC rides showcased here British Columbia Randonneurs Cycling Club is a long-distance cycling club with deep roots: randonneuring in BC dates to 1979, and the club was a founding member of Les Randonneurs Mondiaux, the world body for 1,200 km grand randonnées, in 1983. With regional chapters in the Lower Mainland, Vancouver Island, Southern Interior, and Peace Region, it organizes brevets (timed long-distance rides of 200 km and up), populaires (shorter introductory events), and permanents (self-paced routes available year-round), and publishes the routes on Ride with GPS. Its celebrated Rocky Mountain 1200 drew riders from around the world. Their story + 3 BC rides → Visit British Columbia Randonneurs ↗ The Great Community Route Celebration event organizer 2 BC rides showcased here The Great Community Route Celebration was a global cycling route-creation event hosted by Ride with GPS, running June 11 to July 5, 2020. Participants worldwide created and submitted routes highlighting places and spaces in their own communities, adding points of interest and photos along the way. The event drew 523 route submissions from 51 countries. Their story + 2 BC rides → Visit The Great Community Route Celebration ↗ Trans Canada Trail trail organization 2 BC rides showcased here Trans Canada Trail is a national charitable organization, based in Ottawa, that coordinates and maintains the Trans Canada Trail (also known as The Great Trail) — a roughly 30,000 km multi-use trail network spanning every Canadian province and territory and connecting the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic coastlines. The network supports hiking, cycling, paddling, and other activities, and is built and managed through partnerships with regional and local trail organizations rather than owned as a single continuous trail. Their story + 2 BC rides → Visit Trans Canada Trail ↗ Great Northern Bikepacking Route individual route creator 2 BC rides showcased here The Great Northern Bikepacking Route (GNBR) is a mostly off-road bikepacking route created by Ontario adventure cyclist and writer Matt Kadey, spanning over 13,000 km across 10 Canadian provinces and 3 U.S. states, from the Pacific to the Atlantic — one of the most ambitious route-mapping projects in the country. It is published segment by segment on a dedicated website, with route data on RideWithGPS and gear and provisioning notes alongside the maps. Their story + 2 BC rides → Visit Great Northern Bikepacking Route ↗ Trans Canada Bike Route Network route network 1 BC ride showcased here A volunteer-run, community-collaborative project mapping a proposed coast-to-coast National Cycling Route Network for Canada. It publishes route data as GPX files, a Garmin BaseCamp database (GDB) with points of interest, KMZ files for offline smartphone use, interactive Google Maps, and a curated Ride with GPS collection. title: Let's Go Biking
desc: Let's Go Biking's complete BC cycling route collection — 179 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Let's Go Biking Let's Go Biking guidebook author visit → Let's Go Biking is a British Columbia cycling guidebook series written by Colleen MacDonald, a champion of slow, scenic, family-friendly riding. Her three guidebooks — Around Vancouver; Okanagan and Beyond; and Vancouver Island, the Gulf Islands and Sunshine Coast — come with a companion website of mapped rides, walks, and runs. Their BC collection Let's Go Biking's BC coverage spans all three guidebooks, with 179 mapped rides in this collection. Most are day rides on quiet roads, greenways, dykes, and rail trails, rated easy to moderate, alongside longer options up to multi-day Kettle Valley Rail Trail (KVR) trips. The focus is family-friendly, scenery-first cycling rather than road touring or bikepacking. 179 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Let's Go Biking's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 94 Photo: Let's Go Biking Ridge Meadows Dyke Ridge Meadows Dyke 7 km · 7 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Gentle grades The Ridge Meadows dykes follow an old rail corridor between Pitt Meadows and Maple Ridge, flat gravel the whole way, with the river beside you and farmland stretching out on the other side. It is 7 km one way, 14 km return, and comfortable for almost anyone, kids included. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Pitt Lake (Trails) Pitt Lake (Trails) 50 km · 125 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Gentle grades The Pitt Lake trails run 20 km one way (40 return) from Pitt Meadows through polder farmland and marsh to the shores of one of the world's few freshwater tidal lakes. Flat the whole way but rough gravel in long stretches, so wider tires help. The birdwatching, eagles, herons, and sandhill cranes in season, is among the region's best. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Around the Mountain Around the Mountain 23 km Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Around the Mountain circles Burnaby Mountain in a 27 km loop linking Port Moody, Coquitlam, and Burnaby, climbing through forest with stretches of singletrack and open views from the high point. One of the harder rides in the Vancouver collection, with real climbing and mixed surfaces. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Barnston Island (from Tynehead Park) Barnston Island (from Tynehead Park) 18 km · 22 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Chunky gravel Gentle grades From Tynehead Park in Surrey, roll down to the Fraser and catch the tiny free ferry, a two-minute crossing, to Barnston Island, where a flat, quiet 10 km lap circles riverside farmland full of bird life. No cars to speak of, no hills at all, and a picnic spot around every corner. The road surface runs rough in patches, so take it easy. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Belcarra Park & Sasamat Lake 40km Belcarra Park & Sasamat Lake 40km 21 km · 469 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Max climbing This 26 km loop from Port Moody climbs through forest to Sasamat Lake, one of the Lower Mainland's warmest swimming lakes, and out to the seaside at Belcarra, with singletrack options and historic sites along the way. The hills are honest work, around 470 m of climbing, which is what keeps the roads quiet. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Blue Heron Loop Blue Heron Loop 18 km · 130 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Chunky gravel Some climbing The Blue Heron Loop covers 18 km of quiet dyke gravel, farmland, and forest singletrack between Pitt Meadows and Maple Ridge. Nearly flat but almost all unpaved and rough in stretches, it rewards wider tires and unhurried pace, and the birdwatching, herons especially, is the point. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking BMUT - Burnaby Mountain Urban Trail BMUT - Burnaby Mountain Urban Trail 17 km Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly paved The Burnaby Mountain Urban Trail runs flat along the mountain's forested flank for 8.5 km one way, 17 return. An easy, family-friendly ride that turns quietly spectacular in fall when the deciduous stretches light up. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking BMUT Lougheed to Gastown BMUT Lougheed to Gastown 42 km Moderate Low-traffic riding Mixed surface An extension of the Burnaby Mountain Urban Trail, this 21 km one-way route runs from Lougheed to Gastown, trading forest for waterfront and finishing among historic brick streets. SkyTrain stations at both ends make the logistics effortless: ride one way, train back. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Boundary Bay Dyke Trail Boundary Bay Dyke Trail 25 km · 12 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Gentle grades The Boundary Bay Dyke Trail runs dead flat along Delta's shoreline between sea and farmland, with access points offering rides of 15, 30, or 40 km. This is one of Canada's premier birdwatching areas, hawks and herons in every season, snowy owls in irruption winters, with mountain views across the bay thrown in. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Burnaby Lakes & Creeks Burnaby Lakes & Creeks 28 km · 266 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Some climbing Burnaby Lakes and Creeks loops through the parkland at the city's green heart, 11 to 29 km past Burnaby Lake, Deer Lake, and the creek trails that join them. Family-friendly, mostly gentle, and a reminder of how much forest hides inside the city. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Burrard Inlet Trails Burrard Inlet Trails 7 km Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Chunky gravel The Burrard Inlet Trails run 4 to 20 km out and back between Burnaby and Port Moody, mixing easy waterfront path with rougher forest singletrack. Choose the shoreline sections for a family outing, or add the trail stretches, which run genuinely rocky and rooty, for something livelier. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Campbell Valley Campbell Valley 26 km · 121 m up Easy Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Gentle grades Campbell Valley in South Langley offers everything from a 7 km perimeter trail to a full 27 km loop, wandering regional parkland, horse country, and farmland, with the historic Langley Speedway site a curious side trip. Local wineries dot the surrounding roads, and the terrain stays gentle throughout. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Canoe Pass Trail (Brunswick Point) Canoe Pass Trail (Brunswick Point) 7 km Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Chunky gravel The Canoe Pass Trail at Brunswick Point runs flat and quiet along the dyke near Ladner, 10 to 14 km out and back where the Fraser meets the sea. Wildflowers colour the banks in summer, and this is superb raptor and shorebird country, with snow geese passing through in season. Gravel surface, no hills at all. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Canyon to Coast Trail Loop Canyon to Coast Trail Loop 34 km · 33 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Gentle grades Canyon to Coast follows a riverside dyke trail near Chilliwack, 18 km one way and 36 return, flat the whole way through farmland and parkland on a former rail corridor. A shorter 15 km road option runs nearby. Mountains bracket the valley on both sides, so the views come free. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Central Valley Greenway Central Valley Greenway 25 km · 297 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Some climbing The Central Valley Greenway runs 25 km from Vancouver through Burnaby to New Westminster, flat, mostly paved, and stitched with parkland and riverside stretches. SkyTrain stations along the corridor make it easy to ride exactly as far as you feel like and train home. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Coquitlam Parks Coquitlam Parks 18 km · 240 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing Coquitlam Parks loops 15 to 18 km through the city's green spaces, linking lake, forest, and parkland with public art along the way and SkyTrain access making it car-free friendly. Gentle enough for families, with a bit of climbing to keep it interesting. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking David's Loop David's Loop 18 km · 273 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Lots of climbing David's Loop runs 18 km through forest, riverside, and parkland between Coquitlam and Port Moody, with stretches of easy singletrack. Mostly family-friendly, though the hills are punchier than the parkland setting suggests. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Deep Cove + Spirit Trail East Deep Cove + Spirit Trail East 10 km · 133 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing This 10 km loop out to Deep Cove in North Vancouver mixes seaside path and forest riding, with one honest climb rewarded by open water views over Indian Arm. Deep Cove's cafes and famous doughnuts make the natural halfway stop. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Delta Watershed + Joe Brown Trails Delta Watershed + Joe Brown Trails 35 km · 94 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Gentle grades The Delta Watershed and Joe Brown trails loop 8 to 35 km through a surprisingly deep pocket of forest between Delta and Surrey, mostly gravel with easy singletrack threading the trees. Flat, quiet, and shaded, a local secret for hot days. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Discovery Trail West Discovery Trail West 9 km Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Abbotsford's Discovery Trail crosses the city in two halves, west (9 km one way) and east (11 km one way), for up to 40 km of riding through parkland and farm edges, mostly paved with gentle grades. Good fall colour, and easy to ride in whatever piece fits your day. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Fort to Fort Trail Fort to Fort Trail 12 km · 52 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Gentle grades The Fort to Fort Trail links the site of the original Fort Langley with today's national historic site, following the Fraser through riverside and farmland on flat gravel. Ride 12 to 30 km depending on the combination, adding the Brae Island loop for more. History at both ends, and Fort Langley village's cafes in the middle. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Fraser Loop Fraser Loop 35 km Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mixed surface The Fraser Loop runs 35 km along the river through Burnaby, Vancouver, Richmond, and New Westminster, following the working waterfront where log booms, tugs, and herons share the water. Mostly flat with connecting city streets, a good half-day that shows a side of the region most rides miss. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Fraser Shores Fraser Shores 8 km · 50 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Some climbing Fraser Shores is a quiet, flat out-and-back along the Fraser River between Burnaby and Vancouver, 6 km each way on a mix of gravel and paved path. Simple, calm riverside riding suited to families and unhurried afternoons. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Friesen Loop White Rock to Crescent Beach Friesen Loop White Rock to Crescent Beach 24 km Easy Low-traffic riding Mixed surface This 24 km loop connects White Rock and Crescent Beach in South Surrey, mixing quiet roads with gravel path as it rounds the bay between two of the area's favourite seaside villages. Mostly flat, with beach stops and fish and chips as natural incentives. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Glen Valley Glide Glen Valley Glide 42 km · 243 m up Moderate Shares roads with traffic Mostly paved Gentle grades The Glen Valley Glide loops 30 km through quiet farmland and riverside country between Fort Langley and Abbotsford, following stretches of former rail corridor past small wineries. Rolling rather than flat, and glorious in fall colour. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Golden Dreams Loop - Whistler Valley Trail Golden Dreams Loop - Whistler Valley Trail 15 km · 95 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Some climbing The Whistler Valley Trail links the resort's lakes on paved, nearly flat path: the classic 15 km loop passes Lost Lake, Green Lake, and Alta Lake, and the 26 km five-lake version adds Nita and Alpha via Creekside. Mountain views the whole way, swimming docks in summer, and family-friendly from end to end. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Great Blue Heron Way Great Blue Heron Way 8 km Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Great Blue Heron Way is a short, flat, quiet ride on Tsawwassen First Nation land, 4 km one way and 8 return along the seaside, with wildflowers in season and the namesake herons a common sight on the flats. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Green Necklace Green Necklace 7 km · 147 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Max climbing The Green Necklace circles central North Vancouver in a 7 km greenway loop, linking parks, public art, and heritage streets. Short, paved, and family-friendly, with more climbing than you might expect for its size, and cafes at every compass point. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Green Timbers Park + Greenway Green Timbers Park + Greenway 11 km · 66 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mostly paved Some climbing Green Timbers, the forest that started BC's reforestation story, and neighbouring Tynehead Park combine with a connecting greenway for 2 to 18 km of quiet, mostly flat riding under tall trees in the middle of Surrey. Good birdwatching and easy family terrain throughout. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Harbour Loop Harbour Loop 30 km Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly paved The Harbour Loop circles Burrard Inlet for 32 km, linking Vancouver and North Vancouver's waterfronts by bridge, with container cranes, shipyards, seawall, and historic Gastown along the way. Flat and paved, its length is the only challenge, and the SeaBus offers a shortcut if the day runs long. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking Iona Jetty Iona Jetty 26 km · 5 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Gentle grades The Iona Jetty runs arrow-straight into the Strait of Georgia from Iona Beach on Sea Island, one of the region's most unusual rides: 4 km out over the water with ocean on both sides, part of an 8 to 24 km outing from Richmond. Dead flat, big skies, and world-class birdwatching at the beach and lagoons. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Let's Go Biking North Sunshine Coast North Sunshine Coast 180 km Ambitious Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 39 km Mixed surface The north Sunshine Coast offers rides from a 5.5 km Okeover Arm amble to the coast's big adventures: the ferry-to-ferry road run, the 13 km Inland Lake loop on one of BC's most accessible trails, quiet roads to Lund at the end of Hi

desc: BIKEPACKING.com's complete BC cycling route collection — 26 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / BIKEPACKING.com BIKEPACKING.com bikepacking platform visit → Founded in 2012, BIKEPACKING.com is the leading resource for bikepacking routes, in-depth gear reviews, inspiration, planning insight, adventure stories, news, and events. For over a decade, we've been building, establishing, sharing, and maintaining the largest library of high-quality bikepacking routes around the world. We now have over 240,000 kilometers (150,000 miles) worth of routes in over 70 countries. This includes our Bikepacking Collective Route Network, which is our collection of original and exceptional bikepacking routes designed by our team of experienced Route Architects or skilled contributors from the community. New Bikepacking Collective Routes are partially funded and supported by the Bikepacking Collective , our member community. As we update and refine some of our popular published routes, we'll induct them into the network, along with other distinguished rides. We're a fully independent platform with a core team of editors who strive to inspire readers to get out and explore our planet, discover its wild places, and connect with its diverse cultures, all via the bicycle's elegant simplicity. Their BC collection BIKEPACKING.com's British Columbia routes run from sub-100 km overnighters to multi-week expeditions such as the 1,164 km BC Trail and the roughly 1,046 km Tree to Sea Loop around northern Vancouver Island, with coverage across BC. Its route pages are unusually deep: full logistics (access, resupply, camping, difficulty) and absolutely beautiful photography. It has also singled out the West Kootenay as a destination-level bikepacking region, with a dedicated route network guide centred on Nelson (BIKEPACKING.com/west-kootenay) linking the Kootenay Confluence, Santa Rosa Valleys and Vistas, Bonnington Scrambler, and Frog Peak Loop routes. Terrain is predominantly unpaved gravel and forest service road. 26 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on BIKEPACKING.com's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 5 Photo: BIKEPACKING.com 10 Lakes Overnighter, Powell River 10 Lakes Overnighter, Powell River 103 km · 2357 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Max climbing The name says it: this 103 km loop from downtown Powell River strings together ten freshwater lakes on the Sunshine Coast's vast logging-road network, loosely following the famous Powell Forest Canoe Route. Fast-rolling gravel with a handful of steep climbs, and lakeside camping at spots like Nanton Lake and Fiddlehead make it an easy first overnighter. These are active, radio-controlled logging roads, so stay alert for trucks and give them the road. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Bikepacking the Sea to Sky Trail Bikepacking the Sea to Sky Trail 101 km · 1917 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 14 km Mixed surface Lots of singletrack Lots of climbing The Sea to Sky Trail runs 101 km from Squamish through Whistler to Pemberton, tracing a corridor the Coast Salish and Interior Salish peoples travelled long before highways. Nearly half is flowy singletrack, and the rest mixes doubletrack, gravel, and pavement past turquoise lakes, swimming holes, suspension bridges, and even an old train wreck. Climbs come short and punchy rather than long. Resupply is easy in all three towns, and public transit can carry you back to the start. Guide by Miles Arbour and Nathan Reimer. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Lower Sunshine Coast Bikepacking Route Lower Sunshine Coast Bikepacking Route 101 km · 3107 m up Epic Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Lots of singletrack Chunky gravel Max climbing A forty-minute ferry from Vancouver drops you at Earls Cove, where this route dives into a green tunnel of loamy mountain bike trails made famous by the BC Bike Race, wooden stunts and all. Three-quarters of the 101 km is singletrack, with around 3,100 m of climbing, so this is proper technical mountain biking, not a gravel ride. Sechelt sits at halfway for resupply, coffee, and brunch, and swims at Chapman Creek and Crowston Lake break up the effort. A brilliant first bikepacking trip for confident mountain bikers. Updated by Skyler Des Roches with Ian Hall and the Coast Mountain Bike Trail Association. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Powell River Sampler Powell River Sampler 84 km · 2008 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Lots of singletrack Chunky gravel Max climbing The Powell River Sampler runs one way from Saltery Bay to Powell River, mixing over 50 km of loamy, ribboned singletrack with easy gravel, past waterfalls, lakes, ocean views, and the bird-rich Duck Lake protected area. Community-built cabins and lakeside campsites make the nights comfortable, and an optional hike-a-bike detour climbs to Walt Hill's 360-degree views. Rooty, technical trails call for real mountain bike skills. It links the Lower Sunshine Coast route with the Comox ferry, so the whole coast chains together. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Texada Ridge Runner Route Texada Ridge Runner Route 144 km · 2674 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 12 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing The Texada Ridge Runner traverses the island's spine from Blubber Bay to Anderson Bay and back, 144 km of quiet gravel past old farmsteads, forgotten airstrips, and beaches, with views across to Vancouver Island and the mainland mountains. The climbing is staggering for an island ride, steep and frequent, so two days is a challenge and three is a holiday. Camp oceanside at Anderson Bay or by Bob's Lake, and enjoy a rare bonus: Texada has no bears. Ferry from Powell River. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 7 Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Alberni Bam Bam, Vancouver Island Alberni Bam Bam, Vancouver Island 507 km · 9765 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 62 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches A week-long, roughly 500 km loop from Nanaimo around the south island's wild interior: gravel and rough doubletrack through the Cowichan Valley to Port Renfrew, past the Walbran Valley and Fairy Creek rainforests at the heart of BC's old-growth story, then to Bamfield, where the MV Frances Barkley, a 65-year-old heritage ship, carries you four hours up the Alberni Inlet. Swim spots and quirky communities all the way; long stretches without resupply, so plan carefully. Designed to be ridden car-free from the Departure Bay ferry. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Cowichan Valley 8 Bikepacking Route Cowichan Valley 8 Bikepacking Route 190 km · 1571 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Some climbing A 190 km figure-eight starting and ending at the parliament buildings in downtown Victoria, following the Galloping Goose, Sooke Wilderness Trail, Cowichan Valley Trail, and Lochside Trail through farm and wine country. Mostly gravel and doubletrack with one real climb near Goldstream, it rides comfortably on a gravel bike in a weekend. Note the publisher's caution: the paved stretch between the Kinsol Trestle and the Mill Bay ferry is busy in summer and deserves extra care. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Englishman River Overnighter Englishman River Overnighter 52 km · 496 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of singletrack Some climbing The gentlest introduction to island bikepacking: 52 km out and back from Parksville's beachfront to Englishman River Falls Provincial Park, through mossy rainforest and estuary on multi-use paths and rooty singletrack. Top Bridge's suspension bridge and swimming holes make the perfect halfway stop, and twin waterfalls wait at camp. Logistics are one online campground booking. Front suspension helps on the rootier stretches, but the route forgives. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Jeune Landing Loop Jeune Landing Loop 134 km · 2128 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Lots of climbing A 134 km figure-eight linking Port McNeill and Port Alice on the North Island's rolling gravel, one of the island's most approachable bikepacking routes: no singletrack, gentle climbs, and lakeside rec-site camping all along. The country is karst, and the route passes the Devil's Bath, one of Canada's largest cenotes, and the Eternal Fountain's disappearing waterfall. A cafe in Port Alice marks halfway. The local campground reckons bikepackers are now a fifth of its guests; this is why. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Snowden or Dust, Vancouver Island Snowden or Dust, Vancouver Island 75 km · 1106 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Lots of singletrack Lots of climbing A 75 km overnighter from Campbell River built around the Snowden Demonstration Forest's 100 km of trails: over 40% of the route is singletrack, flowy and sometimes rocky, linked by scenic gravel with lakeside rec-site camping to choose from. Designed as a mountain biker's introduction to bikepacking; bring decent trail skills, a hardtail, and your navigation patience, because the trail network is a maze. Not a gravel-bike route. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com The South Island Sundowner The South Island Sundowner 139 km · 1317 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Some climbing A 139 km loop that never strays far from Victoria yet delivers a real taste of the island's ruggedness: rail trail and fire roads link steep, loose climbs through Thetis Lake and Francis King parks, remote singletrack in the Sooke Hills, and wide views over the Strait of Juan de Fuca to the Olympic Mountains. The numbers look tame, but a couple of kilometres of rocky hike-a-bike and relentless 20% pitches earn its reputation. Cafes and swimming lakes reward a three-day pace; strong riders chase the sundown in two. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Tree to Sea Loop, Vancouver Island Tree to Sea Loop, Vancouver Island 1046 km · 16742 m up Epic Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 92 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches The North Island's bucket-list epic: a roughly 1,046 km gravel loop from Comox linking massive valleys, deep fjords, and coastal villages, Gold River, Tahsis, Zeballos, Port Alice, Holberg and its famously remote pub, on a patchwork of forest service roads. Along the way: whale watching, caves, and some of BC's best waterside camping. Plan on 15 days, a water-taxi leg from Tahsis to Zeballos, unreliable village resupply, and weather that can turn any season. Note the 2026 Strathcona Dam closure reroutes the early kilometres around Campbell Lake. Stops, map + getting there → Thompson Okanagan · 4 Photo: BIKEPACKING.com BC Grasslands Circuit BC Grasslands Circuit 250 km · 4054 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 46 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing A three-day, 250 km loop through the fragile grassland ecosystems south of Kamloops: just one percent of BC's land base, yet home to nearly a third of its threatened species. The route rolls past sprawling historic ranches, including Canada's largest at Douglas Lake, and azure lakes teeming with waterfowl; bring binoculars, this is some of the best birdwatching in the province. Good gravel and quiet pavement, but the climbs are real, around 4,000 m in all, and water is scarce, so carry plenty. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Chute Lake Charcuterie Route, Kelowna Chute Lake Charcuterie Route, Kelowna 103 km · 1690 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Rough, near-MTB Lots of climbing Kelowna's introduction to bikepacking: climb out of the city on the Mission Creek Greenway and Myra-Bellevue's singletrack to the Kettle Valley Rail Trail, spend the night at Chute Lake, in the lodge's glamping tents or the free rec site next door, then descend flowy trails back to City Park. The KVR stretch runs sandy and potholed, so a mountain bike is happiest. Beaches, restaurants, and breweries wait downtown when you roll back in. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Lac du Bois Tranquility, Kamloops Lac du Bois Tranquility, Kamloops 229 km · 4207 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 14 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches North of Kamloops lies a maze of scenic gravel through grasslands, mossy forest, and deep canyons that could be straight out of a Western. This 229 km loop through the Lac du Bois Grasslands climbs to Vidette Lake and back over three to four days, past forgotten homesteads, the Castle Rock Hoodoos, and country thick with stories, from Sasquatch sightings at Red Lake to gold panning on the Tranquille River. Long steep climbs, exposed heat, and no resupply, so carry water and take your time. Lakeside rec sites make camping easy. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com The BC Trail The BC Trail 1164 km · 16531 m up Epic Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 134 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing The flagship BC traverse: about 1,164 km from Cultus Lake to Fernie following the province's spine of decommissioned rail trails, the Coquihalla River Trail, the KVR with its Myra Canyon trestles, and the Great Northern, linked by forest roads and occasional rocky singletrack. Rail grade does not mean easy: many sections run rough, sandy, and washboarded, hard on gear and riders alike. Plan on about 12 days, with good town amenities between the remote stretches. The BC Epic 1000 race follows it from Merritt to Fernie every June. Note: the Hope to Princeton rail trail closure currently reroutes that section via Tulameen. Skyler Des Roches linked the route together; Lennard Pretorius developed the BC Epic 1000 race that follows it. Stops, map + getting there → Kootenay Rockies · 6 Photo: BIKEPACKING.com 8 Rivers Overnighter 8 Rivers Overnighter 206 km · 3251 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Almost all gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches Tucked into the East Kootenays in Ktunaxa and Secwepemc territory, this 206 km loop links one spectacular river valley after another on wide gravel roads and sneaky little connectors, with a dip into Nipika's singletrack partway. The last big pass is the unanimous highlight: wildflowers, meadows, and Rockies views both directions, then hours through the staggering regrowth of old wildfires. Two to three days with creek crossings, and rustic Lussier Hot Springs waits near the start for afterwards. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: BIKEPACKING.com Bonnington Scrambler Bonnington Scrambler 126 km · 3396 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Max climbing A weekend loop out of Nelson for riders who like earning it: Kootenay River trails, an eclectic mix of doubletrack and gravel over the Bonnington Range, then the Great Northern Rail Trail home

title: Gravel Buddies
desc: Gravel Buddies's complete BC cycling route collection — 23 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Gravel Buddies Gravel Buddies cycling club visit → Gravel Buddies is a Vancouver-based cycling community that organizes group gravel rides for women, gender-diverse, and 2SLGBTQIA+ riders, ranging from short evening rides in Stanley Park to multi-day bikepacking trips. Their BC collection Gravel Buddies' BC routes split between Metro Vancouver and North Shore day rides and multi-day trips on Vancouver Island and the Sea-to-Sky corridor. Routes range from short 20 km rides to a 160 km rally day, mostly on mixed paved and gravel surfaces (roughly 20-70% unpaved). The set includes an annual multi-day gravel rally spanning the Vancouver Coast and Mountains and Vancouver Island regions, plus overnight bikepacking trips to Sooke Potholes, Golden Ears, the Sunshine Coast, and the Sea-to-Sky Trail. 23 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Gravel Buddies's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 12 Photo: Hubert Kang West Vancouver, BC Bowen Island Day Trip 28 km · 596 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Chunky gravel Max climbing Bowen Island is the easiest island escape from Vancouver, twenty ferry minutes from Horseshoe Bay, and this 28 km loop makes a full day of it. A mix of quiet paved roads and gravel, with about 600 m of climbing and some genuinely rough patches, plus coffee and lunch options in Snug Cove before the boat home. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Harbour Air Seaplanes Bowen Island, BC Bowen Island Day Trip (shorter) 22 km · 485 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Chunky gravel Max climbing The shorter, gentler version of the Bowen Island day trip: 22 km of quiet island roads and gravel with about 480 m of climbing. Same ferry, same island charm, more time for the bakery. A good pick when the group has mixed legs. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Heath Moffatt Squamish, BC Capilano Salmon Run 20 km · 396 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing An easy 20 km ride tracing the Capilano River through West Vancouver's forest edges, mostly paved with some gravel path. The name is a hint: come in fall and you can watch salmon fighting upstream below the canyon walls, with the hatchery a natural stop. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Jennifer Kleingeltink Agassiz, BC Deep Cove Ramble 27 km · 411 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing One of the prettiest rides on the North Shore: 27 km around Deep Cove mixing mossy forest trails, open fields, and flowy singletrack, with one steep hike-a-bike to keep you humble. Mostly gentle otherwise, and Deep Cove's famous doughnuts wait at the end. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Blake Jorgenson Squamish, BC Lakes and Rivers 50 km · 306 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Some climbing A Gravel Buddies favourite: 50 km wandering through parks and along rivers east of Vancouver, nearly flat, with plenty of spots to stop, swim a toe, and picnic. Perfect for a sunny day when the ride is the destination. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Reuben Krabbe North Vancouver, BC North Shore through Stanley Park 37 km · 684 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing A 37 km link-up of Vancouver's classics: through Stanley Park, over to the North Shore, and back, mixing seawall, forest paths, and gravel with about 680 m of climbing. City riding at its most scenic, with the bridges themselves among the highlights. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Albert Normandin Vancouver, BC North Van Sampler 56 km · 1032 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing A 56 km sampler of North Vancouver's mixed terrain, stitching gravel paths and quiet streets with over 1,000 m of climbing. The North Shore tilts: expect to work on the way up and grin on the way down. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Vision Event Photography Vancouver, BC North Van Shakedown 33 km · 566 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Lots of climbing A 33 km route exploring North Vancouver's hidden neighbourhood connectors, with singletrack, steep climbs, and fast downhills. What goes up comes down, and nowhere is that truer than North Van. Just over half unpaved, and a good shakedown for bike and rider alike. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Michael Bednar Vancouver, Coast and Mountains, BC Upper North Van 28 km · 340 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing An easy 28 km loop through Upper North Vancouver on a mix of leafy streets and gravel paths, with only about 340 m of climbing, gentle by North Shore standards. A relaxed introduction to the area's mixed-surface riding. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Andrew Strain Vancouver, Coast and Mountains, BC Golden Ears Overnighter (out and back) 105 km · 735 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Some climbing An adventure that starts from your doorstep: ride 105 km out and back from Port Moody to Golden Ears, camp beneath the mountains, and be home for dinner the next day. Mostly flat on a mix of gravel and pavement, it is one of the easiest ways in the Lower Mainland to try a first bikepacking trip without a car shuttle. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Blake Jorgenson Whistler, BC Squamish-Whistler (out and back) 96 km · 1622 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 16 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing The Squamish-to-Whistler stretch of the Sea to Sky Trail, ridden as a 96 km out-and-back so no shuttle is needed. The trail follows a corridor Coast Salish and Interior Salish peoples travelled long before the highway, climbing from lush rainforest into pine forest on a mix of flowy singletrack and chunkier wide sections, with clear lakes for swimming and viewpoints all along. About 1,600 m of climbing spread over the day or a night out. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Dolf Vermeulen Halfmoon Bay, BC Sunshine Coast Overnighter 67 km · 1098 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 7 km Mixed surface Lots of climbing A 67 km overnight trip on the lower Sunshine Coast starting near the Langdale ferry, mostly on paved roads that roll and climb hard, about 1,100 m in total. Ferry over from Horseshoe Bay, camp partway, and let the coast set the pace. Expect to share the road on the busier stretches. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 11 Photo: Peter O Hara Ladysmith, BC Rally Day 1 (West Vancouver) 160 km · 1212 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Some climbing The first day of the Gravel Buddies 2025 Rally: 160 km from West Vancouver, ferry across the strait included, onto Vancouver Island's mixed gravel and pavement with about 1,200 m of rolling climbing. A long social day built for steady groups; a gentler alternative route runs the same day. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Landon Copplestone Duncan, BC Rally Day 1 alternative (West Vancouver) 150 km · 965 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 14 km Mixed surface Some climbing The alternative first day of the Gravel Buddies 2025 Rally: 150 km on the same West Vancouver-to-island journey with a bit less gravel and about 950 m of climbing. Same destination, slightly kinder legs. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Graeme Owsianski Cobble Hill, BC Rally Day 2 (Cowichan Valley) 118 km · 795 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mostly gravel Some climbing Day two of the Gravel Buddies 2025 Rally crosses the Cowichan Valley: 118 km, more than half gravel, with about 800 m of rolling climbing through farm and wine country. A shorter alternative runs the same day for anyone saving their legs. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Peter O Hara Shawnigan Lake, BC Rally Day 2 alternative (Cowichan Valley) 95 km · 652 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Some climbing The alternative second day of the Gravel Buddies 2025 Rally: 95 km through the Cowichan Valley with about 650 m of climbing, a little less gravel and a little more mercy than the full day-two route. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Andrea Johnson Salt Spring Island, BC Rally Day 3 (Victoria) 96 km · 993 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Some climbing The final day of the Gravel Buddies 2025 Rally: 96 km around Greater Victoria with about 1,000 m of climbing, the hilliest day of the three despite the capital setting. A shorter alternative runs the same day. Finish-line coffee strongly implied. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Jordan Dyck Ladysmith, BC Rally Day 3 alternative (Victoria) 86 km · 767 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 15 km Mixed surface Some climbing The alternative final day of the Gravel Buddies 2025 Rally: 86 km around Greater Victoria with about 770 m of climbing and less gravel than the main route. Most of the views, fewer of the hills. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Taylor Cave Productions Nanaimo, BC Gabriola Group Ride 23 km · 324 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mostly gravel Lots of climbing A social 23 km gravel ride on Gabriola Island near Nanaimo, rolling past an alpaca and goat farm with an optional detour to the Malaspina Galleries, the island's famous wave-carved sandstone overhang. Mostly unpaved with gentle climbing; built for groups and unhurried days. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Rob Wilson Duncan, BC Cowichan Valley: Stoltz Pool to Nanaimo 78 km · 417 m up Moderate Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 18 km Mixed surface Gentle grades The second leg of a Cowichan Valley crossing: 78 km from the swimming holes at Stoltz Pool on the Cowichan River north to Nanaimo, mostly paved with gravel stretches and about 400 m of climbing. Pairs with the Swartz Bay leg for a car-free island traverse ending at Nanaimo's ferries. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Daniel Baylis Shawnigan Lake, BC Cowichan Valley: Swartz Bay to Stoltz Pool 83 km · 564 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Some climbing From the Swartz Bay ferry terminal, this 83 km leg crosses to the Cowichan Valley and follows trail and quiet roads to Stoltz Pool on the Cowichan River, where the provincial park campground and famous swimming holes wait. Nearly half gravel with about 560 m of climbing. Pairs with the Nanaimo leg for a two-day, ferry-to-ferry island crossing. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Taylor Cave Productions Nanaimo, BC Gabriola 44 km · 596 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mostly gravel Lots of climbing A 44 km wander around Gabriola Island, a twenty-minute ferry from Nanaimo, mixing trails and quiet island roads, more than half unpaved, with about 600 m of rolling climbing. Beaches, sandstone shorelines, and the island's easy pace do the rest. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Daniel Baylis Sooke, BC Sooke Potholes (out and back) 158 km · 822 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Gentle grades The beloved beginner overnighter: from Swartz Bay, follow the Lochside Trail through Saanich farmland and the Galloping Goose's rail-trail wilderness to Sooke Potholes Provincial Park, about 75 km each way with barely a hill, 95% of it on trail. Camp near the river and spend the evening swimming in the famous rock pools; the park squeezes cyclists in even when sites run out. Bike shops and resupply sit right on the route, and the trail never strays far from help. Bring cash for the campground and a book for the beach.
