title: Love Machine
desc: Love Machine's complete BC cycling route collection — 16 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Love Machine Love Machine individual route creator visit → Love Machine is a Vancouver-based gravel cycling project run by two friends, Max and Cam, as a side project — not a brand, shop, or club. It publishes free, downloadable GPX routes across southwestern British Columbia, with a stated goal of keeping gravel cycling welcoming rather than gatekept. Their BC collection Love Machine's routes cluster around Metro Vancouver, the North Shore, and the Sea-to-Sky corridor, from short urban gravel loops in Burnaby, Richmond, and North Vancouver to bigger days in Squamish, Golden Ears, and Cultus Lake, plus a Sunshine Coast overnighter and two Vancouver Island loops near Comox and Campbell River. Routes run 40-110 km on a mix of forest service roads and singletrack, often borrowing flow trails from the North Shore and Squamish mountain bike networks. 16 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Love Machine's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 14 North Vancouver, BC Afterschool Special 43 km · 429 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Some climbing A 43 km, mostly flat gravel loop west of Vancouver, running along the beach, through old growth forest, and down to the Fraser River. Aimed at riders new to gravel, with options to extend via Pacific Spirit Park or Stanley Park. Stops, map + getting there → Burnaby, BC Burnabop 43 km · 666 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing A 42 km loop through Burnaby linking quiet back roads, urban singletrack, and hidden gravel trail entrances through colourful deciduous forest. About half unpaved, low-key with easy bail-out options. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Viranlly Liemena viranlly Coquitlam, BC Burnaby Orbit 48 km · 620 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Lots of climbing A 48 km loop connecting the Trans Canada Trail on Burnaby Mountain with the gravel trails around Burnaby Lake, on mostly smooth, well-graded surfaces. Best ridden clockwise, with a detour option to Port Moody's breweries and cafes. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: The Fraser Valley Group Abbotsford, BC Cultus Shock 73 km · 551 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Some climbing A 73 km route near Abbotsford following the Vedder River past local food stops, then climbing forest service roads before descending to Cultus Lake. An optional shortcut trims it to about 50 km. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: VancityWild North Vancouver, BC Cypress Side Quest 55 km · 1166 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Max climbing A 55 km loop connecting Cypress Provincial Park to Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver, stitching together the area's scattered gravel and dirt sections amid mostly paved roads. Includes narrow community-built singletrack connectors with short hike-a-bike sections. Stops, map + getting there → North Vancouver, BC Discomfort Zone (Thrill Seeker Version) 60 km · 1190 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing A 60 km loop from Chinatown in Vancouver to the North Shore, taking on classic North Shore mountain bike descents (Ned's and Bobsled) before mellowing into smoother gravel back to the Second Narrows. Minimum 48 mm tires recommended. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Hubert Kang Langley, BC Golden Ears Hundo 101 km · 785 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Some climbing A 100 km gravel loop starting and finishing at the Lafarge Lake–Douglas SkyTrain station, reachable without a car. Flat pea-gravel dyke riding through Coquitlam and Pitt Meadows leads into Golden Ears Provincial Park, with a turnaround near North Beach and a climb past Mike Lake on the way back. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Andrew Strain Gibsons, BC Coastal Croissant 53 km · 1688 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 3 km Mostly gravel Max climbing A 53 km gravel day trip on the Sunshine Coast, mixing flowy singletrack with forest service road and paved climbing. Finishes at Persephone Brewing before the ferry back to Vancouver. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Reuben Krabbe Pemberton, BC Riverview Loop 52 km · 417 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Some climbing A 52 km, mostly flat gravel loop starting and finishing in Port Moody, combining pea-gravel dykes, forest paths, and short singletrack. Low-elevation and rideable year-round; can be linked with Burnaby Orbit or Golden Ears Hundred for a longer day. Stops, map + getting there → North Vancouver, BC North Van Local's Lap 41 km · 786 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing A 41.5 km loop in North Vancouver combining quiet roads, gravel paths, and forest service roads, about 40% unpaved. Ridden clockwise from Waterfront Park to front-load the climbing, finishing near the Shipyards breweries. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: entre2escales Squamish, BC Powerhouse Mash 40 km · 578 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing A 40 km loop in Squamish through estuary trails before climbing Powerhouse and Mashiter and descending via paved roads and singletrack. Short enough for an after-work ride, starting and ending near coffee and beer at Locavore/Cloudburst. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Heath Moffatt Whistler, BC Short Exposure 47 km · 900 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing A 47.5 km half-day loop near Whistler, starting at Brandywine Falls and following the Sea to Sky Trail before climbing Cheakamus Lake Road through old-growth forest to Cheakamus Lake. Return passes Function Junction and the Whistler Train Wreck. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Hubert Kang Squamish, BC Squamish Ringer 43 km · 688 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Lots of climbing A 43 km gravel loop out of Squamish, climbing Garibaldi Park Road and Ring Creek North Forest Service Road (FSR) to views of the Tantalus Range, then descending singletrack — Miki's Magic and Cardrona — past Alice Lake back to the Squamish estuary. About 85% unpaved. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Tyler Garnham Delta, BC The Spring Classic 103 km · 159 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Gentle grades A 103 km, mostly flat loop starting and finishing at Bridgeport Canada Line Station near Vancouver, linking seaside trails in Richmond and Iona, a stop in Steveston, and singletrack, doubletrack, and boardwalk trails in Delta. About half unpaved, transit-accessible via SkyTrain. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 2 Photo: Bluetree Photography Campbell River, BC Campbell River Tight Lines 68 km · 899 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Lots of climbing A 68 km route near Campbell River combining well-graded forest service roads with about 15 km of singletrack through the Snowden Demo Forest mountain bike trail system. Mellow, sustained climbing, with rec sites suited to bikepacking overnighters. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Boomer Jerritt Comox, BC NOBL x Love Machine - The Comox ATB Classic 110 km · 1766 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Lots of climbing A 110 km route starting and finishing at NOBL Wheels HQ in Cumberland, mixing forest service roads, gravel paths, and singletrack across the Comox Valley. Includes a calf-high river crossing at km 59, with a winter alternative to avoid it. We're interested in learning more about where you love to ride. Drop us a note and tell us what you publish. hello@bccycletourism.ca

title: Trails BC
desc: Trails BC's complete BC cycling route collection — 12 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Trails BC Trails BC trail organization visit → Trails BC (the Trails Society of BC) is a non-profit charity that advocates for greenway trails for self-propelled recreation and active transportation across the province. Léon Lebrun has been at the heart of that work for nearly three decades, building and championing non-motorized trails across the Lower Mainland and beyond; a bridge in Chilliwack and a trail in Port Moody now carry his name. The rides shown here are a handful of the many he's helped map over the years. Their BC collection Trails BC's routes here range from short 12 km community loops to a 220 km multi-day Kootenay loop, and include several short Trans Canada Trail feeder segments in the Fraser Valley (Chilliwack Lake to Thurston, Cultus Lake to Tamihi, Langley to Clayburn) alongside day loops around Salmo, Kaslo/Slocan, Kimberley, Nanaimo, Squamish, Summerland, and Chilliwack. Coverage spans Kootenay Rockies, Vancouver Coast and Mountains, Vancouver Island, and Thompson Okanagan, with terrain running from flat valley-bottom trail to sustained climbing (over 1,300 m and 2,300 m of ascent on the two longest Kootenay routes). 12 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Trails BC's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 7 Photo: Dannielle Hayes Langley, BC Alternate Tsawwassen Langley 61 km · 231 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Gentle grades The cyclists' link from the Tsawwassen ferry terminal to the Trans Canada Trail at the Golden Ears Bridge: 61 km, easy and mostly flat, following dykes and greenways through Tsawwassen First Nation lands, the 16 km Boundary Bay Greenway, and Surrey's back routes to Fort Langley. Half gravel, half paved, and a practical, pleasant way to start or finish an island trip. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Blake Jorgenson Whistler, BC Chilliwack Lake to Thurston Rec Site 29 km Moderate Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel One of the more challenging Trans Canada Trail sections in the Fraser Valley: 29 km from Chilliwack Lake down the valley to the Thurston recreation site, almost entirely unpaved and best ridden in the downhill direction. Popular with mountain bikers, and a proper backcountry feel so close to town. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Local Wanderer Cultus Lake, BC Cultus Lake to Tamihi Rec Site 17 km Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel A 17 km Trans Canada Trail section from Cultus Lake along the Chilliwack River to the Tamihi recreation site, with pleasant greenway at both ends and forest service road climbing in between. Mostly gravel; allow about two and a half hours. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Robin O Neill Vancouver, Coast and Mountains, BC Langley to Clayburn 28 km Easy Some traffic sharing Mostly gravel This 28 km Trans Canada Trail section links Langley to Clayburn, following the Matsqui Regional Trail along the Fraser toward Sumas Mountain before country roads lead into Clayburn Village, whose brick church and store recall its brick-making origins. Flat riverside riding, about three hours end to end, with some shared-road stretches. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Ben Girardi Squamish, BC Squamish Cycle Loops 79 km Moderate Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 4 km Mostly gravel A set of cycling loops around Squamish, from about 47 km up to a 79 km combination, tracing Howe Sound and the Squamish, Mamquam, and Stawamus rivers on a mix of gravel paths and quiet roads. Mostly gentle grades, with mountain walls on every horizon and shorter options easy to carve out. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Viranlly Liemena viranlly Chilliwack, BC Rotary Loop Trail 12 km Moderate Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel A 12 km loop in Chilliwack taking in the Great Blue Heron Nature Reserve, boglands, the Vedder River, and forested trails. Come in spring when the heronry is busiest; the whole loop takes about an hour by bike, all on gravel. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Kari Medig Pemberton, BC Vedder Sumas River 92 km · 181 m up Easy Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 28 km Mixed surface Gentle grades A 92 km dyke-based loop through the Fraser Valley linking McDonald Park on the Sumas River, the Barrowtown Pump Station, the Vedder River, Sumas Prairie, and the Great Blue Heron Nature Reserve. Mostly flat and easy despite the distance; allow up to four hours, or split it over two days. Half gravel, with some quiet shared roads between dykes. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 1 Photo: Taylor Cave Productions Nanaimo, BC Nanaimo Cycling Trail Loop 63 km · 177 m up Easy Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Gentle grades A 63 km loop through Nanaimo's greenways and parks, linking Bowen Park's forest, Petroglyph Provincial Park's ancient rock carvings, the harbourfront walkway, and the city's rail trails, with a ferry side trip to car-free Saysutshun (Newcastle Island) the highlight worth building in. Mostly flat; allow four to six hours with stops. Stops, map + getting there → Thompson Okanagan · 1 Photo: Thompson Okanagan Tourism Association Summerland, BC Summerland Cycle Loop 55 km · 335 m up Moderate Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 9 km Mixed surface Some climbing A 55 km loop around Summerland taking in beaches, parks, and the high-level Lakeview Trail with views across Okanagan Lake toward Naramata, plus a stretch of the Kettle Valley Railway route past Mount Conkle and over the Trout Creek Trestle. Modest climbing and a mix of pavement and gravel make it a satisfying full-morning ride. Stops, map + getting there → Kootenay Rockies · 3 Photo: Kari Medig Trail, BC Alternate Trail Salmo 109 km · 1368 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mixed surface Lots of climbing Where the main Trans Canada Trail between Trail and Salmo is unsuitable for bikes, this connector offers two rideable options: a shorter, hillier route through the Beaver Valley on Highway 3B, or a longer, quieter loop south toward the Pend d'Oreille River. Up to 109 km with about 1,370 m of climbing, mostly on pavement with some gravel road sections. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Kari Medig Kaslo, BC Loop Kaslo Slocan 221 km · 2320 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mixed surface Some climbing A 221 km loop through the West Kootenay linking Nelson, Kaslo, and New Denver over two days, with an optional cable-car river crossing on the way out and a return leg on the Slocan Valley Rail Trail. About 2,300 m of climbing in all, with a fair amount of highway riding between the trail sections, so expect to share the road. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Kimberley, BC Kimberley Lions Way Northstar Loop 12 km Moderate Low-traffic riding Mixed surface A 12 km loop in Kimberley combining the shaded, creekside Lions Way trail along Mark Creek with the flat, easy Northstar Rail Trail back into town. One of the few loops that runs entirely on the Trans Canada Trail. Dog-friendly, about 45 minutes by bike, and a lovely way to see the town's green edges. title: Bikepack Canada
desc: Bikepack Canada's complete BC cycling route collection — 12 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Bikepack Canada Bikepack Canada bikepacking platform visit → Bikepack Canada is a bikepacking route-sharing platform founded in 2016 by adventure cyclist Ryan Correy, author of the guidebook 'Bikepacking in the Canadian Rockies' and the memoir 'A Purpose Ridden.' Correy died in 2018; the site continues today, hosting routes contributed by bikepackers from across the country. Their BC collection Bikepack Canada's British Columbia routes range from a 75 km alpine overnighter near Squamish to the 1,200 km Kootenay Flathead Fandango loop through BC, Montana, Idaho, and Washington. Coverage concentrates in the Kootenay Rockies and Thompson Okanagan, mixing rail trail, forest service road, and singletrack, mapped by a mix of named route builders — Megan Dunn, Ali Becker and Mat Leblanc, Guy Stuart, Penny Lawless, Cameron Fenton, Dario Dulic, and Peter Fordham — alongside two routes from Ryan Correy's own guidebook. 12 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Bikepack Canada's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 1 Photo: Heath Moffatt Squamish, BC The Nch'Kay 75 74 km · 2730 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Almost all gravel Chunky gravel Max climbing A mostly-singletrack overnighter from Squamish up to the alpine near Mount Garibaldi (Nch'Kay), mapped by Cameron Fenton. 75 km with 2,421 m of climbing, 95 percent unpaved and 85 percent singletrack. Stops, map + getting there → Thompson Okanagan · 4 Photo: Mitch Winton Castlegar, BC Eastern Kettle Valley Railway 538 km · 7570 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 90 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches A 538 km point-to-point route from Kelowna to Kimberley along the historic Kettle Valley Railway and Columbia and Western rail grades, mapped by Guy Stuart. Mostly rail trail and highway grade with some hike-a-bike on Gray Creek Pass, and about 5,740 m of climbing. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Thompson Okanagan Tourism Association Kelowna, BC Kettle Valley Railway Midway Loop 352 km · 3369 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 72 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Some climbing A 352 km loop from Midway through Myra Canyon's Kettle Valley rail grade, then wine country roads around Naramata, Penticton, Oliver, and Osoyoos, back over Anarchist Summit. Mapped by Penny Lawless, it's rated easy to moderate. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Thompson Okanagan Tourism Association Kelowna, BC Okanagan Feast 238 km · 4598 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing A four-day, 238 km loop around the south end of Okanagan Lake from Kelowna, mapped by Cameron Fenton, linking rail trail, gravel backroads, and singletrack. Paced for winery, brewery, and food stops, best ridden at harvest time. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Andrew Strain Kamloops, BC Seymour Arm Overnighter 176 km · 4446 m up Epic Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 3 km Almost all gravel Max climbing Remote stretches A 175 km, mostly unpaved overnighter through two Monashee mountain valleys near Sicamous, mapped by Dario Dulic. Steep gravel climbs up to 20 percent grade and 3,778 m of elevation gain, with a resupply stop in the remote village of Seymour Arm. Stops, map + getting there → Kootenay Rockies · 7 Photo: Mitch Winton Fernie, BC Flathead Valley 292 km · 4048 m up Challenging Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 66 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches A 291 km loop through southern BC from Fernie, one of ten routes in Ryan Correy's guidebook 'Bikepacking in the Canadian Rockies.' Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Cranbrook, BC Kootenay Flathead Fandango 547 km · 9268 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 80 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches A roughly 1,200 km gravel-focused loop from Fernie through the Flathead into Montana, Idaho, and Washington and back into the Kootenays, following portions of the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route and BC Epic 1000. Mapped by Megan Dunn, it mixes forest service roads, some pavement, a short singletrack stretch, and one demanding hike-a-bike descent through bear country, with a free ferry crossing of Kootenay Lake near Nelson. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Kari Medig Crawford Bay, BC Kootenay-Miller Pass 79 km · 1377 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches An 80 km overnight loop from Nipika Mountain Resort into the East Kootenays, mapped by Peter Fordham, climbing to Miller Pass before a rugged, overgrown descent that calls for bike-hiking and solid navigation. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Kari Medig Kaslo, BC Lakes and Hot Springs Loop 551 km · 9866 m up Challenging Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches A 550 km figure-eight route through the Central Kootenays from Nakusp, mapped by Ali Becker and Mat Leblanc, passing fourteen lakes, three hot springs, and two free ferry crossings plus a cable car over Carpenter Creek. Moderate to challenging, mostly for its remoteness through grizzly, black bear, cougar, and wolf territory. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Castlegar, BC The Great Granby Loop 477 km · 7345 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 80 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches A 475 km, five-to-seven day loop through the West Kootenays from near Castlegar, mapped by Ali Becker and Mat Leblanc. Rail trails, forest service road climbs, and paved connectors through old mining and forestry towns, with a free cable ferry and side trips to hot springs and alpine lakes. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Cranbrook, BC Top of the World 347 km · 6340 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 15 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches A 347 km loop through southern BC from Cranbrook, one of ten routes in Ryan Correy's guidebook 'Bikepacking in the Canadian Rockies.' Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Invermere, BC Two Lake Tootle 145 km · 2093 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Almost all gravel Lots of climbing A 145 km, two-to-three day gravel loop from Invermere up to lakeside Recreation Sites at Cleland Lake and Dogleg Lake, with an optional cafe detour to Spillimacheen. Two significant climbs, and free first-come-first-served lakeside camping along the way. title: Bike Gear Database
desc: Bike Gear Database's complete BC cycling route collection — 10 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Bike Gear Database Bike Gear Database route network visit → Bike Gear Database is a Canadian online publication covering gravel and bikepacking gear reviews, rider stories, and community-submitted route guides. Routes are organized by country and region, including a Canada section with several British Columbia rides — and every route in the library has actually been ridden by the community before it's published. Their BC collection Bike Gear Database's British Columbia routes are mostly single-day gravel and mixed-surface rides of 43–124 km, spread across Vancouver Island, the Vancouver Coast and Mountains region, the Thompson-Okanagan, and the Cariboo Chilcotin Coast, plus one 510 km multi-day bikepacking route across Haida Gwaii in northern British Columbia. Surface mix ranges from fully paved to mostly unpaved (up to 83% unpaved), with difficulty from moderate to hard. 10 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Bike Gear Database's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 2 Photo: Hubert Kang North Vancouver, BC Gravel Guide Vancouver: Seymour Valley Loop 69 km · 1234 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Lots of climbing A Vancouver gravel staple: 69 km linking protected bike lanes from downtown to the Seymour Valley, where a closed-to-cars paved trailway leads deep into the forest. The route visits the Seymour Dam, source of much of Metro Vancouver's drinking water, then returns on Spur 4 Road and Fisherman's Trail past a salmon hatchery and through pockets of old growth. About 1,200 m of climbing spread gently over the day. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Alex Guiry Bowen Island, BC Texada Island Two Step 124 km · 2886 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 12 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Max climbing A hardy 124 km lap of Texada Island, reached by ferry from Powell River. Mostly gravel, never busy, and far hillier than an island ride has any right to be: the climbing comes constantly in steep pitches, nearly 2,900 m of it. Come with low gears and a full day, or split it with a night at one of the island's campgrounds. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 5 Photo: Taylor Cave Productions Nanaimo, BC Barry's Loop 58 km · 618 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Chunky gravel Some climbing A 58 km mixed-surface loop out of Esquimalt near Victoria, about 40% unpaved with 600 m of climbing and some genuinely rough stretches. A local's line through the South Island's backroads, named for the rider who shared it. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Ben Giesbrecht Port Renfrew, BC Gordon River & Tall Trees 123 km · 3217 m up Challenging Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 59 km Mixed surface Max climbing Remote stretches From Lake Cowichan, this 123 km mixed-surface ride crosses to Port Renfrew and back through some of the island's most storied country: ancient forest, crystal-clear rivers, and long quiet logging-road stretches. About 3,200 m of climbing and remote in the middle, so carry what you need. The tall trees are not a figure of speech. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Peter O Hara Courtenay, BC Gravel Loop Comox Valley 64 km · 603 m up Moderate Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 8 km Mixed surface Some climbing A 64 km rolling loop through the Comox Valley near Courtenay, mixing quiet pavement with gravel stretches and about 600 m of gentle climbing. Farm country riding with the Beaufort Range on the horizon and the valley's food-and-cider scene close at hand. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Taylor Cave Productions Nanaimo, BC Metchosin Caper 83 km · 791 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mixed surface Some climbing An 83 km rolling loop out of Victoria through Metchosin's rural roads and trails, about a third unpaved with 800 m of climbing. Farm stands, ocean glimpses, and forest stretches trade places the whole way around; a local's tour of the capital's quiet west. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Peter O Hara Shawnigan Lake, BC Mill Bay Rambler 100 km · 1136 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mostly gravel Some climbing A 100 km road ride from Esquimalt up the Saanich Inlet coast toward Mill Bay and back, with about 1,100 m of climbing. Classic South Island road touring: shoreline stretches, forested climbs, and enough distance to make the coffee stop count. Stops, map + getting there → Thompson Okanagan · 1 Photo: Abby Cooper Thompson Okanagan, BC Goose / McConnell Goodness w/ Katie 48 km · 756 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Lots of climbing A 48 km ride on Thompson-Nicola backroads, about three-quarters gravel, with roughly 750 m of climbing that arrives in steep pitches rather than long grinds. A solid half-day out in quiet country. Stops, map + getting there → Cariboo Chilcotin Coast · 1 Photo: Robin Ryan Clinton, BC Tutti Loves Poutine 50 km · 205 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Gentle grades Remote stretches A mostly flat 50 km gravel loop built for cruising, strung with lakes and quiet forest roads. Halfway around, a roadside restaurant serves authentic Quebec-style poutine, and the Chasm viewpoint is worth the photo stop. Almost all gravel, barely any climbing, and long stretches with nobody around. Stops, map + getting there → Northern British Columbia · 1 Photo: Shayd Johnson Skidegate, BC Haida Gwaii: Magic, Mystery and Mayhem 510 km · 5573 m up Challenging Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 235 km Mixed surface Some climbing Remote stretches A 510 km multi-day route through Haida Gwaii, the remote archipelago off BC's north coast. The riding threads temperate rainforest and rugged coastline, passing near ancient Haida village sites, with about 5,500 m of climbing along the way. Roughly a third is unpaved, and services are few and far between. The published account of riding it solo is a story of connection as much as cycling: this is a place you visit on its terms. title: BT 700 Bikepacking
desc: BT 700 Bikepacking's complete BC cycling route collection — 10 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / BT 700 Bikepacking BT 700 Bikepacking individual route creator visit → BT 700 Bikepacking is a route-publishing site run by Ontario adventure cyclist and writer Matt Kadey, one of Canada's most prolific bikepacking route builders. It grew out of the original BT700 gravel loop in southwestern Ontario and now offers downloadable route files for gravel and bikepacking rides across Canada, including several in British Columbia. Their BC collection BT 700 Bikepacking's British Columbia routes are side trips, bypasses, and connectors along The Big Griz, its 2,380 km Victoria-to-Banff flagship — from 37 km connectors up to a 304 km multi-day route into Castlegar. Six are concentrated in the Kootenay-Rockies region (Fernie, Nakusp, New Denver, and the Central and East Kootenay), two are on Vancouver Island (Bamfield, Port Renfrew), and one extends into the Thompson-Okanagan. Most are unpaved or mixed-surface gravel routes with significant climbing, rated moderate to hard. 10 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on BT 700 Bikepacking's website. Vancouver Island · 2 Photo: Jordan Dyck Tofino, BC BT700 Bamfield 110 km · 972 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 9 km Almost all gravel Some climbing Remote stretches A 110 km mostly-gravel leg into Bamfield, the remote boardwalk village on Barkley Sound reached otherwise by boat or the same long logging roads you will ride. Steady climbing, rough stretches, and long quiet distances; the reward is one of the west coast's most distinctive destinations. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Rob Wilson Vancouver Island, BC BT700 Port Renfrew 174 km · 3731 m up Challenging Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 51 km Mixed surface Max climbing Remote stretches A 174 km BT700 leg from the Victoria area out to Port Renfrew on the island's wild west coast, on a near-even mix of pavement and gravel with a serious 3,700 m of climbing. Remote in the middle third and shared with traffic on the road sections. Big trees and the Pacific wait at the end. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Thompson Okanagan · 1 Photo: Tina Bryan Grand Forks, BC BT700 Castlegar 304 km · 3490 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 13 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Some climbing Remote stretches A 304 km multi-day BT700 stretch running down to Castlegar, about three-quarters unpaved with 3,500 m of climbing spread over gentle grades. The surfaces are the challenge here rather than the hills: expect long rough stretches where fatter tires and patience both pay off. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Kootenay Rockies · 7 Photo: Mitch Winton Fernie, BC BT700 Fernie Alternative 76 km · 1119 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mostly gravel Lots of climbing An alternative leg of the BT700 near Fernie: 76 km, mostly unpaved, with steady forest-road climbing adding up to about 1,100 m. The option for riders who want more gravel in their East Kootenay traverse. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Fernie, BC BT700 Fernie Sparwood 37 km · 569 m up Challenging Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 2 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing The BT700's connector between Fernie and Sparwood through the Elk Valley: 37 km, about three-quarters unpaved, with some genuinely chunky surfaces and around 570 m of climbing. A solid half-day link between the two towns. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Nakusp, BC BT700 Gray Creek Bypass 174 km · 1991 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Some climbing The BT700's paved alternative through the Central Kootenays via Gray Creek: 174 km with about 2,000 m of rolling climbing, nearly all on pavement and highway, so expect to ride with traffic. The practical choice when your bike or the conditions make the rougher passes a bad idea. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Lindsay Marie Stewart Kaslo, BC BT700 Kaslo 85 km · 2103 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 30 km Mostly gravel Max climbing An 85 km BT700 leg with one of BC's more memorable trail moments: a hand-pulled cable-car river crossing on the Galena Trail out of New Denver. From there the Wagon Trail runs rough and chunky into Kaslo, then paved highway follows Kootenay Lake south to Balfour, with about 2,100 m of climbing along the way. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Nakusp, BC BT700 Nakusp Rosebery 43 km · 513 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Almost all gravel Chunky gravel Some climbing Remote stretches A 43 km BT700 leg linking Nakusp and Rosebery, entirely unpaved and nearly flat, with only about 500 m of climbing. The kind of stretch where you settle into a rhythm: quiet gravel, forest, and long sections with nobody around. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Kari Medig Nelson, BC BT700 Slocan Valley 76 km · 744 m up Moderate Some traffic sharing Mixed surface Some climbing A 76 km BT700 leg through the Slocan Valley on a mix of rail trail and quiet valley roads, about a third unpaved, with gentle rolling terrain and around 750 m of climbing. Mellow riding through one of the Kootenays' loveliest valleys. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Darren Robinson Princeton, BC The Big Griz 2261 km · 38186 m up Epic Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 530 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches BT700 BC flagship, 2,380 km from Victoria to Banff with about 62% on gravel and dirt and climbing that never really stops. The nine other BT700 routes here are its side trips and bypasses. Our map shows the BC leg; route files are on bt700.ca. Route created by Matt Kadey of BT 700 Bikepacking. title: Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society
desc: Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society's complete BC cycling route collection — 7 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society touring organization visit → The Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society (CCCTS) is a non-profit cycling club founded in 1982, based in British Columbia with a chapter in Ottawa. In its own words, it is a club for active adults of all ages; members are mainly retired people who love recreational cycling. Volunteers organize weekly day rides plus multi-day and cross-Canada tours, some of which have run continuously since the 1980s. Their BC collection The Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society's BC routes range from short day rides of about 84 km to a 1,511 km cross-provincial tour toward Calgary. Most of its routes here are on Vancouver Island, with others in the Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley and one crossing northern British Columbia, the Cariboo-Chilcotin Coast, and the Thompson-Okanagan. Most routes are on paved roads with rolling-to-climbing terrain, and the set includes several multi-day touring routes and one route linked by four ferry crossings. 7 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 1 Photo: Viranlly Liemena viranlly Fort Langley, BC Bakerview to Fort Langley 84 km · 490 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly paved Gentle grades A rolling 84 km paved day ride through the Fraser Valley between Bakerview and Fort Langley, with about 490 m of climbing. The destination earns the miles: Fort Langley's national historic site and cafe-lined village make a natural turnaround. Club-style road riding, so expect to share the road. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 6 Photo: The Number Creative Nanaimo, BC Sunshine Coast Tour Day 5 110 km · 1135 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Some climbing The fifth day of a Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society multi-day tour, riding 110 km in the Nanaimo area with about 1,100 m of rolling climbing, nearly all paved. Club-style road touring: steady pace, shared roads, coffee halfway. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Danika McDowell Comox, BC 4 Ferry Odyssey 165 km · 1662 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Some climbing The 4 Ferry Odyssey links Campbell River, Quadra Island, Cortes Island, Lund, and Powell River in a 165 km island-hopping tour with four water crossings, three ferries and a water taxi. The riding is nearly all paved but deceptively hilly, and the crossings set an unforgiving rhythm, which is why the club recommends it for strong riders. Few routes pack in more Salish Sea per kilometre. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Rob Wilson Duncan, BC Duncan to Chemainus 108 km · 729 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Some climbing A rolling 108 km paved day ride between Duncan, the City of Totems, and Chemainus, famous for its outdoor murals, through the Cowichan Valley's farmland. About 730 m of climbing on shared roads; the two towns' public art makes better-than-average turnaround entertainment. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Jarrett Lindal Cumberland, BC Gold River 2 109 km · 1421 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Lots of climbing Remote stretches An out-and-back paved ride on Highway 28 from the Elk Portal parking area to Gold River and on to the salt water at Muchalat Inlet, about 109 km with 1,400 m of climbing. Quiet mountain highway riding through the edge of Strathcona country, with long empty stretches, so carry what you need. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Ben Giesbrecht Victoria, BC Touring Victoria 84 km · 413 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Mostly paved Gentle grades An 84 km rolling day ride through Greater Victoria, mostly paved, sampling the capital region's shoreline drives, quiet neighbourhoods, and rural edges with only about 400 m of climbing. A club-style tour that shows how much variety hides within an afternoon of the city. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: The Number Creative Cowichan Bay, BC Victoria - Port Renfrew - Lake Cowichan - Duncan - Victoria 264 km · 2993 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Some climbing A classic South Island road tour: start at the Empress Hotel in downtown Victoria, ride the coast road to Port Renfrew, cross the island's interior to Lake Cowichan and Duncan, and return, 264 km over two or three days with nearly 3,000 m of climbing. Paved throughout, remote and lightly serviced on the west-coast leg, and about as varied as island road riding gets. title: Adventure Cycling Association
desc: Adventure Cycling Association's complete BC cycling route collection — 6 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Adventure Cycling Association Adventure Cycling Association touring organization visit → For over 50 years, Adventure Cycling Association has been mapping the most iconic bike routes in North America, including the TransAmerica Trail and the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route. It hosts over 90,000 kilometres of bikepacking and bike touring routes, leads dozens of guided tours each year, and advocates to protect the routes, access, and infrastructure that make bike travel possible. Supported by members and donors, Adventure Cycling's nonprofit mission is to inspire, empower, and connect people to travel by bike. Their BC collection Adventure Cycling Association's routes touching British Columbia fall into two groups: multi-day bikepacking and touring loops around Greater Vancouver and Vancouver Island (paved and mixed surface, roughly 460-660 km), and long-distance touring and gravel routes through the Kootenay-Rockies and northern BC that continue into Alberta, Yukon, and the United States, including the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route, Great Parks North, Selkirk Splendor, and the Alaskan Golden Circle Tour. Terrain is mostly rolling, with surfaces ranging from fully paved to substantially unpaved gravel. Its flagship Pacific Coast route also touches BC, starting in Vancouver before running the length of the US West Coast. 6 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Adventure Cycling Association's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 1 Photo: Albert Normandin Langley, BC ACA Pacific Coast (BC Only) 65 km · 442 m up Moderate Shares roads with traffic Mostly paved Some climbing One of Adventure Cycling's flagship routes, the Pacific Coast runs roughly 3,000 km of paved coastal touring from Vancouver to the US-Mexico border. The BC leg is its opening chapter: 65 km from Vancouver south to the Peace Arch crossing, flat to rolling on city routes and suburban highway. Modest riding on its own, but every ride to Mexico has to start somewhere. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 1 Photo: Jordan Dyck Duncan, BC Vancouver Crossing Loop 503 km · 3165 m up Moderate Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 21 km Mixed surface Some climbing A 503 km multi-day loop, ridden clockwise, that circles the Salish Sea region on a chain of trails and ferries, crossing between Vancouver Island and the Lower Mainland. Nearly half unpaved but gently graded throughout, with about 3,200 m of climbing spread over the distance. The ferries are half the fun; the trail connections do the rest. Stops, map + getting there → Kootenay Rockies · 3 Photo: Steve Ogle Kootenay Rockies, BC Great Divide Mountain Bike Route (BC Only) 307 km · 3108 m up Challenging Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 52 km Mostly gravel Some climbing Remote stretches The British Columbia section of the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route, the famous off-pavement ride tracing the Continental Divide from Canada to Mexico. The BC leg crosses the Flathead Valley, one of the wildest corners of the Canadian Rockies, mostly on gravel and dirt roads far from traffic. About 307 km with around 3,100 m of climbing and long gaps between services, so treat it as a self-sufficient backcountry ride. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Toby Stier Fernie, BC Great Parks North (BC Only) 373 km · 3252 m up Challenging Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Some climbing Remote stretches Adventure Cycling's Great Parks North runs from the Jasper area south into the United States, and its British Columbia leg gives you 373 km of it through the Kootenay Rockies. Nearly all paved and rolling, with around 3,200 m of climbing, built around big mountain scenery. Expect to share the road: this is classic highway touring, best for riders comfortable riding with traffic. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Mitch Winton Creston, BC Selkirk Splendor (BC Only) 355 km · 5532 m up Challenging Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mixed surface Lots of climbing The British Columbia stretch of Adventure Cycling's Selkirk Splendor, about 355 km through the Selkirk Mountains before the route drops toward Sandpoint, Idaho. Mostly paved and never flat: the BC leg piles up around 5,500 m of climbing through lake and mountain country. A committed road tour for riders happy sharing the highway. Stops, map + getting there → Northern British Columbia · 1 Photo: Robin O Neill Smithers, BC Alaskan Golden Circle Tour (BC Only) 130 km · 1971 m up Epic Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Lots of climbing Remote stretches The British Columbia stretch of the Alaskan Golden Circle, a roughly 890 km loop through Alaska, the Yukon, and northern BC, famously closed by about 250 km of ferry travel to and from Haines, Alaska. The 130 km BC leg is paved highway riding through genuinely remote northern country, with long gaps between services. Plan carefully and expect to share the road. title: Elbow Valley Cycle Club
desc: Elbow Valley Cycle Club's complete BC cycling route collection — 6 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Elbow Valley Cycle Club Elbow Valley Cycle Club cycling club visit → Elbow Valley Cycle Club is a Calgary-based recreational cycling club, one of the largest in Western Canada with roughly 700 members. It organizes about 250 events a year, including road, gravel, and multi-day touring rides, several of which cross into British Columbia. Their BC collection Elbow Valley Cycle Club's BC routes span road touring in the Kootenay Rockies, a long-distance gravel route through the Thompson-Okanagan, Kootenay Rockies, and Vancouver Coast and Mountains regions, and shorter day rides on Vancouver Island and in the Thompson-Okanagan. Most routes are paved road rides in the 30-120 km range, alongside one multi-day gravel route exceeding 1,300 km with 67% unpaved surface. Terrain ranges from rolling valley roads to sustained mountain climbing, including sections of the club's flagship Golden Triangle tour through the Rockies. 6 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Elbow Valley Cycle Club's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 1 Photo: Viranlly Liemena viranlly Chilliwack, BC Van to Can Day 1 115 km · 811 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 9 km Mostly paved Some climbing The opening day of the Elbow Valley Cycle Club's Vancouver-to-Canmore tour: 115 km of mostly paved, mostly flat riding east out of the city through the Fraser Valley, with about 800 m of gentle climbing. Straightforward touring with traffic for company. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 1 Photo: Peter O Hara Comox, BC Campbell River 33 km · 147 m up Easy Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 10 km Mostly paved Gentle grades An easy 33 km rolling ride around Campbell River, taking in the oceanfront and the town's edges with barely 150 m of climbing. Campbell River calls itself the salmon capital of the world, and the seawalk's fishing pier makes a fitting stop. Stops, map + getting there → Thompson Okanagan · 2 Photo: Ryan Flett Castlegar, BC BC Gravel (BC Only) 1300 km · 17063 m up Epic Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 177 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches BC Gravel crosses about 1,300 km of southern British Columbia, from the Coast Mountains through the Okanagan to the Kootenays, roughly two-thirds unpaved with over 17,000 m of climbing. A multi-week undertaking on quiet backroads, best planned with the same care as any long bikepacking traverse. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Kari Medig Thompson Okanagan, BC Shuswap No. 6: Carlin, White Lake, Blind Bay 42 km · 506 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly paved Lots of climbing A 42 km paved loop in the Shuswap near Salmon Arm, linking Carlin, White Lake, and Blind Bay with about 500 m of gentle climbing. Pretty lake-country roads, though you will share them with local traffic. Stops, map + getting there → Kootenay Rockies · 2 Photo: Mitch Winton Golden, BC Golden Triangle Day 2 107 km · 635 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Gentle grades The middle day of the classic Golden Triangle road tour: 107 km of pavement from Radium Hot Springs to Golden through the Columbia River Valley, home to North America's longest contiguous wetland. Rolling rather than mountainous, with a new shoulder added in both directions in 2023. Highway riding, so expect traffic. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Kari Medig Kootenay Rockies, BC Golden Triangle Day 3 87 km · 1546 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Lots of climbing Remote stretches The climbing day of the Golden Triangle tour: 87 km from Golden up through Yoho National Park past Field to Lake Louise, gaining about 1,500 m along the way. All paved, all highway, and all Rockies: this is the leg the tour is remembered for. Expect traffic on Highway 1. body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / British Columbia Randonneurs British Columbia Randonneurs cycling club visit → British Columbia Randonneurs Cycling Club is a long-distance cycling club with deep roots: randonneuring in BC dates to 1979, and the club was a founding member of Les Randonneurs Mondiaux, the world body for 1,200 km grand randonnées, in 1983. With regional chapters in the Lower Mainland, Vancouver Island, Southern Interior, and Peace Region, it organizes brevets (timed long-distance rides of 200 km and up), populaires (shorter introductory events), and permanents (self-paced routes available year-round), and publishes the routes on Ride with GPS. Its celebrated Rocky Mountain 1200 drew riders from around the world. Their BC collection The club's routes in this set are populaires of 100 to 160 km with 400 to 820 m of climbing over rolling terrain, on mostly paved roads with some mixed-surface sections. Two start in Metro Vancouver (Vancouver and Langley) and one on southern Vancouver Island (Saanich), consistent with the club's day-length, brevet-style long-distance riding format. 3 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on British Columbia Randonneurs's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 2 Photo: Kindred Scout Vancouver, Coast and Mountains, BC Cherry Blossom Populaire 102 km · 438 m up Ambitious Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 3 km Mostly paved Gentle grades A 102 km populaire from Vancouver in the BC Randonneurs tradition: a friendly, non-competitive distance ride timed for spring, when the city's cherry trees are in bloom. Nearly flat and nearly all paved, it is a fine first step into randonneuring or simply a good long day out. Ride the route any time; the club event happens once a year. Stops, map + getting there → Photo: Viranlly Liemena viranlly Chilliwack, BC Maple Leaf Populaire 159 km · 823 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Fast-road sections · 39 km Mostly paved Gentle grades A 159 km populaire starting in Langley, in the BC Randonneurs tradition of long, sociable, non-competitive rides. Rolling Fraser Valley terrain with about 800 m of climbing, mostly paved with a few gravel stretches, and enough distance to make the finish feel earned. Ride it any time; the club event runs once a year. Expect to share the road. Stops, map + getting there → Vancouver Island · 1 Photo: Daniel Baylis Sooke, BC Iron Mine Bay Grando 102 km · 769 m up Ambitious Low-traffic riding Mostly gravel Some climbing A 102 km populaire from Saanich in the BC Randonneurs tradition, rolling out toward Iron Mine Bay on a near-even mix of pavement and gravel with about 770 m of climbing. Sociable, non-competitive distance riding; the route is there year-round even when the club event is not. body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / The Great Community Route Celebration The Great Community Route Celebration event organizer visit → The Great Community Route Celebration was a global cycling route-creation event hosted by Ride with GPS, running June 11 to July 5, 2020. Participants worldwide created and submitted routes highlighting places and spaces in their own communities, adding points of interest and photos along the way. The event drew 523 route submissions from 51 countries. Their BC collection Two BC routes were submitted to the Celebration. One is a 346-kilometre multi-day gravel-and-paved loop through the Cariboo-Chilcotin Coast, starting and ending in Quesnel, largely rustic with limited services. The other is a 112-kilometre paved climbing loop on Vancouver's North Shore in the Vancouver, Coast and Mountains region. Together the two range from remote multi-day backcountry touring to a demanding single-day road climb. 2 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on The Great Community Route Celebration's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 1 Photo: Kindred Scout North Vancouver, BC Triple Crown, Vancouver, BC (loop) 112 km · 2410 m up Ambitious Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Max climbing The Triple Crown is Vancouver road cycling's rite of passage: climb the North Shore's three big paved ascents, Cypress, Grouse, and Seymour, in a single ride. This 112 km loop stays on the North Shore and routes you back to your start, collecting about 2,400 m of climbing along the way. All paved, all shared with traffic, and all reputation-earning. Stops, map + getting there → Cariboo Chilcotin Coast · 1 Photo: Bonnie Grenon Quesnel, BC Fish, Fishpot Lakes & Snaking River Loop 346 km · 4005 m up Challenging Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 41 km Mostly gravel Some climbing Remote stretches A 346 km loop starting and ending in downtown Quesnel, wandering Cariboo backroads past Fish Lake, the Fishpot Lakes, and the Snaking River. About 70% gravel, with roughly 4,000 m of climbing spread over several days. Very rustic and far between services, so sort out your resupply before leaving town. title: Trans Canada Trail
desc: Trans Canada Trail's complete BC cycling route collection — 2 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Trans Canada Trail Trans Canada Trail trail organization visit → Trans Canada Trail is a national charitable organization, based in Ottawa, that coordinates and maintains the Trans Canada Trail (also known as The Great Trail) — a roughly 30,000 km multi-use trail network spanning every Canadian province and territory and connecting the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic coastlines. The network supports hiking, cycling, paddling, and other activities, and is built and managed through partnerships with regional and local trail organizations rather than owned as a single continuous trail. Their BC collection Two Trans Canada Trail cycling routes cover British Columbia. The southern route runs about 1,768 km from the Kootenays through the Okanagan and the south coast to Vancouver Island, linking rail trails, greenways, and road sections across four regions. The northern route follows the Alaska Highway corridor about 1,031 km from Dawson Creek toward the Yukon border — the land connection between the rest of the Trans Canada Trail and the Arctic coast. Both are long-distance corridors best suited to experienced touring cyclists rather than casual day rides. 2 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Trans Canada Trail's website. Kootenay Rockies · 1 Photo: Kari Medig Castlegar, BC Trans Canada Trail South (BC Only) 1768 km Epic Low-traffic riding Fast-road sections · 65 km Mostly gravel Chunky gravel The southern leg of the national Trans Canada Trail, about 1,765 km of cycling sections from Victoria to the Alberta border. It threads Vancouver Island, the Lower Mainland, the Kettle Valley Rail Trail through the Okanagan, and the Kootenays. This is a network of segments with meaningful gaps between them, not one continuous line, so expect road links and detours. A few stretches, including much of the KVR Coquihalla corridor, are closed for now. Some of the Trail is hilly, on roads, on rough gravel, and/or remote: look into the details so you are prepared. Stops, map + getting there → Northern British Columbia · 1 Photo: 6ix Sigma Productions Mackenzie, BC Trans Canada Trail North (BC Only) 1031 km Epic Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Remote stretches The far-north leg of the Trans Canada Trail in BC, about 1,028 km following the Alaska Highway corridor from Dawson Creek toward the Yukon. Highway riding, big country, long distances between towns and very remote: plan your stops and resupply with care. desc: Great Northern Bikepacking Route's complete BC cycling route collection — 2 rides — on Get Inspired, BC Cycle Tourism Society.
body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Great Northern Bikepacking Route Great Northern Bikepacking Route individual route creator visit → The Great Northern Bikepacking Route (GNBR) is a mostly off-road bikepacking route created by Ontario adventure cyclist and writer Matt Kadey, spanning over 13,000 km across 10 Canadian provinces and 3 U.S. states, from the Pacific to the Atlantic — one of the most ambitious route-mapping projects in the country. It is published segment by segment on a dedicated website, with route data on RideWithGPS and gear and provisioning notes alongside the maps. Their BC collection The British Columbia section of the GNBR is split into two long RideWithGPS routes covering roughly 1,770 km combined, from Vancouver-Coast and Mountains through the Thompson-Okanagan, Cariboo-Chilcotin Coast, and Kootenay-Rockies. Both are multi-day, high-climbing bikepacking routes on mixed surfaces, with Part Two mostly unpaved (67%) and Part One closer to an even paved/unpaved mix (47% unpaved). 2 of their BC rides # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Great Northern Bikepacking Route's website. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains · 1 Photo: Kari Medig Lillooet, BC Great Northern Bikepacking Route, BC Part One 583 km · 11950 m up Epic Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 213 km Mixed surface Max climbing The first half of the Great Northern Bikepacking Route's British Columbia section: about 583 km from Richmond through the Coast Mountains into the Interior, on mixed pavement and gravel. The climbing is the story, nearly 12,000 m of it, as the route fights its way up from sea level through some of the steepest country in the province. A committed multi-day leg of a much longer journey. Route created by Matt Kadey. Stops, map + getting there → Kootenay Rockies · 1 Photo: Aaron Hagen Cranbrook, BC Great Northern Bikepacking Route, BC Part Two 1187 km · 18412 m up Epic Some traffic sharing Fast-road sections · 196 km Mostly gravel Lots of climbing Remote stretches The second half of the Great Northern Bikepacking Route's British Columbia section: nearly 1,200 km through the Kootenay Rockies and Thompson Okanagan, mostly unpaved, with an enormous amount of climbing, over 18,000 m in total. A committed multi-week undertaking through big, quiet country. Route created by Matt Kadey. body: Home / Get Inspired / Route makers / Trans Canada Bike Route Network Trans Canada Bike Route Network route network visit → A volunteer-run, community-collaborative project mapping a proposed coast-to-coast National Cycling Route Network for Canada. It publishes route data as GPX files, a Garmin BaseCamp database (GDB) with points of interest, KMZ files for offline smartphone use, interactive Google Maps, and a curated Ride with GPS collection. Their BC collection The BC portion of the network totals roughly 5,400 km of mapped riding across all six regions of the province, from Vancouver Island to the North. It is long-distance, self-supported touring — the western spine of a route that ultimately crosses the whole country, mapped entirely by volunteers. 1 of their BC ride # Open any ride for its welcoming stops and how to get there. The full writeup, map, and directions live on Trans Canada Bike Route Network's website. Thompson Okanagan · 1 Photo: Mirae Campbell Kelowna, BC Trans Canada Bike Route (BC Only) 5446 km Epic Shares roads with traffic Mostly fast roads Mostly paved Remote stretches The British Columbia portion of the proposed Trans Canada Bike Route, a national coast-to-coast cycling network still taking shape. The BC section maps about 5,400 km of connected riding, nearly all on paved roads, reaching from Vancouver Island through the southern Interior to the Cariboo. A planning framework and a dream to follow rather than a signed trail: expect ordinary highway conditions. How we describe routes → The British Columbia stretch of the Alaskan Golden Circle, a roughly 890 km loop through Alaska, the Yukon, and northern BC, famously closed by about 250 km of ferry travel to and from Haines, Alaska. The 130 km BC leg is paved highway riding through genuinely remote northern country, with long gaps between services. Plan carefully and expect to share the road. Rather not haul your own gear that far north? Sockeye Cycle , a bike outfitter in Haines, runs a guided Golden Circle tour and a self-guided package with rental bike, camping gear, and shop-to-shop logistics between Haines and Skagway. How we describe routes → “When most people think of British Columbia, they picture towering, glacier-capped mountains and vast conifer forests. In the south-central part of the province, however, lies a unique and environmentally significant grassland landscape. B.C.’s grasslands make up just one percent of its land base but provide habitat for almost a third of the province’s threatened and endangered species, according to the Grasslands Conservation Council of British Columbia. This route is designed to explore part of this environmentally important landscape. It begins in Kamloops and will inspire with its great beauty. You’ll marvel at endless views over sprawling ranches, the azure lakes teeming with waterfowl, and the thousands of birds flying through the air as you tackle the route’s many climbs and descents.” — BIKEPACKING.com Get the route on BIKEPACKING.com → Where this ride goes # Approximate line Get the real route ↗ Map key & layers Show stops Mute other bike trails Food & Drink Supplies Camping Bike Services Riding near fast traffic Fastest stretches Dashed line = our rough sketch of where the ride goes. How we describe routes → “The Frog Peak Loop is a non-technical and logistically straightforward gravel route, making it the perfect intro to bikepacking in the Kootenays. The official starting point is in Nelson, but it’s possible to start anywhere in the Slocan Valley or at the revered Frog Peak Café if you need a caffeine hit before you ride. At 107 kilometers (66 miles) long, the route can be tackled in a single day but is best enjoyed extended over a weekend to soak in the beauty of the West Kootenays. Despite feeling remote at times, this is offset by its proximity to small communities, delicious food stops, and well-traveled rail trails. If you’re looking for a route to convert the first-time bikepacker, this is it. The route has ample swimming spots, resupply points, and campgrounds, making it an ideal weekend trip.” — BIKEPACKING.com Get the route on BIKEPACKING.com → Where this ride goes # Approximate line Get the real route ↗ Map key & layers Show stops Mute other bike trails Food & Drink Attractions Supplies Camping Accommodation Bike Services Dashed line = our rough sketch of where the ride goes. body: Photo: Andrew Strain Vancouver, Coast and Mountains, BC Home / Get Inspired / Vancouver, Coast and Mountains / Golden Ears Overnighter (out and back) Golden Ears Overnighter (out and back) A ride described at Gravel Buddies Ambitious How we describe routes → Ambitious A real undertaking. Demanding on a couple of fronts, like rough surfaces plus steady climbing, or a long stretch on busier roads. Difficulty Our overall read of how demanding a route is. We score surface roughness, climbing, singletrack, and how far it runs from services. The route publisher's own rating, a lot of busy road riding, or sheer scale can push the tier up, never down. Derived from OpenStreetMap. Good data, not perfect. Spot something wrong? Tell us . How we describe routes → The beloved beginner overnighter: from Swartz Bay, follow the Lochside Trail through Saanich farmland and the Galloping Goose's rail-trail wilderness to Sooke Potholes Provincial Park, about 75 km each way with barely a hill, 95% of it on trail. How we describe routes → The Salish Sea Trail links the South Island's best rail trails, the Lochside, the Galloping Goose, and the Cowichan Valley Trail, into one big 175 km loop with a Salt Spring Island ferry hop in the middle. Most of it is calm rail-trail riding through forest and farmland; the road stretches through wine country roll and climb a bit more. Ride a 15 km piece, or take a few days and go all the way around. How we describe routes → The Kettle Valley Rail Trail from Penticton to Midway is one of Canada's most-loved off-pavement tours: 214 km of historic rail grade through Naramata's benchlands, up past Chute Lake, through the Kelowna highlands and Beaverdell, and down to Midway. Access points all along mean you can ride anything from 11 km to the whole thing. The grades stay gentle, but surfaces vary from smooth to rough and sandy, and services thin out in the middle, so plan your days around the towns. How we describe routes → The southern leg of the national Trans Canada Trail, about 1,765 km of cycling sections from Victoria to the Alberta border. It threads Vancouver Island, the Lower Mainland, the Kettle Valley Rail Trail through the Okanagan, and the Kootenays. How we describe routes → “The Tree to Sea Loop takes advantage of the gravel roads north of Campbell River, linking together small coastal villages, incredible landscapes, and impressive granite mountains into a 1,000-kilometre bucket-list bikepacking route. How we describe routes → The Triple Crown is Vancouver road cycling's rite of passage: climb the North Shore's three big paved ascents, Cypress, Grouse, and Seymour, in a single ride. How we describe routes → A 503 km multi-day loop, ridden clockwise, that circles the Salish Sea region on a chain of trails and ferries, crossing between Vancouver Island and the Lower Mainland. Nearly half unpaved but gently graded throughout, with about 3,200 m of climbing spread over the distance. The ferries are half the fun; the trail connections do the rest.
