title: BC Bike Stops: How It Works
desc: What our accreditation means: the criteria behind each of the seven stop categories, the four badge tiers, and how businesses join the BC Bike Stops program.
body: Home / BC Bike Stops / Guides Guide to the BC Bike Stops directory Every touring cyclist in BC is doing the same detective work: Will the hostel store my bike? Does the bus take three bikes? Will I be able to fill up my water bottle mid-ride? 18,500+ cycling stops 906 BC communities 7 stop types BC Bike Stops is an accreditation program developed by the BC Cycle Tourism Society to highlight businesses that genuinely serve cycle tourists. Seven categories of stops, criteria designed for each facility type, and every listing tells you what you're getting before you arrive. Already know what you're looking for? Open the interactive directory → The seven stop types # What we require of each, at a glance. Each type has its own guide: what the criteria mean, what else we track, and a few stops that show the range. Accommodation 1,534 stops Secure overnight bike storage, because knowing your bike is safe lets you sleep well. Read the guide → Browse all 1,534 → Camping 1,395 stops A commitment not to turn away a cyclist arriving for the night. Read the guide → Browse all 1,395 → Food & Drink 10,910 stops Bike parking or a sightline to your bike, a water bottle refill, and washrooms. Read the guide → Browse all 10,910 → Supplies 2,611 stops Groceries, pharmacies and gear, with bike parking and a water bottle refill. Read the guide → Browse all 2,611 → Bike Services 201 stops Staff help with urgent mechanical issues, and a pump you can use. Read the guide → Browse all 201 → Attractions 1,653 stops Museums, parks and viewpoints with bike parking, a water bottle refill, and washrooms. Read the guide → Browse all 1,653 → Transport 209 stops A commitment to carry bikes. Read the guide → Browse all 209 → Riding your own route? See the welcoming stops along it → Those are the required basics. On top of them, each type carries a standardized set of optional amenities , from a dozen for supplies up to twenty-plus for camping, chosen for what actually helps a cyclist, whether you're loaded up for a week of bikepacking or out for an afternoon on a rail trail: covered bike parking, a water bottle refill, laundry, somewhere to bring your bike inside, Wi-Fi, a bike wash. Every amenity is recorded on each listing, and you can filter any category down to just the stops that have the ones you need. What the badges mean # Every listing carries one of four badges, so you can tell at a glance how much we know. Accredited Verified to meet all accreditation criteria, by application, our own research, or community recommendation. Welcoming Meets our cyclist-welcoming criteria on the info we have, but hasn't been formally accredited. Info Listed for reference; details are mostly assumed from public data. Bikes Unwelcome Known not to accommodate bikes, flagged so you can plan around it. Every listing shows which criteria are confirmed and which are still assumed from public data , so you know what you are getting before you arrive. Riders and businesses can correct any listing . How we build this The BC Cycle Tourism Society starts from open data — OpenStreetMap, open government datasets, and public sources — and uses AI to match places to cycling routes and draft each listing against its category's criteria. Businesses can also apply directly — a 10-minute form where they confirm they meet their category's criteria and share local knowledge for cyclists. We review every application ourselves, usually within two weeks. Accreditation lasts two years, then we check in to confirm the listing is still accurate. Want the backstory? Read how and why we built this in our Field Notes Newsletter. Common questions # What is BC Bike Stops? It's an accreditation program from the BC Cycle Tourism Society, and a directory of places across BC that are glad to see you arrive by bike. Seven categories of stops, each with criteria built for that kind of place, so every listing tells you what you're getting before you arrive. What does “cycle tourism” mean? Travelling by bike for the trip itself. It might be a day ride around one town, a few days linking rail-trails and quiet roads, or a loaded bikepacking route. Not commuting, not racing. Just exploring BC under your own power and choosing stops along the way that make the ride easier and more enjoyable. How is this different from a regular tourism listing? A normal listing tells you a place exists. Ours tells you whether it works when you arrive on a bike. Each category carries its required basics plus a standardized set of optional amenities, from a dozen for supplies up to twenty-plus for camping, all chosen for what actually helps a cyclist on the road. Does it cover all of British Columbia? Yes, all of it. The directory spans 906 communities, from the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island to the Kootenays, the Okanagan, the North, and the Interior. Coverage is denser in some areas than others, and it keeps growing as more stops are added. How can I find cycle tourism spots along my planned route? For now, browse stops by community along your route and filter each category down to the amenities you need. We're also building route-planning tools that will show cyclist-welcoming stops right along your route, so you can plan a whole trip in one view. Those are coming soon, stay tuned! Can I find budget options, or higher-end ones? Both. Accommodation, food and drink, and attractions carry a price indicator ($ to $$$), so you can pick a cheap campground meal or a nicer stay depending on the trip you want. The listings don't push you either way. They just show what's there so you can choose. I ride an e-bike. Is this useful to me too? Yes. E-bike riders are a growing part of the touring crowd, and the directory tracks what matters to you. “E-bike charging” is a flagged amenity on accommodation, camping, food, and attraction listings, so you can find places to top up the battery. We also try to make clear whether a bike shop can service e-bike motors and batteries, and whether transport accepts e-bikes, weight and battery rules included. We don't have complete details everywhere yet, but it keeps getting better. Is this directory useful if I'm hiking or paddling instead of cycling? It's built for people travelling by bike, and the criteria reflect that, like secure bike storage and whether a bus will carry your bike. That said, a lot of what it tracks, water refills, washrooms, welcoming places to stay, and local route knowledge, is useful to anyone exploring BC under their own power. How do you decide what counts as Indigenous-owned? We don't decide it ourselves. The Indigenous-owned and Indigenous-operated tags come from Indigenous Tourism BC and Destination Indigenous , where businesses self-identify and are listed by the Indigenous tourism organizations themselves. A few band-operated facilities, like Nation-run campgrounds in provincial parks, are tagged from public operator records. Culture & heritage is broader: it means a place centres Indigenous culture, art, or heritage you can experience as a visitor, whatever its ownership. If we've got something wrong, or your business should be here and isn't, please tell us and we'll fix it. We care about recognizing Indigenous-owned and Indigenous-operated listings correctly and respectfully. Is it free to use? Yes. Browsing the directory and planning your trip is completely free. Listing a business or becoming accredited is free too. Our goal is a comprehensive directory that benefits every cycle tourist in BC. I run a business. What are the benefits of being listed or accredited? Cyclists plan their trips around places that welcome them. In Quebec, where the Bienvenue cyclistes! program has run for decades, 31% of overnight cycle tourists adjust their itinerary based on certification. Listing is free. Accreditation brings a full, customized listing with the teal Accredited badge, highlighted placement in our route-planning tools, features in our newsletter and social channels, and a digital "BC Bike Stops" badge for your own website if you'd like one. The form takes about 10 minutes, we review every application ourselves within two weeks, and accreditation lasts two years. Apply on the Apply for accreditation page. I have a suggestion that would help other cycle tourists. Where do I send it? We'd love to hear it. If you know a great cyclist-welcoming stop we're missing, or you spot something that needs fixing, head to the Suggest or update a listing page and tell us. The directory gets better every time a rider shares what they know, so thank you! Get involved # Help us make the BC Bike Stops directory better. Want to welcome cyclists? Join the BC Bike Stops program as an accredited business and tell touring riders exactly what you offer. Apply for accreditation → Know a business that should be listed? Rode past a café with a bike rack? Stayed at a hostel that stored your bike? Tell us about it. Suggest or update a listing → Got feedback on the program? We'd love to hear it. Contact us or email hello@bccycletourism.ca .

title: Field Notes
desc: Deep dives on cycling infrastructure, policy, and BC's path to becoming a world-class cycle touring destination.
body: Home / Field Notes Field Notes from the BC Cycle Tourism Society Deep dives on cycling infrastructure, policy, and BC's path to becoming a world-class cycle touring destination. Deep dives # The longer reads: features, announcements, and policy. Ride BC indoors this winter Three BC rides to pedal along to on YouTube, free on any indoor bike, and the 45 BC rides on Rouvy, with what you need and what it costs. November 2026 BC gifts for people who ride (and where they're really made) Gifts for people who ride, from under $5 to $300, each one labelled with where it's really made. November 2026 Where can I camp this fall? Most BC campgrounds close by the end of October. Here's when they close, region by region, and where you can still pitch a tent this fall and winter. October 2026 Who to thank for our BC trails Find out who looks after the BC trails and rec sites you rode this summer, and easy ways to say thanks this Thanksgiving. October 2026 Society guest on Bike Sense Podcast I (Founding Director Heather Piwowar) talked with Peter Ladner on the BC Cycling Coalition's podcast about what BC is missing, why PDF maps don't cut it anymore, and how much cycle tourists really eat. The full transcript, plus more episodes for people who love touring in BC. September 2026 Riding through Indigenous BC Plan your next BC bike trip around Indigenous cultural sites, public art, and Indigenous-owned places to eat, stay and learn along the way. September 2026 Plan Your To and Fro: which buses, trains, and ferries take your bike Pick two BC places and see every way we know to move you and your bike between them. 115 places, floatplanes included. August 2026 The Trailside Buffet: a cyclist's guide to BC's wild berries Late August is huckleberry and blackberry season. What to look for, where and when to find it, and where picking is actually allowed. August 2026 145 places in BC that want you to visit with your bike The first 145 accredited places are live on BC Bike Stops. No paid placements, and nobody gets in just by asking. Each one showed us, in their own words, how they welcome cyclists. July 2026 BC road rules are being rewritten BC is consulting on changes to the Motor Vehicle Act. Most of the attention goes to city streets. Here are five proposed changes that matter most when you're touring. July 2026 Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore. Quebec and Ontario figured this out years ago. BC Bike Stops is a business directory built for what touring cyclists actually need to know. May 2026 Calling everyone who loves exploring BC by bike! We're starting by listening. Subscribe, tell us what you know, and help us build BC into one of the best places in the world to explore by bike. May 2026 How to # Practical guides for getting yourself and your bike around BC. Know when to replace your helmet When to replace your bike helmet, how to tell how old it is, and what to do with the old one. November 2026 Put your bike on a BC Transit or TransLink bus bike rack Almost every city bus in BC has a bike rack on the front. Here's how to load your bike, with BC Transit's short video and the rules for e-bikes, big tires, and kids' bikes. November 2026 Store your food when you're camping by bike No car to lock your food in at night? Here's what works at BC campgrounds, from bear canisters to the bear-proof garbage bin. October 2026 Snack vegan on a bike tour Portable vegan and vegetarian bike snacks, sweet and salty, that almost everyone can eat. September 2026 Eat enough on a bike tour Riding all day takes a lot of food. More than most of us expect, and much more than you eat at home. September 2026 Get a bike mechanic to come to you Awkward to get your bike to a bike shop? In BC, sometimes the bike shop can come to you. Mobile repair vans don't do roadside assistance, but they can still save a touring trip. August 2026 Plan around wildfire smoke in BC Fire season is part of BC riding now. The forecasting tools are genuinely good, BC is enormous, and a bit of planning usually means changing your trip, not losing it. August 2026 Take your bike in a taxi or rideshare No bike rack required. With a little prep, a bagged bike rides fine in a cab, an Uber, or a Coastal Rides car. July 2026 Keep your drivetrain happy on a multi-day ride Mat from Trip Longer cleans his chain every night on tour, and it takes five minutes. Here's his routine. July 2026 Take your bike on a coach bus Coach buses are one of BC's most underrated tools for cycle tourists: economical, low-carbon, and they usually accept bikes. Here's how to pack and ride along. May 2026 No Field Notes match that search. Loading... Ride along with us! Monthly Dispatch: hot news and deep dives on cycling infrastructure, policy, and BC's path to becoming a world-class cycle touring destination. Subscribe From the dispatches Nov 29 The Bicycle Film Festival comes to Nanaimo on Sunday, November 29, at Malaspina Theatre at Vancouver Island University (VIU), for $30 online. It's in Vancouver on Thursday, December 3, at the Rio Theatre, with two programs from $27. Nanaimo tickets → Vancouver tickets → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov Kettle Valley Rail Trail: closed from Trout Crossing to Summerland after the Bald Range wildfire, likely for two to three years. Trout Crossing is where the trail meets Princeton-Summerland Road, about 13 km up the road. No detour has been posted. Galloping Goose, Victoria: closed between Viaduct Park and Dupplin Road until spring 2027 for BC Hydro cable work. Detours are signed. The Neighbourhood Bikeway is also detoured between Gorge Road East and Culduthel Road, along Washington and Whittier avenues. George Massey Tunnel shuttle: weekdays only until April 1. Southbound from Richmond at 6, 7, and 8 am and 4, 5, and 6 pm; northbound from Delta half an hour later. Kettle Valley closure → Galloping Goose detours → Massey shuttle schedule → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Oct 22 The Island Corridor Foundation has started building a path beside the E&N rail line in Qualicum Beach, from Memorial Avenue to the back of the train station. It's due to finish this month. Story in the Nanaimo Bulletin → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov 19 Reservations for BC's national park campgrounds open at 8 am on these dates: Jan 13: Glacier, Mount Revelstoke, and Gulf Islands Jan 15: Pacific Rim (Green Point) Jan 19: Kootenay and Yoho (8 am mountain time, which is 7 am in Vancouver) Every campground and time is on Parks Canada's launch dates page. Missed your date? Check back, since sites open up all season. BC's provincial parks work differently: campsites open for booking three months ahead of your arrival date, at 7 am every day. Launch dates → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov 23 BIKEPACKING.com's seventh Good Night campout runs December 19 to 31. All you have to do is spend one night out with your bike, and your backyard counts. Want to go farther? Our campground seasons map shows which BC campgrounds are still open in late December. Pick a night and see. November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov The third group start on the Great Northern Bikepacking Route leaves Mile 0 in Victoria at 9 am on Sunday, May 16, 2027. The full route is 13,700 km (!), and it's not a race. Sign up on the route's site. Group start details → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov 10 GoByBike BC has started a series on BC communities to visit by bike. First up is Nanaimo, with its waterfront, downtown cafés, restored E&N station, and bike trails. Read it on GoByBike BC → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov 1 The Outdoor Recreation Council of BC's Outdoor Recreation Fund is open to trail groups until January 20. Grants run from $2,000 to $10,000. You need to match half, and volunteer time counts at $25 an hour. BC charities, nonprofits, and Indigenous governments can apply. Fund details → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov Peter Gostelow rode Canada and Alaska for 158 days, mostly wild camping, and posted what it cost: about £1,170 (about $2,200) for food, £251 (about $470) for six ferries, and £51 (about $95) for four nights of paid camping. He notes that bikes ride free on BC Ferries. Cost breakdown on Facebook → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Oct 11 Dara Poon linked a World Rivers Day ride and the BC Randonneurs Cycling Club annual general meeting into one week-long bikepacking trip, and visited a residential school site on September 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. The whole trip came to 1,552 km in eight rides. Routes and photos on Komoot → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Oct 15 A rider spent three fall days on the Cowichan Valley 8, which is singletrack, a lot of rail trail, and city paths. The first day started cold and sunny, it drizzled under low cloud on the second, and they had the northern half almost to themselves. "Fall really can be a great time to get out there." Trip report on Reddit → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Oct 23 Four friends took cameras on their first bikepacking trip, three days in the Chilcotin. Video at Bike Mag → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov 12 Vern Dewit added the Okanagan Rail Trail to both ends of a local gravel race route, climbed into a maze of forest roads with no cell service, and rode home along the lakes with stops for a swim. Video on YouTube → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Nov 10 A Cumberland mountain biker bought a flat-bar gravel bike and rode two days from Seal Bay to Forbidden Plateau on 70 km of logging roads and singletrack, many gated to cars. Lesson learned: bring more phone battery. Story at Flow → November 2026 Dispatch (in progress) Oct 7 Registration is still open for the BC Cycling Coalition's Active Transportation Summit in Victoria, October 28 to 30. Bursaries are still available and take 50% off registration for all three days. If cost is a factor, you're eligible. When you register, you can also ask to be matched with others to carpool, share a taxi, or cycle in together. Day 1 is half-day workshops, $59 each, on topics like walking and biking to school and the Motor Vehicle Act, and they're filling up fast. BC Cycle Tourism Society (Colleen and Heather) are presenting on Thursday afternoon. Bursary → Workshops → Register → October 2026 Dispatch Sep 30 Amtrak Cascades has started running its new Airo trains. Each one has racks for 18 bikes, some of them in the passenger cars, so you can keep your bike near you rather than only in the baggage car. Two Airo trains are running so far: one arrives in Vancouver from Seattle at 12:30 pm, and one leaves Vancouver for Seattle at 4:45 pm. The rest of the fleet switches over by early 2027. You still need a bike reservation, and Amtrak's booking system may cap them at six per train until it catches up. E-bikes are allowed under 50 lb, with tires no wider than 2". Amtrak → October 2026 Dispatch Oct 2 Building Momentum Bikepacking runs a free gear library for women and gender-diverse riders: bikepacking bikes, bags, tents, and other camping gear, borrowed for up to a week (two with a renewal) and picked up in Nelson. Since it opened in late July, 35 people have borrowed 67 items. Gear library → October 2026 Dispatch Oct 6 Adventure Cycling Association (ACA) is a US non-profit, but a few of its routes run through BC, including the Vancouver Crossing Loop, the start of its Pacific Coast Route, and part of the Great Divide Route. (This month it also launched an Eastern Canada Route, 1,500 km from Toronto to Québec City, roughly two-thirds car-free, swoon!) ACA members get Adventure Cyclist, a beautiful touring magazine, in print or digital. New this year are Campfire Chats, small monthly online conversations for members. October's is about eating on tour (Oct 21, 4 pm Pacific). Campfire Chats → October 2026 Dispatch Sep 9 Not a trip report exactly, but a lovely ten minutes of riding in the South Cariboo. Kelly Servinski and Erin Yeo sold everything to open the Tutti Gravel Inn in Clinton, which they call Canada's first gravel bike hotel. The film follows them and a few riders out on the gravel roads around town. It was made with support from the region's tourism association and two bike brands, it's a polished look at what a stay built around bikes can be like. Since filming, wildfires have hit the area hard, with an evacuation order and homes and businesses lost. The inn came through fine, but the community has a hard road ahead. It's a great time to consider making the trip and supporting local businesses along the way. Video on YouTube → October 2026 Dispatch Oct 2 Nine riders from Building Momentum Bikepacking rode from Winlaw along the Slocan Valley Rail Trail to lunch in Slocan, then climbed to camp at the Little Slocan Lake rec site. They hung their food in a tree. Ride report on Substack → October 2026 Dispatch Sep 28 A northern BC rider linked the Babines loop to Telkwa Pass: 205 km over three and a half days, including 30 km of purpose-built alpine singletrack. Cronin Pass still had snow in mid-July. Their tip: if you time it right, you can take VIA Rail from Terrace back to Smithers. Trip report on Reddit → October 2026 Dispatch Sep 11 Eden Sun's second bikepacking trip: 400 km over four days, along the Juan de Fuca coast to Sombrio Beach and back through Lake Cowichan. Three crashes and two falls along the way, and a bus to get past a stretch closed to bikes. Trip report at the UBC Varsity Outdoor Club → October 2026 Dispatch Sep 22 A photo trip into the Valhallas near McKean Lakes, then down to Burton on a recently decommissioned ATV road. No bears, though lots of bear scat. Trip report on Reddit → October 2026 Dispatch Sep 18 Twenty-four Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society riders based themselves in Penticton for a week of hub-and-spoke riding: Summerland backroads past the Trout Creek Trestle, Oliver and Okanagan Falls, and a last ride through the Little Tunnel to Naramata, just after the Bald Range fire. Trip report in the CCCTS Newsbrief → October 2026 Dispatch Aug 12 Kate Bradley rode about 2,190 km of the Great Northern Bikepacking Route in 43 days, through Nelson and Fernie. Her rear hub failed at Elk Pass, on the Alberta border, and that ended the trip. Trip summary on Substack → October 2026 Dispatch Mid-September Heading for the Tsawwassen ferry? The free bike shuttle through the George Massey Tunnel has moved, it now picks up southbound riders at the Highway 99 on-ramp at Steveston Highway, not Rice Mill Road. Each trailer takes up to eight bikes, and e-bikes under 25 kg are fine. Schedule → September 2026 Dispatch Oct 17 and Oct 24 BC votes twice this fall: local elections October 17 and the provincial election October 24. Going in, local governments at the Union of BC Municipalities convention voted on two asks for the province that matter for cycling. title: Calling everyone who loves exploring BC by bike!
desc: We're starting by listening. Subscribe, tell us what you know, and help us build BC into one of the best places in the world to explore by bike.
body: Home / Field Notes / Calling everyone who loves exploring BC by bike! Calling everyone who loves exploring BC by bike! May 27, 2026 Lower Seymour Conservation Reserve, North Vancouver, BC The BC Cycle Tourism Society wants to make British Columbia an easier, safer, and more welcoming place to explore by bike. We're starting with building out practical information for riders, communities, and businesses. We'll share more soon about our plans and structure... but we don't want to wait until everything is finished before we start listening. A great bike trip is made of two pieces, right? A beautiful, interesting place. We have that covered: BC is incredible. The other piece is the people you meet along the way. So we're starting with an invitation: we'd love to hear from you. Subscribe, and tell us what interests you # The simplest way to help right now is to sign up for the newsletter . Knowing there is an audience for this work helps when we talk with communities, tourism organizations, businesses, funders, and partners. It shows that people care about making BC a better place for cycle touring (which for us absolutely includes bikepacking, rail trail explorations, scenic road treks, and everything in between). Delta, BC When you subscribe, there's a place to tell us what interests you. Please do: a human reads every response. Hi, I'm Heather :) You can instead email me directly at heather@bccycletourism.ca . Tell us what you know # If you see something wrong, missing, or confusing, please let us know. We also want to know what's ready in your community, and what isn't yet. Where is the best coffee shop stop? Where can riders refill water in the middle of nowhere? Which businesses are happy to let cyclists charge their phones or the e-bikes? What looks fine on a map, but is not actually great for a loaded bike? This helps us improve BC Bike Stops , our developing directory of places that are useful and welcoming for cycle tourists. Check it out and let us know what you think. Tell us what would help you ride more of BC # What information would help you get out on your bike and explore another part of the province? What advocacy issues matter to you? What rules, gaps, missing connections, or outdated assumptions make cycle tourism harder than it needs to be? Help us find the right people # Cycle tourism sits between recreation, transportation, tourism, small business, community development, and stewardship. The right conversations matter. If there is someone in your community we should talk to, please let us know. That might be a tourism organization, local government staff person, campground operator, cyclist-welcoming business, bike shop, trail society, cycling club, chamber of commerce, visitor centre, Indigenous tourism organization or community contact, or quiet local expert who just knows how things really work. Introductions are incredibly helpful. Share photos, stories, and evidence # Lazy Boy Trail, Kamloops, BC BC is so pretty, and real trip photos beat stock art any day. If you have BC photos of ferry crossings, small-town stops, beautiful views, or real life on the road, send them our way. Please only share photos you own or have permission to share, and let us know how you would like to be credited. We'd also love to hear your stories of cycle camping and bike travel in BC. Where did someone make room for you? Where did a small kindness change the day? Where did a policy, missing connection, or lack of information make the trip harder than it needed to be? Those stories matter. They help us understand what is happening on the ground, and they may help us frame the case to policy makers, funders, and partners. Want to help in a hands-on way? # If you've got some time to spare, we'll need help manually checking listing accuracy and connecting with key businesses, campgrounds, and services that may be a good fit for BC Bike Stops. If you'd like to review listings, confirm details, or make friendly introductions, please get in touch. We'll provide guidance so the outreach is clear and consistent. Do you edit OpenStreetMap? Vancouver and Victoria have great coverage of bike parking, public washrooms, and water fountains but they aren't as well captured elsewhere... more data helps us and many others too. If you are a business or organization in the cycle tourism sector, we'll also be rolling out an Industry Partnership program, including some founding partner opportunities. Stay tuned. We don't have a bank account set up yet, but financial support will be welcome later. We won't be issuing charitable tax receipts (tourism isn't a charitable purpose), but donations, sponsorships, and in-kind support will help us build practical resources for cycle tourism in BC. Keep in touch # We have big plans for the next year: more routes, more digital tools, more partnerships, and more ways to help BC become one of the best places in the world to explore by bike. For now, we're starting by listening. Subscribe , send us what you know, tell us who we should talk to, and check back in as this grows. We'd love to build it with you. — Heather

title: Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore.
desc: Quebec and Ontario figured this out years ago. BC Bike Stops is a business directory built for what touring cyclists actually need to know.
body: Home / Field Notes / Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore. Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore. May 27, 2026 Whistler, BC When I planned my ride on the Sea to Sky Trail with my family, I had questions I couldn't fully answer from my desk. Would the hostels have somewhere to store our bikes inside overnight? Would the buses take three bikes? The Squamish Connector said two maximum. SkyLynx would take three but only bagged… what kind of bag, exactly? We found out, eventually. The Whistler hostel had a ski room. The Squamish hostel had locked cargo containers. The bus took all three bikes despite what the website said. I overnighted a bike bag from Amazon and packed my bike in a parking lot. Every answer required a phone call, an email, or a calculated guess. Every touring cyclist in BC is doing the same detective work. That's the problem BC Bike Stops is designed to fix. What we built, and why # Quebec figured this out a long time ago. Their Bienvenue cyclistes! program has been running for decades, and 31% of overnight cycle tourists in Quebec adapt their itinerary based on Bienvenue cyclistes! certification. Ontario By Bike has done the same since 2007 and now has over 1,600 certified businesses. BC has had pieces of this, GoByBike BC's directory among them, but nothing built for touring. Until now. BC Bike Stops is the BC Cycle Tourism Society's accreditation for businesses that serve bikepackers and cycle tourists well. Seven categories, criteria written for what each one needs. The part I care about: every listing tells you what you're getting before you arrive. Squamish Adventure Inn, Squamish, BC For accommodations, secure indoor overnight storage is required. Not a bike rack out front. The arrangement gets described in the listing, so you know whether it's a locked room, a garage, or bikes-in-rooms before you book. (Whistler hostel: would have passed.) Campgrounds commit to always having space for self-contained cyclists arriving by bike. Not "we'll try." A real commitment, for groups up to six, for one night. Restaurants have to give you somewhere to park where you can keep an eye on your loaded bike. Anyone who's parked a fully loaded bike at a rack 2 blocks away while trying to enjoy lunch knows why. Squamish, BC And transportation — buses, ferries, shuttles, luggage transfer — is its own category in our criteria, with the listing telling you about bagging requirements, advance booking, and bike fees. (SkyLynx: would have told me about the bag.) How it works # Apply through our website. We review applications ourselves. You'll hear from us. Approved businesses appear in the directory, filterable by category, region, and the amenities that matter to a touring cyclist. If you run a business that's great for cyclists, Apply for accreditation → . If you know one, send them our way. If you're planning a trip, search the directory → . We built these criteria for cyclists like the three of us, sorting out bike bags in a Whistler bus loop ... and cyclists like you. If we missed something, tell us: contact us → . — Heather ** Bikes on BC buses and ferries is its own saga! More in a future issue. ** Sources: Bienvenue cyclistes! attestation program , Vélo Québec; Ontario By Bike business directory , Ontario By Bike.

title: HOW TO: Take your bike on a coach bus
desc: Coach buses are one of BC's most underrated tools for cycle tourists: economical, low-carbon, and they usually accept bikes. Here's how to pack and ride along.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Take your bike on a coach bus HOW TO: Take your bike on a coach bus May 27, 2026 Vancouver Pacific Central Station, Vancouver, BC Coach buses are one of BC's most underrated tools for cycle tourists. They're economical, reasonably low-carbon, and they usually accept bikes. With a bus, you can ride point-to-point without a car. Coach services in BC # eBus has the most extensive network for cyclists. BC stops include Vancouver, Surrey, Chilliwack, Hope, Merritt, Kamloops, Salmon Arm, Sicamous, Armstrong, Vernon, Kelowna, Revelstoke, Golden, Quesnel, Williams Lake, and Prince George. Bike fee: $30. Rider Express runs two BC-relevant routes: the Vancouver–Calgary corridor (Vancouver, Surrey, Abbotsford, Chilliwack, Hope, Merritt, Kamloops, Salmon Arm, Sicamous, Revelstoke, Golden) and a separate Kelowna–Salmon Arm route (Kelowna, Vernon, Armstrong, Enderby, Salmon Arm). Bike fee: $60, or $50 if booked online in advance. YVR Skylynx runs Vancouver to Squamish to Whistler. One bike per passenger is free. All three of these operators require your bike to be in a bag or box for transport, which we cover below. IslandLink unfortunately DOES NOT ACCEPT BIKES . BC also has several regional coach and shuttle operators... many of them don't require special bike handling, just show up with your bike and put it on the rack. NOTE: E-Bikes have different policies not covered here. Bus coach at Bay 6, Vancouver, BC Step by step # 1. Buy your ticket. Specify you are bringing a bike. 2. Decide if you are going to box or bag your bike. We'll cover boxing in a different how-to. The advantage to bagging a bike is that the bag is more portable, so it's easier to bike to or from the bus station. 3. Get a bike bag. We've had good luck with a large one made of sturdy material: the "Bike Carry Bag Bike Travel Case for 26-29 inch Folding Bike MTB Road Bike Transport Carrying Case" , the 29-inch version, for $60.99 on Amazon.ca. It's also available directly from the manufacturer Rhinowalk as the "27.5 inch/700C Portable MTB Storage Bag" for about $60. It fits a straight-bar bike or a drop-bar bike. 4. Bike to the bus station with the bike bag. Bike and bag rolled up at the station 5. Take all the bags off your bike , but you can probably leave your racks and accessories on it. 6. Turn your front handlebars sideways , so they are parallel to your bike. On a drop bar bike you may also have to rotate the curl of your handlebars so they tuck in a bit. Here is a video on how to do that. Handlebars rotated parallel to the frame 7. Take off your front wheel. 8. Put your bike in the bike bag , minus the front wheel. Front wheel removed, bag laid out beneath 9. Pad the disc brake rotor of your front wheel (I used spare bike shorts... try not to touch or get oils on the shiny rotor part) if you have disc brakes, then put the wheel in the bike bag beside your bike frame. Use a bungee cord to secure it to the frame if you want. Front wheel beside the frame inside the bag Bungee-cording the wheel to the frame 10. Zip up the bike bag and you are ready to go! No need to remove the pedals with this size of bike bag, take off the seat, or do anything else fancy. Because you are going to be with your bike for almost all of its movement, we haven't found it necessary to pad the bike within the bag. Note: if your bike is a fragile, expensive go-fast bike, you may want to pad it more. Zipped and ready 11. Kill a bit of time! In our experience, packing the bike into a bag takes less than 20 minutes after you've done it a few times. Give yourself extra time to decrease stress, but you probably won't need it. 12. Carry the bike in its bag (awkward! but it has handles you can put over your shoulder) to the ticket taker, then to the side of the bus , along with your other luggage. 13. The bus driver will load your bike bag into the bottom of the bus. Loaded into the luggage compartment 14. Enjoy your trip! Look out the window and admire beautiful BC. 15. When you get to your destination, the bus driver will take the bike out of the bottom of the bus for you. Arrived in Kamloops, BC 16. Put your front wheel back on, straighten out your handlebars, roll up your bike bag, and cycle off into your adventure. Arrived in Kamloops, BC Accurate as of May 2026.

title: HOW TO: Keep your drivetrain happy on a multi-day ride
desc: Mat from Trip Longer cleans his chain every night on tour, and it takes five minutes. Here's his routine.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Keep your drivetrain happy on a multi-day ride HOW TO: Keep your drivetrain happy on a multi-day ride July 27, 2026 Five minutes of care at the end of each riding day keeps your bike shifting smoothly for the whole trip. Mat Leblanc of Trip Longer filmed his nightly routine at camp, and it's the best short demo of trail-side drivetrain care we've seen: View this reel by @trip.longer on Instagram The routine # As Mat runs it: Prop the bike so the pedals can spin freely. Wipe down the chain with a rag. He keeps his in a ziplock bag so it doesn't dirty everything else. Get the derailleur's jockey wheels and the front chainring while you're in there. Shake the chain lube well, find the master link so you know where you started, and give every link a dab. Backspin the pedals about a dozen times to work the lube in. One last wipe of the chain, then let it sit overnight. Ready to ride in the morning. Why bother? Dust and chain lube mix into a fine grinding paste that wears out cassettes and chainrings surprisingly fast. A nightly wipe-and-lube costs you five minutes and saves your gear, especially on BC's gravel and rail trails. About Mat and Ali # Mat Leblanc and Ali Becker are the West Kootenay couple behind Trip Longer. They created several of the routes BC bikepackers ride, including the Great Granby Loop and the Lakes and Hot Springs Loop, and in 2024 they became two of the first three people to ride the 15,000 km Great Northern Bikepacking Route across Canada. Follow them at @trip.longer for honest, useful posts from the road.

title: HOW TO: Take your bike in a taxi or rideshare
desc: No bike rack required. With a little prep, a bagged bike rides fine in a cab, an Uber, or a Coastal Rides car.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Take your bike in a taxi or rideshare HOW TO: Take your bike in a taxi or rideshare July 27, 2026 Sometimes the last 10 km are the hard ones. The bus depot is across town, the ferry leaves early, a wheel died, or the forecast turned. A cab or rideshare can get you there, bike and all. It goes best when the driver knows the bike is coming and it doesn't look like a hassle. Both halves of one travel day: the taxi and the bus it was catching. Kamloops, BC Tell them early # Drivers say no to surprises, not to bikes. Give the heads-up before anyone is standing at the curb. For taxis, skip the app and phone the dispatcher. When I tried to order a van through the taxi app in Kamloops it took ages to confirm; one phone call later a car was there in 10 minutes, and my bagged bike rode flat in the back of an ordinary Toyota Prius v wagon, backpacks and me along too. Say this on the phone: "I have a bike, packed small and clean, and one passenger. I need a car it'll fit in, like a hatchback please." Ready for pickup Uride's options in Kamloops, July 2026: an XL tier and a Pickup Notes field For app rides, pick a large car (see below) then use the text fields. Uride has a Pickup Notes box right on the booking screen, so the driver knows before they accept. On Uber or Lyft, message the driver once the ride matches. Message this in the app: "I have a clean bike and one passenger, ok?" We've never had a driver decline. Coastal Rides makes it easiest of all: when you request a ride, their app lets you specify how many bikes you're bringing, helping match you with drivers who have bike racks. The exception to booking ahead is the airport taxi lineup, where the fleet comes to you: in most major cities it works to just wait in line for a minivan taxi; a hatchback works too if you don't have a bike box. Shrink the bike # Match the prep to the vehicle: Van or a rideshare XL showing up? Your bike will probably fit without any dismantling, even in a bike box. If it isn't in a box, your prep is a clean-up: wipe the frame and tires, and bring a garbage bag or old towel for under the chain. Clean is all the prep there is. Ordinary car? Front wheel off, seats down, drivetrain side up. Fits more often than you'd think, hatchbacks included. You'll probably have to sit in the front seat, which means if you are travelling with someone you may each need a car. Want the guaranteed yes? A soft bike bag. Wheel off, bike in, zip closed: now it's luggage, not a bike, and you can feel the driver relax when they see it. We use the Rhinowalk 27.5 inch/700C bag (about $60, also on Amazon.ca ). Five minutes, full step-by-step in our coach bus how-to . A bagged bike, flat in the back of a Kamloops Cabs Prius v A cardboard bike box is the exception: boxes only really work in vans. Phone ahead and ask for one, or at the airport wait in the lineup for a minivan to cycle through (intended ;) ); most major airports have plenty. Who to call # Taxis , everywhere in BC. Phone ahead, especially for early departures. Coastal Rides on the Sunshine Coast, Sea to Sky, Tofino and Ucluelet, and much of Vancouver Island. A BC-grown, accredited BC Bike Stop that actively courts cyclists, down to suggesting point-to-point rides in their own bike road trip guide . Uber and Lyft in Metro Vancouver and beyond; request an XL for extra room. Uride in Kamloops, Kelowna, Vernon, Penticton, Nanaimo, Courtenay and Comox, and Prince George, with an XL tier. Know before you call. We track the taxi and ride-hail operators we've found bike information for in the directory: taxi and ride-hail listings on BC Bike Stops . Had a ride, or found a policy we're missing? Tell us and we'll add it. Kami Cabs, Kamloops, BC Last tips: allow extra time, keep the greasy side away from the seats, and tip like someone who wants the next cyclist to get a yes too. Also check out our tips on taking your bike on a coach bus in case you are going further afield.

title: BC road rules are being rewritten
desc: BC is consulting on changes to the Motor Vehicle Act. Most of the attention goes to city streets. Here are five proposed changes that matter most when you're touring.
body: Home / Field Notes / BC road rules are being rewritten BC road rules are being rewritten July 29, 2026 Gitwinksihlkw, BC · Photo: Marcus Paladino You're descending into Hope on Highway 3. A truck passes at 110 km/h, close enough to feel. Whether that pass is safe, legal, or enforceable depends on BC's Motor Vehicle Act (MVA), a law written mostly with cars in mind. That law is being rewritten. The province amended it in 2024 to require a minimum passing distance, and consultations on the next round of changes are underway now. Two BC cycling organizations, HUB Cycling and the BC Cycling Coalition, have put forward 25 recommendations for what those changes should be. Their highest-priority recommendations are strong: 30 km/h default limits on neighbourhood streets, no right turns on red, and a three-second following distance behind people on bikes. We read all 25 with a different rider in mind. Not the commuter on Commercial Drive, but the person three days into a loaded tour, on a rural highway, crossing a rail corridor, rolling into a town they've never seen. Cycle tourists spend long days on roads where there are no protected bike lanes, only the choices made by the people driving around them. Some of the recommendations that matter most for that rider sit well down the urban priority list. Here are our five. Space at railway crossings # Rail crossings can be hazardous for cyclists, especially when tracks cross the road at a shallow angle. Touring riders often need to move across the lane to line up a safer crossing, and doing that with a vehicle close behind can be one of the most stressful moments on a ride. At one rail crossing in Tennessee, redesigning the approach so cyclists crossed the rails at a steeper angle reduced observed single-bike crashes by 98 percent. Recommendation 23 would require drivers to give cyclists room to cross railway tracks and cattle guards safely. Side-by-side riding # Pairs and groups tour together, yet current law effectively requires single file. That makes nearly every touring group technically offside and gives impatient drivers a pretext. Recommendation 17 would make riding two abreast legal where it's safe. Dangerous driving by large vehicles # In the city, the answer to traffic danger is protected infrastructure. On a rural highway there usually isn't any. Safety depends on whether the driver of the truck gives you room. Recommendation 13 would lower the threshold for licence suspension, raise fines for the largest vehicles, and make retraining routine after repeat offences. Stop signs as yields # On a multi-day ride you stop at a lot of empty rural intersections. The "Idaho stop" lets cyclists treat a stop sign as a yield: slow, look, proceed if clear. Idaho's cyclist injuries dropped 14.5 percent in the year after the law took effect, and HUB Cycling already advocates for it here. Recommendation 11 would bring it to BC. Safer highway speeds # The speed gap between a loaded bike and highway traffic is largest exactly where cycle tourists ride. Recommendation 10 would expand GPS-aware speed limiters: the vehicle knows the local speed limit and resists being driven far past it. The European Union already requires them in new vehicles. The full list, with our take on all 25, is in the appendix at the bottom of this page. None of this replaces the urban priorities. It's the same reform, seen from a loaded bike on an unfamiliar road. Have your say # The BC Cycling Coalition (BCCC) is surveying riders to shape what goes to the province, and they'll be sharing the results with government. You need to be a BCCC member to take the survey; joining is free and takes a minute. Take the survey . They especially need to hear from people who ride outside the cities. — Heather Appendix: all 25 recommendations, through a cycle tourist's lens # The full list of HUB Cycling and the BC Cycling Coalition's 2024 Motor Vehicle Act reform recommendations , presented in their original order, with our take on what each one means for people touring BC by bike. # Recommendation Our take 1 Default 30 km/h limit on local streets without centre lines Moderate. Every tour passes through towns, and slower streets make unfamiliar ones gentler. Mostly a residential-street change. 2 No right turns on red for motor vehicles Moderate-high. Removes a common conflict point at the intersections you meet entering and leaving town. 3 Welcome wheelchairs and mobility scooters on cycling routes Low for touring specifically, though it makes shared paths more welcoming for everyone. 4 Allow small children on sidewalks at walking speed Minimal for touring. Matters for families, not multi-day trips. 5 Three-second following distance behind vulnerable road users High. Being followed too closely by fast traffic is a familiar experience on rural highways. An enforceable buffer matters most where there is no bike lane to retreat to. 6 Fines for blocking bike lanes, with automated enforcement Moderate. Mostly protects urban bike lanes. Relevant when your route crosses a city. 7 Let cyclists use the pedestrian head-start signal at intersections Moderate. Simpler intersections help riders who don't know them. 8 Remove the mandatory adult helmet law Mainly affects spontaneous and urban visitor cycling, especially bike share. Touring riders generally bring helmets, so the impact on multi-day trips is small. 9 Make "elephant's feet" crossings a provincial standard Low. A consistency fix with a small benefit at town crossings. 10 Expand GPS-aware speed limiters High. The speed gap between bikes and traffic is biggest on the rural highways where tours happen. Anything that brings vehicle speeds down there cuts the worst risk. 11 Stop sign as yield for cyclists (the Idaho stop) High. Touring means hundreds of rural stop signs. Slowing and proceeding when it's clearly empty beats coming to a complete stop at every one. HUB Cycling already advocates for this. 12 Allow passing on the right on shoulders and bikeways Low. A technical legal fix, rarely an issue on touring routes. 13 Stronger penalties and retraining for dangerous driving, higher fines for the largest vehicles High. On a rural highway there is no protected lane, just the driver's choices. Heavy vehicles pose one of the greatest risks to touring cyclists on rural highways. 14 Allow bicycles in rightmost bus lanes Low. Urban only. 15 Modernize cyclist signalling rules Low. A clarification, though a welcome one on a loaded bike when taking a hand off the bars is unsafe. 16 Clarify right-of-way at roundabouts and traffic circles High. Roundabouts are increasingly common in resort towns, and visitors often aren't sure who yields to whom. Clear rules help everyone. 17 Allow side-by-side riding where safe High. Pairs and groups tour together, and the single-file rule makes that technically illegal, which some drivers treat as an invitation. 18 Require side guards on heavy trucks High. Side guards reduce the risk of cyclists being pulled beneath turning trucks. Particularly relevant where touring cyclists and heavy vehicles share the same road. 19 Drivers must yield to a cyclist continuing through an intersection High. Getting cut off by turning vehicles is a constant hazard when you're following a route through unfamiliar intersections. 20 Tighten safe passing to 1.5 m at speeds under 50 km/h Moderate. Since 2024, drivers are required to give you 1.5 m at highway speeds but only 1 m in town. This would make the full 1.5 m the rule everywhere. 21 Clarify that cyclists ride as near to the right as is safe , not as far right as possible High. Loaded bikes need room to avoid debris, grates, and rough shoulders. Legal clarity protects riders who are already doing the right thing. 22 No duty to pull right just because a driver honks Moderate. A horn should not be able to legally push you into the gravel. 23 Drivers must give cyclists space to cross railway tracks and cattle guards Very high. Touring riders sometimes need to move across the lane to line up a safer crossing. Having room to do that matters. Especially relevant on rural roads with rail crossings or cattle guards. 24 Rename the Act to the "Road Safety Act" Symbolic. No practical effect on a ride. 25 Let cyclists proceed past the stop line to trigger a signal Low, but real: plenty of signals never detect a bicycle. Sources: Modernizing the BC Motor Vehicle Act , HUB Cycling and BC Cycling Coalition (2024); rail crossing research, University of Tennessee ; stop-as-yield fact sheet, NHTSA .

title: 145 places in BC that want you to visit with your bike
desc: The first 145 accredited places are live on BC Bike Stops. No paid placements, and nobody gets in just by asking. Each one showed us, in their own words, how they welcome cyclists.
body: Home / Field Notes / 145 places in BC that want you to visit with your bike 145 places in BC that want you to visit with your bike July 30, 2026 Smithers, BC · Photo: Andrew Strain We hit a milestone this month: the first 145 accredited places went live on BC Bike Stops. These aren't paid placements or self-nominations we took on faith. Each one earned it the same way: by showing us, in their own words, how they welcome cyclists. Red Beard Cafe in Kamloops was one of the first to be accredited. "Red Beard is just off the Rivers Trail on the flat North Shore of Kamloops. We have many bike racks, and locks if you forget yours." Locks if you forget yours. That's exactly the kind of detail we were hoping to find. Red Beard Cafe, Kamloops, BC · Photo: Red Beard Cafe In Vancouver, Our Community Bikes has been fixing bikes and teaching people to fix their own since long before we showed up. "We strive to create an environment where all people feel safe, included and respected." Our Community Bikes, Vancouver, BC · Photo: Our Community Bikes And Accent Inns has made bike-friendliness a chain-wide promise across five BC locations. "Love your bike? Bring it to your room." There's also a wash station and a 37-piece tool kit. It's not just cafes, shops, and hotels. At The Butchart Gardens , "it is always a pleasure for us to welcome bikers." And Kelowna's Okanagan Heritage Museum encourages visitors to arrive by bike. The full directory now covers more than 18,000 places across BC, from water refills to welcoming beds. New to BC Bike Stops? We introduced the program in our launch announcement . The accredited ones are where someone has gone further and put it in writing, on their website or to us directly. Know a business that belongs on the list? Send them to bccycletourism.ca/apply . — Heather

title: The Trailside Buffet: a cyclist's guide to BC's wild berries
desc: Late August is huckleberry and blackberry season. What to look for, where and when to find it, and where picking is actually allowed.
body: Home / Field Notes / The Trailside Buffet: a cyclist's guide to BC's wild berries The Trailside Buffet: a cyclist's guide to BC's wild berries August 30, 2026 Hikers may get the close inspection, but nobody covers more berry habitat in a day than a cyclist. Fifty kilometres of trail is fifty kilometres of sunny, disturbed edge: old rail grades, road shoulders, clearing margins. Which happens to be exactly where berries thrive. We ride through a buffet most of the summer without noticing. Late August is peak season for two of the best. Here's what's ripe now, what to look for, and what's already done for the year. That part's for next summer. One rule before anything else: If you're not sure, don't eat it. Every berry below made this list because it has no dangerous lookalikes, and a free app like Seek by iNaturalist helps while you're learning. Ripe right now (late August) # Black huckleberry Black huckleberry. Photo: Jason Hollinger, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0) Interior mountains Vaccinium membranaceum , native When: late July to September; August is the classic month, later at high elevation Where: open subalpine slopes, roughly 1,000–1,800 m: Kootenays, Okanagan highlands, Interior ranges Many British Columbians will tell you this is the best-tasting berry in the province: intense, dark, almost wine-like. The berries hang singly on the stem, blue-black to dark red. If you're climbing, you're in huckleberry country. Blackberries, both of them Himalayan blackberry. Photo: Ragesoss, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) Trailing blackberry. Photo: Leslie Seaton, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0) Coast & southern lowlands Rubus ursinus (native) and Rubus armeniacus (introduced) When: in season from midsummer into fall; late August is prime, and the Himalayan peaks into September Where: low-elevation roadsides, rail-trail margins, and forest edges, coast to southern Interior BC has two. The trailing blackberry (Rubus ursinus) is our native: a slender vine hugging the ground at forest edges, with small berries that beat the big ones on flavour. The Himalayan blackberry (Rubus armeniacus) is the introduced one, those towering, arching thickets that line low-elevation roadsides and rail trails from the coast to the southern Interior, famously crowding the Galloping Goose and Lochside trails near Victoria. Telling them apart is easy once you know the tells: Himalayan grows thick, ridged canes taller than you are, leaves in fives, and big plump berries; trailing stays at ankle height on thin stems with a whitish, waxy coating, leaves in threes, and smaller fruit. The Himalayan is officially an invasive plant, which means eating as many as we can hold is a public service. Not actually from the Himalayas. The Himalayan blackberry has never been near the Himalayas. It's native to Armenia and northern Iran, and it got here through the famous California plant breeder Luther Burbank, who in 1885 grew seeds that had been shipped to him from India, so he called his prize new berry the "Himalaya Giant." By 1894 he was marketing it to growers in the damp Pacific Northwest, where it promptly hopped the garden fence. Within fifty years it had run the length of the Pacific coast, and today it's BC's most widespread invasive shrub, and in practice the most-picked wild berry in the province. Salal Salal. Photo: Darren Giles, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) Coast Gaultheria shallon , native When: late July into September Where: coastal forest understory and trail margins: Vancouver Island, Gulf Islands, Lower Mainland, north coast The glossy-leaved shrub we've all ridden past a thousand times on any coastal route. The dark purple berries at the branch tips are ripe from late July into September. Eaten raw they're mild and a bit mealy; cooked into jam or syrup they're much better. Coastal First Nations have valued salal for a very long time, traditionally eating it fresh or drying it into cakes for winter. Oregon grape Oregon grape. Photo: VIEX, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) Most of BC Mahonia aquifolium , native When: late June through August Where: dry-to-moist forest understory and open slopes across southern BC Holly-like spiny leaves, dusty-blue clusters, completely unmistakable. Perfectly safe, and comically sour raw: offer one to a riding partner and watch their face. Makes an excellent jelly for anyone willing to carry some home. We just missed these: mark next year's calendar # Salmonberry Salmonberry. Photo: Kristof Zyskowski & Yulia Bereshpolova, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0) Wet coast Rubus spectabilis , native When: April through June, the first berry of the year Where: moist coastal forest and streamside thickets Raspberry-shaped berries in colours from gold through salmon to deep red, all edible at full ripeness, in wet coastal forest and streamside thickets. Wild strawberry Wild strawberry. Photo: Vintagenie, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) Most of BC Fragaria species, native When: May to July Where: meadows, roadsides, and forest edges, lowland to subalpine Tiny, and better than anything in a store. Classic strawberry leaves in threes, miniature fruit, intense flavour. Saskatoon Saskatoon. Photo: Walter Siegmund, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) Dry southern Interior Amelanchier alnifolia , native When: late June and July, a little later at elevation Where: roadsides, open forest, and dry slopes; classic Okanagan cycling terrain Sweet with a hint of almond, at home in dry Interior country. The saskatoon is also one of the most culturally significant foods in the region: in Syilx (Okanagan) tradition it is siya̟ , one of the Four Food Chiefs, and the first ripening berries are honoured in ceremony before the harvest begins. Thimbleberry Thimbleberry. Photo: Fernsebner, Wikimedia Commons (CC0) Forest edges everywhere Rubus parviflorus , native When: July into August Where: cool, part-shade forest edges and clearings at low-to-mid elevation, province-wide A soft red dome that slides off its core like a thimble. The trail's most fragile berry: eat it where you stand, because it will not survive a pannier. Wait, can we pick here? # Here's the part that surprised us: picking anything in a BC provincial park is prohibited by default , berries included. That has a very practical consequence for cyclists: the Myra Canyon trestles, the most famous stretch of the Kettle Valley Rail Trail, sit inside Myra-Bellevue Provincial Park. Perfect-looking huckleberry country. Look, don't pick. Outside the parks it's simpler. On provincial Crown land outside parks, which is much of BC's rail-trail and backroad riding, picking berries for personal use is generally permitted. On private land, ask first. On First Nations reserve land, don't forage without an invitation. Regional and municipal trails vary by operator, so check locally. Forage like a guest # Take a little, leave lots. Pick from several plants rather than stripping one, and remember we're sharing: berries are serious food for wildlife (huckleberries are a major late-summer food for grizzly bears in southeastern BC), and they're traditional foods for the people whose territories these trails cross. A handful for the ride is the right amount. The tame side of the buffet # Most of BC's berries aren't wild at all. This province grows about 95 percent of Canada's cranberries and is the largest highbush blueberry-growing region in the world. Abbotsford is the official Raspberry Capital of Canada, with the Fraser Valley producing most of the country's raspberries. All of it is rideable. In September and October, the dyke trails of Richmond and Pitt Meadows pass flooded cranberry bogs: vast ruby-red lakes being corralled by harvesters, one of the best free spectacles in BC agriculture (Let's Go Biking's Cranberry Trail route rides right through it). From mid-July through August, u-pick blueberry farms run from Langley to Chilliwack, happy to top up a pannier. June is strawberry month, late June to July is raspberry time, and a farmers' market is a good excuse for a ride in any month. Next April it starts over, with salmonberries on the wet coast. We've marked the calendar. Sources: BC Parks, Responsible Recreation ; Invasive Species Council of BC ; The Tyee on the Burbank story ; USDA black huckleberry plant guide ; Sierra Club BC EcoMap ; BC Cranberry Marketing Commission ; Statistics Canada on BC highbush blueberries ; Tourism Abbotsford . Berry photos: Wikimedia Commons contributors, credited under each image.

title: HOW TO: Plan around wildfire smoke in BC
desc: Fire season is part of BC riding now. The forecasting tools are genuinely good, BC is enormous, and a bit of planning usually means changing your trip, not losing it.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Plan around wildfire smoke in BC HOW TO: Plan around wildfire smoke in BC August 30, 2026 You've got a trip planned, and the forecast has gone that grey-orange colour. Cancel? Maybe. Here's how to think it through. The forecasting tools are genuinely good, BC is enormous, and a bit of planning usually means changing your trip, not losing it. Before you commit to a trip plan, answer two questions # 1. Where are the fires, and what's closed? The BC Wildfire Service map shows every active fire and its perimeter. EmergencyInfoBC lists evacuation orders and alerts. If your route passes near an active fire, reroute. No forecast needed for that one. If you plan in Ride with GPS, the same fire picture is available right on the planning map: turn on the wildfire layer (added August 2026) to see active and contained fires, prescribed burns, and estimated perimeters next to your route. One distinction worth knowing: a fire's perimeter, the official closures around it, and its smoke plume are three different things. A fire can be barely growing while the closures around it stay wide and firmly enforced. Closures are posted by whoever manages the land: area restrictions from the BC Wildfire Service for backcountry areas, BC Parks advisories for parks, Rec Sites and Trails BC for rec trails and forest service roads, and DriveBC for highways. (Evacuation orders and alerts are different again: they apply to communities, and they're what EmergencyInfoBC lists.) Here's what those tools look like. Every screenshot below was taken the same afternoon (August 30, 2026), and each one links to the live page. Click through and check your own route. BC Wildfire Service map: every active fire, its status, and its perimeter wildfiresituation.nrs.gov.bc.ca/map EmergencyInfoBC: current evacuation orders and alerts emergencyinfobc.gov.bc.ca BC Parks active advisories, filtered to wildfire risk bcparks.ca/active-advisories Rec Sites and Trails BC: map of closed sites and trails sitesandtrailsbc.ca Ride with GPS with the wildfire layer on: the fire picture right on your planning map ridewithgps.com DriveBC with its Wildfires layer on: closures and fire perimeters over the highway network drivebc.ca 2. Where will the smoke be? FireSmoke.ca runs the BlueSky Canada model out of the University of British Columbia (thank you, UBC): an animated forecast of where smoke will be, hour by hour, up to two days ahead. For today's actual conditions, check the Air Quality Health Index (AQHI) for the communities on your route. FireSmoke.ca: animated forecast of where the smoke will be firesmoke.ca The AQHI summary for BC: current values and forecasts by community weather.gc.ca/airquality Should I ride today? # The AQHI runs from 1 to 10+. The official guidance is written for the general population; here's how we read it for loaded touring, which is strenuous exercise for hours at a stretch: 1–3 (low): ride as planned. 4–6 (moderate): officially, most people can carry on with normal outdoor activities unless symptoms show up. Loaded and climbing is not normal outdoor activity, so consider shortening the day, easing the pace, or picking the flatter route. 7–10 (high): officially, consider reducing or rescheduling strenuous outdoor activity. For a touring day, our read: postpone, reroute, or make it a rest day. 10+ (very high): avoid strenuous activity outdoors. Smoke this thick makes it a no-riding day. If asthma, heart disease, or another condition makes you more vulnerable to air pollution, follow your doctor's advice; the guidance asks people at higher risk to cut back sooner than the numbers above. Whatever the number says, listen to your body: stinging eyes, coughing, wheezing, a headache, dizziness, or unusual fatigue are reasons to slow down or stop. Repeated exposure adds up too, so don't treat a string of moderate-smoke days as harmless just because no single day crosses a line. A well-fitted N95 can cut how much smoke you breathe when you have to be out in it. And don't ride on an old forecast: check the AQHI and the FireSmoke.ca forecast the morning you roll out, and again before a long climbing stretch in case you'll want to slow down or take some extra breaks. If your plan smokes out: remember BC is big # When one region is smoky, another usually isn't. Smoke that has settled into the Okanagan may leave Vancouver Island, the Kootenays, or the North clear, and the FireSmoke.ca forecast shows you which. So if the forecast turns before you leave, look at riding a different corner of the province instead of cancelling. Our Plan Your To and Fro pages show which buses, trains, and ferries can carry you and your bike to each region. Then bookmark the original plan. The route will still be there next year, and a community that spent this summer fighting a fire will usually be glad to see visiting cyclists in a future year when it is rebuilding its economy. What if it smokes out mid-trip? # Book accommodation you can cancel where possible. Before you leave, find out which buses or trains serve the towns on your route, so a smoky day 4 is a ride to the bus stop instead of a grind. Download offline maps of a much larger area than your planned route, so you can navigate a detour when a closure appears where cell service doesn't. And check the trail operator's own status page before setting out each day: closures from active fires, like this summer's KVR closure near Trout Creek, show up there first. One more thing about towns near a fire: even when the road is open, a community preparing for evacuation may need its roads, rooms, and groceries more than a passing cyclist does. If your resupply town is under an evacuation alert, that's a reroute. Further reading # Adventure Cycling Association's Bike Touring During Wildfire Season: What to Know and When To Bail (updated July 2026) goes deeper on health thresholds, masks, and when to abandon a trip. Note it uses the US air quality scale (AQI), which runs 0–500 rather than the Canadian 1–10+. For a longer read on how fire seasons are reshaping route choices across the West, Are Wildfires Changing Bikepacking? at bikepacking.com is worth your time. And our Be Prepared page keeps the year-round checklist: emergencies and cell coverage, conditions, wildlife, and rules of the road. If you've toured through a smoky BC summer and learned something we missed, tell us and we'll add it. Accurate as of August 2026. Screenshots taken August 30, 2026; conditions shown are that day's, not today's.

title: HOW TO: Get a bike mechanic to come to you
desc: Awkward to get your bike to a bike shop? In BC, sometimes the bike shop can come to you. Mobile repair vans don't do roadside assistance, but they can still save a touring trip.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Get a bike mechanic to come to you HOW TO: Get a bike mechanic to come to you August 30, 2026 Awkward to get your bike to a bike shop? In BC, sometimes the bike shop can come to you. Mobile repair vans don't do roadside assistance, alas, but they can still save a touring trip. Here's how it works. You might have biked past one of the big red Velofix vans, like I did, and wondered whether they'd be any use mid-tour. I stopped to ask. Mitchell from velofix Vancouver gave me the low down, then posed for photos in his rolling workshop. Mitchell in the velofix Vancouver van: repair stand, wall of tools, parts drawers How it works # 1. Find who serves your area. Skim the list below. Most of BC's mobile mechanics cover one metro region each. 2. Book online. Every outfit here takes bookings through its website: pick a service, say what's wrong, choose a time. It's an appointment, not a rescue line. Depending on the season they may have an opening tomorrow or be booked up for weeks, so give them a call to check. 3. Give the van somewhere to park. Home and office are the usual spots, but a hotel or campground works too. If your bike limps into town mid-trip, phone and ask: if the schedule has room, they may come to you on short notice. 4. Hand over the bike. The van is a complete workshop. Stay and chat while the work happens, or walk away and come back to a fixed bike. A few more things Mitchell told me about the Velofix vans: they stock a fair amount of touring bike parts, they work on e-bikes, and prices are similar to a bike shop's, with a bit more white-glove service for the difference. That matches what riders say online. The tell: a Mercedes Sprinter wearing a giant chainring Why this is worth knowing as a touring cyclist # Mid-trip, it means you don't have to figure out how to limp a broken bike across a strange town. Before a trip, it means the tune-up happens in your own driveway. Who comes to you in BC # Vancouver and the Lower Mainland Nootka Bicycle Co. — strong on e-bikes; texts you before arriving The Bike Stand VanCycle — a full shop in a truck, parts and accessories included Nomadic Mechanic — based on the North Shore Velofix — two territories: Vancouver and Richmond and Fraser Valley and Tri-Cities Sea to Sky Nomadic Mechanic — covers the corridor True Mobile Bike Mechanics — Squamish to Pemberton, mountain-bike specialty Velofix Sea to Sky — West Vancouver to Whistler Okanagan On A Roll — Kelowna McGeeCycle — Kelowna Velofix Okanagan Greater Victoria Velofix Victoria and Capital Region We didn't find mobile mechanics in every region: nothing surfaced for Vancouver Island outside Greater Victoria, the Kootenays, Kamloops, or the north. If you're headed somewhere not listed here, search "mobile bike repair" plus the town name, and tell us what you find so we can add it. Book online, and this parks outside your door Accurate as of August 2026. Thanks to Mitchell for the tour and the photos.

title: Plan Your To and Fro: which buses, trains, and ferries take your bike
desc: Pick two BC places and see every way we know to move you and your bike between them. 115 places, floatplanes included.
body: Home / Field Notes / Plan Your To and Fro: which buses, trains, and ferries take your bike Plan Your To and Fro: which buses, trains, and ferries take your bike August 30, 2026 How do you bike somewhere that is too far away to get to by bike? Drive? But then you have to find a place to park your car for a while, and it doesn't solve getting home from a point-to-point ride, and is awkward for those of us without a car. What about transit? Is there transit? Buses, trains, ferries, and floatplanes can be a lovely way to see the province. It hasn't been easy to figure out how practical it is to travel that way between two communities, let alone with your bike in tow. But now it is :) Doesn't Google Maps already do this? # Surprisingly, no. Ask Google Maps for transit from Castlegar to Kamloops and it says, "Sorry, we could not calculate transit directions," then offers to route you there by car. The buses exist; most of BC's intercity carriers just never make it into the big trip planners. Our page for that pair shows what actually runs: a weekly Kootenay coach that does the long haul, and the one direct bus chain that breaks because its Kelowna leg ( Silver City Stagelines ), alas, won't take your bike. Sites like Rome2Rio come closer, and they were part of our inspiration. But none of them will tell you whether the bus takes bikes, whether yours needs to be boxed, what it costs, or whether an e-bike is welcome. That gap is why we built Plan Your To and Fro . How it works # Go to Plan Your To and Fro , then pick two BC places from the dropdowns. You get a page listing every way we know to move yourself and your bike between them, step by step: buses, trains, ferries, water taxis, floatplanes, carpools, even a one-way rental car where that's genuinely the only link. There are 115 places to choose from. Seattle and Calgary are in the dropdowns too, as honorary BC cities: if you live there, we'd love to make it easy to come ride here. What we don't have, at least for now, is schedules or prices on the page. We know the map, not the timetable, so each option links to the operator for times and fares so you can look those up before your trip. We do try to list whether you need to box or bag your bike, if e-bikes are ok, if reservations are required. And if you know more than we've got listed, let us know so we can add it to the tool. When you'd reach for it # Riding point to point. You've ridden Castlegar to Kamloops; now you and the bike need to get home . Riding a loop somewhere else. The riding is in the Kootenays but your front door isn't. Get there, ride the loop, come home. Changing plans late. A smoked-out forecast, or plain whim. The pages show which buses and ferries can move the whole trip to a clearer corner of the province; our wildfire smoke how-to covers that move in detail. Things we learned building it # BC Transit holds the province together. It shows up in the answers for more than 8 of every 10 pairings: front rack, no fee, all over BC. Obviously BC Transit isn't perfect, but it is a workhorse: thanks, bus driver. The intercity spines are alive and take bikes. Ebus and Rider Express cover the interior corridors, Mountain Man Mike's links Vancouver to the Kootenays all the way to Fernie, BC Bus North covers the highways out of Prince George, and VIA Rail checks bikes through the mountains. You can take your bike on a floatplane. Harbour Air will carry it with the front wheel off for $20 plus the weight fee of the bike, on all of their routes. Just don't book a Twin Otter on the Vancouver to Victoria route. Alas, some key carriers don't take bikes. Island Link, we are looking at you, and a few others, making some connections much more challenging. We will advocate for better bike connections in these corridors, but in the meantime the tool shows these options while showing plainly that you cannot take your bike on these carriers. Carpools and one-way car rentals fill gaps. Do you know about Poparide , the carpool platform? Poparide drivers who take bikes mark it with a bicycle icon, super easy! Where no bus or boat crosses a gap, we list one-way rental car options too. It's not just BC Ferries on the water. Hullo crosses the Strait, inland ferries are free and fun, the SeaBus views are fantastic, and water taxis let you get far from town. (Our ferry directory lists many more boats, including the international runs to Port Angeles and Seattle.) Every carrier has its own packaging rules. Ebus wants bikes bagged in cloth, not plastic. Rider Express charges $50, non-refundable. VIA Rail checks bikes as baggage, but only at staffed stations. The pages spell out each carrier's quirks so you find out at home, not at the curb. E-bikes are a patchwork. Roll onto BC Ferries freely, but Hullo says no, most airlines say no, and BC Transit takes them only under 25 kilograms with the battery carried on board. If you ride electric, read the bike facts on your option before you commit. The network goes further than we expected. The longest pair with a real answer runs from Haida Gwaii to Sparwood, the Elk Valley coal town in BC's far southeastern corner that keeps the world's biggest truck parked by the highway: 1,244 kilometres as the crow flies, chaining a BC Ferries sailing, a VIA Rail train, two Ebus legs, and Mountain Man Mike's to finish. The page for Haida Gwaii to Sparwood: 1,244 kilometres, one itinerary Haida Gwaii to Sparwood: one sailing, one train, three buses Missing info? # Behind every option is a listing in our directory with the operator's bike policy and where we found it. Things change: routes get cut, policies get rewritten, ferries go on refit. Every page has a tell-us link, and we mean it. If you find something wrong or out of date, that report fixes the page for the next rider too. Reading this from the USA? Come ride in BC! # For the sake of making it easy for you to figure out how to get here, we've included Seattle WA as an honorary BC town in To and Fro . Check out all the great ways to get here: you can take a ferry up to Victoria, a train to Vancouver, or heck even a floatplane. Come north, bring your bike, and stay awhile! Try it # Start with the trip you've been putting off because getting there seemed like the hard part: Plan Your To and Fro . We'd love to hear what you think. Accurate as of August 2026. Place counts are from the August 2026 build of the To and Fro pages.

title: Riding through Indigenous BC
desc: Plan your next BC bike trip around Indigenous cultural sites, public art, and Indigenous-owned places to eat, stay and learn along the way.
