body: Home / Field Notes / Riding through Indigenous BC Riding through Indigenous BC September 30, 2026 Hazelton, BC · Photo: Mattias Fredriksson September 30 is the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It's a day to remember the children who were sent to residential schools, and the ones who never came home. It's also a good day to think about whose land we ride on, and where our money goes when we travel. A bike gives you time for both. You move slowly, you stop in small places, and you spend your money close to where you sleep. Indigenous Tourism BC suggests choosing the Indigenous-owned lodge over the chain hotel, or a meal with an Indigenous host over a fast-food stop. Most of us are curious, too: the Conference Board of Canada found 88% of people in Canada are interested in Indigenous cultural activities. A night in a lodge isn't reconciliation. But it's a start to know whose territory you're riding through, and to spend some of your trip with the people who live there. Bike paths with Indigenous art and signs # Many paths you probably already ride have new art and signs made by local First Nations. Chilliwack, BC · Photo: Viranlly Liemena Vancouver. Next time you ride the Seawall, stop at Brockton Point in Stanley Park for the poles and Susan Point's three carved gateways. In Port Moody, five Coast Salish house posts went up along the Shoreline Trail between 2025 and this spring, one from each of five host Nations. Ride the paved path. Some posts sit on the gravel trail or the Pigeon Cove boardwalk, where you walk your bike. Nearby, the Traboulay PoCo Trail follows the Coquitlam River past "Continuum," panels made with the Kwikwetlem First Nation. Chilliwack. On the Vedder Rotary Trail, Peach Park has the Lhewá:mel Welcome Portal and Gathering Place , led by the Ts'elxwéyeqw Tribe. Victoria. Around the Inner Harbour, seven bronze spindle whorls by Songhees carver Butch Dick mark places the Lekwungen people named. A spindle whorl is the carved wooden disc Coast Salish weavers use to spin wool. Start at Songhees Point . The walkway there is for people on foot, so walk your bike from one whorl to the next. The E&N Rail Trail itself was built with the Songhees and Esquimalt Nations as partners. Okanagan. On the Okanagan Rail Trail, the gateway at Km 0 by Kalamalka Lake has panels on Syilx people, language and culture, written in n̓syilxcən. The Okanagan Indian Band's fluent speakers set the spelling, and the words are written without capital letters, as a sign of equality. The Km 0 page has audio for the pronunciations. Riding out of Kelowna, turn off at Pelmewash Parkway in Lake Country, where three sculptures by Syilx artists Clint George and Les Louis stand a short distance from the trail. Duncan, BC · Photo: Rob Wilson Cowichan. Duncan calls itself the City of Totems. Its self-guided tour follows yellow footprints painted on the streets past 43 poles. It's a walking tour, so lock your bike downtown. Look for Coast Salish artist Charlene Johnny's mural, Nanum'IyusTth'ele (A Meeting of Happy Hearts). A few things to know: some poles are meant to weather and return to the earth, so a leaning or mossy pole isn't a neglected one. Mortuary and memorial poles honour the dead. At burial grounds, like the one in Alert Bay, view from the road. And if a sign says a road or an area is closed or local traffic only, that includes you on a bike. Indigenous cultural stops in five regions # Tofino and Ucluelet ʔapsčiik t̓ašii and the Tofino multi-use path. Tofino, BC · Photo: Jordan Dyck ʔapsčiik t̓ašii is the 25 km paved path between Tofino and Ucluelet through Pacific Rim National Park Reserve. An Elders' working group from the Tla-o-qui-aht and Ucluelet First Nations named it when it opened in 2022. The name means "going the right way on the path," and it also carries the teaching to speak the truth. It's pronounced "ups-cheek ta-shee," and Parks Canada has a recording of Tla-o-qui-aht Elder Kaamatḥ, Levi Martin, saying it. Indigenous-led cycling businesses are still rare. T̓iick̓in E-bikes is one, a family business with deep roots in the Ucluelet First Nation. They rent e-bikes at the Tofino–Ucluelet junction, right where the path starts. Their hours change with the season, so call ahead (250-266-3482). You can also pick up their bikes at Tin Wis. Sleep at the Tla-o-qui-aht Nation's Tin Wis Resort , an 85-room hotel on tinwis Beach about 400 m from the Tofino path, or at the Ucluelet First Nation's Wya Point , with oceanside tent sites and hot showers on 600 acres of old growth, 1.4 km off the path. In downtown Tofino, Himwitsa Lodge shares a building with the House of Himwitsa gallery and its smoked fish store. Roy Henry Vickers' gallery , which he built in 1986, is 300 m from the path. South Okanagan The Kettle Valley Rail Trail and the South Okanagan–Similkameen bike network. The Osoyoos Indian Band's sx̌ʷəx̌ʷnitkʷ campground at Okanagan Falls is about 100 m from the Kettle Valley Rail Trail, beside the river's little falls. Ride south on the bike network to Osoyoos, where the band runs the Nk'Mip Desert Cultural Centre , a campground on Osoyoos Lake, Canada's warmest, and Nk'Mip Cellars , which calls itself the first Indigenous-owned winery in North America. All three are within about a kilometre of each other, a good argument for a two-night stop in Osoyoos. The band's sẃiẃs (Haynes Point) campground is on the same network. (The Penticton Indian Band's section between Summerland and Kaleden is closed, so you can't ride the trail down from Penticton.) Up the valley in Westbank, the Sncewips Heritage Museum and Kekuli Cafe are both worth a stop. Victoria to Port Renfrew The Port Renfrew–Cowichan loop. The route heads into old-growth country on BC's southwest coast, and Port Renfrew, where the San Juan River meets the sea, has been Pacheedaht territory for thousands of years. Their campground sits right on the route: beachfront, riverside and forest sites between two rivers, open year-round. Start the ride at Ship Point on the Inner Harbour, where Songhees Tours leaves for canoe and walking tours with Lək̓ʷəŋən hosts. North Island by ferry The Island touring route north from Courtenay, with ferries to Quadra and Alert Bay. Alert Bay, BC · Photo: Jordan Dyck From Campbell River, a short ferry reaches Quadra Island, where the We Wai Kai campground borders Rebecca Spit, and the Nuyumbalees Cultural Centre at Cape Mudge holds part of the potlatch collection that came home in 1979. Call ahead for hours. Farther north, take the ferry from Port McNeill to Alert Bay for the U'mista Cultural Centre , which holds regalia the government took after a 1921 potlatch and that has since come home. If you stay the night, the 'Namgis First Nation has fourteen cabins with kitchens. At the top of the Island, the Kwa'lilas Hotel in Port Hardy is right on the last few kilometres of the route. Kwa'lilas means "a place to sleep" in Kwak̓wala. Gwa'sala-'Nakwaxda'xw Elders chose the art and design inside, and there's a pub and restaurant downstairs. Highway 16 and Haida Gwaii Highway 16 along the Bulkley and Skeena rivers, then the ferry and the Haida Gwaii route. Near Hazelton, 'Ksan Historical Village sits on Gitxsan land where the Skeena and Bulkley meet, with a museum, longhouses and a campground, 2 km off the route. At Witset, the Widzin Kwah Canyon House Museum overlooks the canyon where Witsuwit'en people still fish. Between Terrace and Prince Rupert, Kitsumkalum's Kasiks is right on the highway with hot showers and a restaurant on site, so there's no dinner to carry. Skidegate, BC · Photo: Shayd Johnson Haida Gwaii, BC · Photo: Shayd Johnson The ferry from Prince Rupert takes you to Haida Gwaii, an archipelago the Haida have called home for at least 13,000 years. Old-growth cedar runs to the edge of the sea, the towns are small, and the art is everywhere. The Haida Heritage Centre at Ḵay Llnagaay in Skidegate has the Haida Gwaii Museum, carving sheds and a restaurant, 100 m off the route. Near North Beach, the Old Massett Village Council's longhouse cabins at Hiellen have wood fireplaces, with tent sites beside them. A few more places worth a stop These don't belong to a single route, but each is worth planning a day around. Whistler. The Squamish Lil'wat Cultural Centre in the Upper Village is under a kilometre from the Sea to Sky Trail. Kamloops. The Secwépemc Museum & Heritage Park is run by Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc. Its programs include the history of the former Kamloops Indian Residential School, which stands next to the park. North Shore. Takaya Tours takes you out from Cates Park in 35-foot ocean-going canoes, with Tsleil-Waututh guides. The North Shore bike routes get you there easily. Lillooet. On the Great Northern Bikepacking Route north of town, Xwísten Experience Tours brings you to the Bridge River fishing rocks, a salmon fishery thousands of years old, with a grill on site. Vancouver. Among the big institutional museums, the University of British Columbia's Museum of Anthropology (MOA) is the one to see. It holds a major collection of Northwest Coast art, admission is free for Indigenous visitors, and their own directions warn that the ride up to campus is hilly. Victoria. The Royal BC Museum closed its First Peoples galleries in 2022. Jonathan Hunt House and Our Living Languages have since reopened, but Totem Hall is still closed. Indigenous-owned places to stay # This is just a selection of Indigenous-owned accommodations, those near a trail. For more Indigenous businesses across BC, see Indigenous Tourism BC . Fraser Valley Fraser River Lodge , Cheam First Nation, near Agassiz. A kilometre off the Canyon to Coast Trail loop, with dining on site, Mount Cheam out the window and a resident bison herd. Vancouver Island Pacheedaht Campground , Port Renfrew. On the Port Renfrew–Cowichan loop; beach, river and forest sites, open year-round. Snaw-naw-as Campground , Nanoose Bay. Right on the Island touring route. Qualicum First Nation Campground , where the Big Qualicum River meets the sea. On Highway 19A, first-come tent sites, May to September. Puntledge RV Park and Campground , K'ómoks First Nation, Courtenay. Under a kilometre from the Courtenay Riverway and a short walk from downtown; showers and laundry. We Wai Kai Campground , Quadra Island. Beside Rebecca Spit, a paved ride from the ferry, tent sites. The Cabins at Alert Bay , 'Namgis First Nation. Fourteen cabins with kitchens, a short ride from the ferry. Kwa'lilas Hotel , Port Hardy. On the touring route's last kilometres; pub and restaurant downstairs. Tin Wis Resort , Tla-o-qui-aht Nation, Tofino. 85 rooms on tinwis Beach, breakfast included, 400 m from the Tofino path. Tsawaak RV Resort , Tla-o-qui-aht Nation, Tofino. 300 m from the path, only five tent sites, so book early. Himwitsa Lodge , downtown Tofino. Gallery and smoked fish store in the same building. Wya Point , Ucluelet First Nation. Oceanside tent sites and hot showers on 600 acres of old growth, 1.4 km off ʔapsčiik t̓ašii; reserve online, no walk-ups. Lillooet and the Fraser Canyon (bikepacking routes) Retasket Lodge , T'it'q'et community, Lillooet. A 20-room motel on a hilltop above town, right on the Great Northern. Lil'tem' Mountain Hotel , Tsal'alh Band, Seton Portage. Hotel and cabins between Anderson and Seton lakes, on the Great Northern and The Big Griz. Spapium Farm , Nlaka'pamux heritage farm near Lytton, farmed since 1882. Ten campsites on the Coast Mountains Bikepacking route. Tuckkwiowhum Campground , Boston Bar First Nation. 400 m off Highway 1, with showers and a heritage village on site. South Okanagan sx̌ʷəx̌ʷnitkʷ (Okanagan Falls) Campground , run by the Osoyoos Indian Band. 100 m from the Kettle Valley Rail Trail. sẃiẃs (Haynes Point) Campground , Osoyoos, run by the band. On the South Okanagan–Similkameen bike network. Nk'Mip Campground , Osoyoos Lake. Beach and indoor pool, a kilometre from the network; priced for RVs more than tents. Kootenays Ainsworth Hot Springs Resort , owned by the Lower Kootenay Band (Yaqan Nukiy) of the Ktunaxa Nation since 2015, right on the Kaslo–Slocan loop above Kootenay Lake. The hot pools include a 150-foot horseshoe cave the Ktunaxa have used for healing since time immemorial. Nearby, the Slocan Valley Rail Trail has panels at Slocan Narrows and Vallican about more than 3,000 years of Indigenous settlement. Highway 16 and Haida Gwaii Key-oh Lodge , Burns Lake. A 42-room hotel right on Highway 16. Witset Campground , beside the Bulkley. Showers, laundry and charging; the canyon museum is a short walk. Kasiks , Kitsumkalum, between Terrace and Prince Rupert. Right on the highway, hot showers and a restaurant on site. Crest Hotel , Prince Rupert. Gitxaała-owned since 2023. Haida House at Tllaal , Tlell. Lodge rooms, cabins and a dining room on the river, on the Haida Gwaii route. Gwaii Naay Island House , Masset. The first Haida-owned hotel in town, six rooms in a former Red Cross hospital. Hiellen Longhouse Village , North Beach, run by the Old Massett Village Council. Cedar longhouse cabins with wood fireplaces, and tent sites. More resources # The BC Bike Stops directory has an "Indigenous tourism" filter in the sidebar with three boxes: Owned, Operated, and Culture & heritage. Tick any of them and the map shows only those places, in every category from campgrounds to cafes. That link opens it with all three ticked. Zoom in on your route to see what's along the way. Indigenous Tourism BC has a free app , too. And read their Travel Responsibly page before a trip; it's short and good. Accurate as of September 2026.

title: Society guest on Bike Sense Podcast
desc: I (Founding Director Heather Piwowar) talked with Peter Ladner on the BC Cycling Coalition's podcast about what BC is missing, why PDF maps don't cut it anymore, and how much cycle tourists really eat. The full transcript, plus more episodes for people who love touring in BC.
body: Home / Field Notes / Society guest on Bike Sense Podcast Society guest on Bike Sense Podcast September 30, 2026 This summer I had a wonderful chat with Peter Ladner on Bike Sense, the BC Cycling Coalition's podcast. We talked about why BC doesn't have a Vélo Québec yet, why PDF maps don't cut it anymore, what cycle tourists actually spend (they eat a lot), and what the society is working on next. Thank you to Peter and the BC Cycling Coalition for having me. Links to the audio and the full transcript are below, as well as links to past Bike Sense podcast episodes with more great BC cycle tourism related content. Listen # On the BC Cycling Coalition's site Apple Podcasts · Spotify · Amazon Music More Bike Sense episodes for cycle tourists # Cycle tourism BC's Future as a Global Cycle Tourism Destination (Oct 2025). Colleen MacDonald, author of the Let's Go Biking guidebooks, on the New Zealand comparison and the economic case. Putting Nelson on the Map: Bikepacking for All in the West Kootenays (Apr 2026). Moe Nadeau on the West Kootenay Bikepacking Route Network, five routes built for everyday riders. Trails built with First Nations leadership How a First Nation Saved a Rail Trail, and Changed the Region (Jun 2026). Phil McIntyre-Paul on the Splatsin to Sicamous rail trail, and how Splatsin leadership brought the region together to buy and build it. Heron Way, Healing Way (Dec 2025). Elder Ruth Adams of Tsawwassen First Nation on the Great Blue Heron Way, an Indigenous-led route along the Fraser River and the Salish Sea. Indigenous Communities Moving Ahead with Active Transportation (Jan 2025). Chawathil First Nation Councillor Aaron Pete on the Coast to Canyon Trail near Hope. More trails and routes Riding the Okanagan Rail Trail (Jul 2023). Matt Vader of the District of Lake Country on the 50 km trail from Kalamalka Lake to downtown Kelowna. MLA Josie Osborne on Biking the Pacific Rim (Jun 2023). The multi-use trail from Tofino to Ucluelet. Rails vs Trails: Vancouver Island's 289 km Rail Corridor (Jul 2025). Alastair Craighead of Friends of Rails to Trails Vancouver Island on the old E&N line. Trailblazers Unite! Connecting the Sunshine Coast from Langdale to Lund (Oct 2024). Tannis Braithwaite on the Connect the Coast trail. The Trail Builder's Playbook (Aug 2025). Allan Kindrat on the Cycle 16 path between Smithers and Telkwa. Salt Spring's Crucial Bike Route Gap (Jul 2024). Steve New on the 180 km Salish Sea Trail loop. The Worst Place To Bike (Pender Island) Finally Gets a Bike Path (Mar 2026). Trials and Tribulations on the Trans Canada Trail (May 2025). Léon Lebrun of Trails BC. The Road Nobody Repaves: Rural BC Highways and the Active Transportation Gap (May 2026). Andy Davidoff of the Regional District of Central Kootenay on chip seal on rural highways. Transcript # Peter Ladner: Welcome to Bike Sense, the BC Cycling Coalition's podcast, where we talk about all things related to active transportation advocacy in BC. I'm your host, Peter Ladner, Chair of the Board of the BC Cycling Coalition. I hope you enjoy the show. My guest today is Heather Piwowar, the volunteer founding director of the BC Cycle Tourism Society, which was incorporated this spring. Its purpose is to unlock BC's huge cycle tourism potential, and we'll get into that. Before we do, I want to explain what a remarkable person she is: she's got an electrical engineering and computer science degree from MIT, a PhD in biomedical informatics, whatever that is, and she co-founded and grew her own multi-million-dollar nonprofit based on open data research. She's a doer, she's smart, she's passionate, and she's fun, and I'm convinced she's going to make this work. Welcome, Heather. Heather Piwowar: Peter, thank you. What an amazing introduction. I'm thrilled to be here. Peter Ladner: It's great to have you here — I've been waiting for this opportunity, because I've known about this initiative and we've been waiting until you'd got some things done that we could talk about. But before we get to that, tell me — what was your latest bike ride? Heather Piwowar: I went up to Whistler to visit some friends, and I had no idea the Valley Trail Network was so extensive — it's amazing. We biked around for days, and then, since I live in Vancouver, I brought my bike home on a coach bus, because I'm experimenting with how I can get around BC with my bike using different transportation methods. So that part was fun too. Why BC Can Win Cycle Tourism Peter Ladner: I've looked at your website and seen the part where you talk very explicitly about how you put your bike on various buses and ferries and so on. Tell me the big picture — what are you trying to do here? Heather Piwowar: We're really trying to make cycle tourism in BC explode. In New Zealand, they make a billion dollars a year on their cycle tourism economy, and New Zealand obviously has a lot in common with BC, so I really think we could do that here too. Our goal is to be a world-class cycle tourism destination, just like New Zealand and Quebec. We've got lots of the routes already — the Whistler network I was just talking about, obviously the Kettle Valley Railway, the Galloping Goose, all sorts of bikepacking routes. I consider bikepacking to be part of cycle tourism, and on bikepacking.com there are 27 routes or so in BC. You had Moe Nadeau on one of your podcast episodes — she was talking about the Kootenay network. So we've got a lot of the trail network. What we don't have is a coordination piece to market and advocate the way other places like New Zealand and Quebec do. BC hasn't had that, and that's what this society is trying to achieve. Peter Ladner: You mentioned Quebec — what do they have, and what are they doing that we're not? Heather Piwowar: Vélo Québec has existed for decades — it's a well-funded, centralized, all-things-cycling organization in Quebec. A long time ago they developed La Route Verte, their connected network system in Quebec. It didn't start off connected — it started in pieces — but they had a long-term strategy and invested in it: the trail network itself, but also the inventory of amenities along the way, like the hotels, campgrounds, grocery stores, and points of interest. They've invested over time, and we think that's what's been missing in BC. Now is exactly the time for BC to jump in and focus on this area. Peter Ladner: It sounds like it's not just a matter of having trails out there — you've got to have directions to them. You're going to be the starting point for all that. How would it work — say I'm coming from Spain and I think, "I'm a big cyclist, I want to go cycling in BC" — they go to your website, then what do they do? Heather Piwowar: Right now, there's no central place that says "BC is a great place to go do cycle tourism." There is, if you want to do mountain biking or skiing in BC, but not cycle tourism — so actually establishing that website is one of the main things that will help someone from Spain say, "Oh, BC, right, I should go there." Right now they'd have had to find the Kettle Valley Railway, for example, on their own, or the Galloping Goose, and then figure out what guided tours exist around there, or whether they'd rather do it solo and can rent a bike and figure it out themselves. We're hoping this website will pull together the routes and the amenities, get their imagination going, and then show them practically how to make it happen. It's BCCycleTourism.ca — I'll say that one more time, BCCycleTourism.ca . I know it's not very catchy, so we're actually working on a more catchy name, but that's where it is right now. What BCCycleTourism.ca Offers Now Peter Ladner: So you've built this website — what's the state of it now? Heather Piwowar: Cycle tourism is cool because it's really got two different audiences. One is the economic-driver audience, people coming from afar; the other is a recreational aspect for locals. Frankly, if you take a coach bus to some other part of the province, you count as a visitor too. Anyway, right now we're really focusing on locals coming to the website and exploring what cycle tourism there is in our province. It includes a list of routes and ways to get around the province by bike, and a list of campgrounds and hotels that welcome your bike inside your room. There's lots there already — go check it out and see what's there. It's early days, so feedback on the website is super useful. Peter Ladner: So at this point you've got the website, it's coming together, you're looking for feedback. Then what has to happen — you've got to promote it somehow. Who's going to help you promote it? Heather Piwowar: So far the society is mostly just me as a volunteer, because we don't have any funding yet. The next step is actually to start getting some funding, to build a sustainable future for the society. Funding the Work Through Tourism Peter Ladner: Where are you going to get that funding, and how much do you need? Heather Piwowar: Other countries and provinces that do this tend to have a staff of about two, three, or four people doing what's called "sector development" and sector marketing — where the sector is cycle tourism instead of golf or mountain biking or whatever. We're looking for enough funding to sustain that size of organization over the next few decades. When these other places got going, they tended to get money from a centralized government — the provincial government, or in New Zealand's case the federal government — as a jobs program, which is great. We were hoping BC might see it the same way, as an investment and jobs program, because I think the potential is there, but that's not how it's structured in BC. So we looked into how tourism is actually financed in BC, and it's through a hotel tax — about two or three percent, charged on top of a hotel bill in most communities, and that money stays in the community to fund tourism development and marketing there. We're hoping to offer services to tourism communities around BC to help them grow their cycle tourism, and in return they'd pay us, and we could use that to invest in cycle tourism around the province. Peter Ladner: I've been to some places in BC and found lots of information about cycling on their tourism websites. Are some communities already doing this well on their own? Heather Piwowar: Great point. Mountain Biking BC has done an amazing job promoting mountain biking in BC — partly because we've got great terrain, so it sells itself, but mountain biking as a sector organization has really helped push tourism around it. When we're talking about cycle tourism, we mean recreational biking — gravel biking, multi-day trips — and there are far fewer websites that talk about that. We found fewer than half the tourism websites cover it at all, and only about 25% cover it in any depth. Only three out of the 100 tourism communities in BC have digital maps or digital routes — most will show you a static PDF map. Of course, we don't navigate our cars that way anymore, and people don't navigate on their bikes that way either — the websites haven't caught up. So although you might have seen some content, it isn't nearly as pervasive, high-quality, or welcoming as we hope to build it to be. Peter Ladner: I'll ask about the content in a second — does the mountain biking association get money from the hotel tax in different regions of the province? Heather Piwowar: Good question — I'm not sure if they do. They do get some money from Destination BC, our province-wide tourism association, which has funding mechanisms for sector organizations that we hope to apply for too, in time. Moving Past PDFs With GPX Peter Ladner: You've said some communities are stuck on PDFs — basically glorified paper on a screen. But yours is going to be more interactive — how's yours going to work? Heather Piwowar: I bet a lot of your listeners use their phone to navigate on their bike, or a Garmin device, or something that gives turn-by-turn directions — either read off the handlebars or spoken aloud. That's the most common approach to cycle tourism navigation. Adventure Cycling Association — celebrating their 50th anniversary this year, the cycle tourism granddaddy of North America — is transitioning away from paper maps and PDF maps to GPX files, which display on your phone or Garmin device for navigation. It's basically like Google Maps navigation on your phone, but customizable and not tied to Google. Peter Ladner: This sounds like a whole new level of service and information for cycle tourists. Heather Piwowar: Yep, it is — but it's also just the standard people expect now. It's what European visitors expect, frankly what we should expect, and what a lot of people are already building for themselves using Ride with GPS and Komoot. But that adds a barrier. One of the things I really hope this society does is tear down barriers — make it easy for people who haven't gone on their first cycle tourism adventure to think, "I can do that, close to home or far away, without being tech-savvy." We're hoping to help with that, including through navigation. If you're a bikepacker on bikepacking.com , it's easy; increasingly a few other route-makers are making it easy too, but our tourism offices aren't — and that's not their area of expertise. One thing a sector organization brings is that expertise. So we hope to say, "Here's actually how cycle tourists do it — let us help you describe your riverfront path in a GPX file, one that passes all your farm stands selling blueberries, one that connects to your ferries. Let us help you showcase your region the way cyclists expect." Aggregating Routes and Grading Difficulty Peter Ladner: Heather, you're clearly not doing all this research yourself — I know we'll get into AI, but you have partners, or existing research you're referencing, that you're aggregating and presumably upgrading or standardizing. Who are some of the people, or what are some of the sources, you're drawing on that are particularly useful? Heather Piwowar: Thanks, Peter — I appreciate the chance to do these shout-outs. The website starts with routes that already exist and have been published by people who've worked hard to figure out where in BC is a great place to bike. We're showcasing 300 different routes right now, easy to hard, pulled from about 10 different route publishers. That includes bikepacking.com ; it includes Let's Go Biking by Colleen MacDonald, who you've had on a previous podcast episode — she's passionate about cycle tourism and is actually on the board of the society. She contributes easier routes, often single-day rides in different communities around BC. There are some routes from a maker called BT 700 — the BT stands for Butter Tart, because he started off making routes in Ontario connecting good butter tart bakeries. Clearly that's the kind of thing we want to promote here — we could have a donut version. He's got all sorts of great routes in BC too

title: HOW TO: Eat enough on a bike tour
desc: Riding all day takes a lot of food. More than most of us expect, and much more than you eat at home.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Eat enough on a bike tour HOW TO: Eat enough on a bike tour September 30, 2026 Riding all day takes a lot of food. More than most of us expect, and much more than you eat at home. Eating enough keeps your legs going, helps you recover, and keeps your mood up. How much are we talking? # Roughly, riding at a steady pace burns something like 500 to 700 calories an hour . A long day on the bike can take 3,000 calories or more, before you add hills, headwinds or a loaded bike. It's a lot. Eat every hour or two # Don't wait until you're hungry. By then you're already behind. Eat something every hour you're riding, even if it's small. Kamloops, BC · Photo: Andrew Strain Eat carbs # Racers have learned this one the hard way. Pro cyclists now eat 100 to 120 grams of carbohydrate an hour , well above the older advice of 60 to 90. You're not racing, but the lesson holds at touring pace too. In one study , cyclists rode for three hours at an easy-to-moderate effort. On water alone, two of the six gave out at two and a half hours as their blood sugar dropped. With carbs, everyone finished. For a long day at your own pace, aim for 50 to 60 grams an hour, about a banana and three Oreos, or two mandarins and a box of raisins. Bread, bananas, dried fruit, granola bars, candy and cinnamon buns all count. A touring day is not the day to go low-carb. Riding with others? Our vegan snack how-to has ideas everyone can share. Pemberton, BC · Photo: Ben Girardi Eat after a scare # A close pass from a logging truck, a skid on gravel, a dog out of nowhere. Pull over, catch your breath, and eat something. It's easier to make good decisions about what to do next when you're topped up, and a snack gives you a few minutes to settle before you ride on. Keep a package of Skittles beside the band-aids in your first aid kit for exactly this. (This is for a scare, not an injury. If someone's hurt, first aid comes first.) Eat to hunger # On a multi-day trip, listen to your appetite. If you're hungry, eat, even if you just ate. Second breakfast is a delightful part of touring. Keep eating after you get home # The hunger doesn't stop when the trip does. Expect to be extra hungry for a few days, maybe a week. Keep eating. Your body is still recovering. Accurate as of September 2026.

title: HOW TO: Snack vegan on a bike tour
desc: Portable vegan and vegetarian bike snacks, sweet and salty, that almost everyone can eat.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Snack vegan on a bike tour HOW TO: Snack vegan on a bike tour September 30, 2026 Picking up some snacks to share can feel complicated if you're travelling with people who eat differently than you. Or maybe you just want some new ideas! Here are some portable vegan and vegetarian sweet and salty bike snacks that almost everyone can eat. Wondering how much to eat? See how to eat enough on a bike tour . From the bakery # Crusty bread like baguette and sourdough is usually just flour, water, yeast and salt. Plain bagels often are too (skip egg bagels and ones made with honey). Pastries, cinnamon buns, donuts and pie crusts usually have butter, lard, eggs or milk, but lots of bakeries now label their vegan treats, so ask. From the farm stand or farmers' market # Kelowna, BC · Photo: Andrew Strain In summer and fall, BC's farm stands and farmers' markets are some of the best snack stops there are. Look for cherries from about late June, peaches from late July, and apples into late October. Most farmers' markets run one day a week, so check the day before you plan around one. From the grocery store # Sweet snacks Fruit: fresh (apples, oranges, bananas, grapes) and dried (raisins, apricots, dates). Dark chocolate: not milk chocolate. The darker it is, the less likely it'll melt on a hot day. Candy: Sour Patch Kids, Jolly Ranchers, Fruit Roll-Ups, Skittles, Twizzlers, Swedish Fish (check the label for beeswax), Cracker Jacks. Cookies: Oreos, Nutter Butters (not the fudge-covered ones), Lotus Biscoff. Bars: Larabars, MadeGood granola bars (also nut-free), most Clif bars. Salty snacks Veggies: cherry tomatoes, carrot sticks, snap peas. Nuts and seeds: mixed nuts, pumpkin seeds, roasted chickpeas, and trail mix from Vancouver Island's Own in Victoria (their West Coast Trail mix, for one). Spreads and wraps: peanut butter or another nut butter on a tortilla (squish-proof and cheap), hummus, single-serve nut butter packets. Most tortillas are vegan, but some are made with lard, so check the label. Crackers: Triscuits, Wheat Thins (Original, and Sundried Tomato & Basil). Chips: Lay's Classic, Ruffles Original, Fritos, Doritos Sweet Chili Heat, and Hardbite chips from Maple Ridge (every flavour but Honey Dijon). Packaged: roasted seaweed, pretzels and pita chips (check the ingredients), Harvest Snaps. From the gas station # On a lot of BC routes, the only store for a long stretch is a gas station. You can often still find bananas, plain chips, nuts, Oreos and Skittles there. A few label notes # Vegan means no meat, fish, eggs, dairy or honey, so watch for sneaky ones like gelatin, whey and beeswax. If your riding companions have gluten or nut allergies, check the labels for those too. Most vegan food is also kosher and halal. When in doubt, check with your eater. Accurate as of September 2026.

title: HOW TO: Store your food when you're camping by bike
desc: No car to lock your food in at night? Here's what works at BC campgrounds, from bear canisters to the bear-proof garbage bin.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Store your food when you're camping by bike HOW TO: Store your food when you're camping by bike October 7, 2026 If you arrive at a campground by car, your food goes in the trunk at night. If you arrive by bike, your whole kitchen is in your bike bags, and your bags are next to your tent. Unfortunately, the food still has to go somewhere an animal can't get at it. BC Parks says food and anything else with a smell goes in "a locked vehicle, hard-sided trailer, bear-proof cannister, or bear-resistant locker, where provided." This isn’t just to deter bears. Parks Canada calls the crows, deer, rodents, and raccoons at Pacific Rim "efficient and creative scavengers." Keeping your food (even an unopened package of chips!) in your bags isn’t enough to keep critters from gnawing through your pannier or frame bag to get to it. We’ve learned this the hard way: RIP Doritos and breakfast. Why not just keep it in the tent? # Your tent won't keep an animal out. At best, you could wake up to a hole in your tent. At worst, you've taught an animal that campsites are a good place to find food. Best: a canister or a locker # Many campgrounds have food lockers , which are metal boxes animals can't get into. Golden Ears Park , east of Maple Ridge, is one. Saysutshun (Newcastle Island Marine) Park, off Nanaimo, is another --its BC Parks page says to store all food there “including toothpaste” (!). For campgrounds without food lockers, ideally we’d all pull up with a bear-resistant canister . It's a hard plastic container with a lid that animals can't open. That said, it's too big for most bikepackers to want to carry. Bite-proof bags (like Ursack, which has versions for deterring bears, small critters, or both) can be a good substitute because they aren’t quite as bulky. No locker and no canister? Some other ideas # Ask a neighbour with a car. A car trunk counts as a "hard-sided vehicle" in both BC Parks and Parks Canada rules. Most people say yes. Ask before dark, and arrange when you'll pick it up…. you don't want your breakfast locked in someone else's car when you're ready to leave. Use the washroom or outhouse, if the door closes. Tuck your food bag into a corner where it's out of everyone's way. This works well against raccoons, squirrels, and birds, less so in bear country. Put it beside the garbage in a bear-proof garbage bin. Yes, really. Mat Leblanc of Trip Longer learned this trick from a park ranger. It isn't an official food locker, but it's one workaround bikepackers have used when the usual options aren't available: View this reel by @trip.longer on Instagram Use a clean, tightly closed bag so it doesn't end up smelling like the bin. Whatever you use # Everything with a smell goes in. That includes garbage, dishes, toothpaste, sunscreen, and the granola bar in your handlebar bag. BC Parks puts it this way: "Keep it bare when you're not there." Pack it so it’s easy. Keep the food and other smelly stuff together. It's much easier to put everything away when you aren't hunting for that last granola bar in three different bags. Don't hang your food at a frontcountry campground (BC Parks' term for anywhere within 1 km of a road). BC Parks asks campers not to do it at campgrounds, because the smell draws animals in and puts other campers at risk. Cook, eat, and clean away from your tent. For more on wildlife and staying safe out there, see our Be Prepared page. Accurate as of October 2026.

title: Who to thank for our BC trails
desc: Find out who looks after the BC trails and rec sites you rode this summer, and easy ways to say thanks this Thanksgiving.
body: Home / Field Notes / Who to thank for our BC trails Who to thank for our BC trails October 7, 2026 Ridge Meadows Dyke · Photo: Let's Go Biking Happy Thanksgiving! Whether your long weekend includes a long ride, a short ride to make room for pumpkin pie, or no ride at all, here's one more thing to be thankful for: the people who look after BC's recreational bike trails. If you rode a rail trail in BC this summer, someone cleared the fallen trees before you got there. Someone fixed the culverts, raised the money, or spent years asking for the trail to exist at all. Whether it's your local trail or a favourite stretch you discovered while passing through on a bike trip, there are people behind it worth thanking. Usually, it's a mix of people. A regional district or city might own a trail, while volunteers have spent years getting it built or turn up every spring to clear the brush. This Thanksgiving, let's pass some of that thanks along. Here's who to thank, and a few fun ways to do it. Who to thank, trail by trail # Here are the groups behind many of the trails touring and gravel riders love, with a favourite detail about each. Vancouver Island Cowichan Lake back roads. The Cowichan Lake Trail Blazers build and maintain trails on working forest land around Cowichan Lake, by agreement with the landowner. Members can join trail-building days on November 14 and December 12. Gabriola Island. Volunteers with the Gabriola Land and Trails Trust meet twice a month on Sunday afternoons to cut back brush and clear fallen trees. Log Train Trail, Port Alberni. This old rail grade is shared by cyclists, walkers, and horse riders, and it's a horse club, the Alberni Valley chapter of the Back Country Horsemen of BC , that puts in volunteer hours and grant money. The Alberni-Clayoquot Regional District leases it from the Province. Vancouver, Coast & Mountains Squamish's in-town gravel paths. Squamish Trails Society volunteers brushed, resurfaced, and realigned part of the Finch Creek Loop last year, and cleared downed trees off Loggers Creek Trail. Sea to Sky Trail, Squamish to Pemberton. The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District (SLRD) looks after it and takes donations for it. The idea began in 1991 with a volunteer society that wanted one trail linking communities from Squamish to D'Arcy. Volunteers still help build and maintain it. Through Whistler it follows the Valley Trail , more than 50 km of paved path the Resort Municipality of Whistler keeps up, clearing about 38 km of snow every winter. Vedder Rotary Trail, Chilliwack. This flat gravel loop along the Vedder River is part of the Trans Canada Trail. Kilometre 0 of the 100 km stretch to Hope is a trail pavilion near the Lickman Road parking lot. The City of Chilliwack runs it, and Chilliwack's Rotary clubs helped build it. Trans Canada Trail, Chilliwack River Valley. Volunteers from the Chilliwack Outdoor Club and Trails BC look after the 36 km from Deer Creek Bridge to Chilliwack Lake, and Paleface Pass beyond it. They put in more than 3,000 volunteer hours last year. This fall they reopened a flooded stretch near Thurston Campground, now raised high enough to stay dry all year. Bikes are welcome on the Tolmie section, between Tamihi and Anderson creeks. Thompson Okanagan Myra Canyon trestles. BC Parks runs the park. The Friends of the South Slopes have looked after the trestles and trails for more than 30 years. Remember to walk your bike across the trestles. Okanagan Rail Trail. Four owners run it together: the City of Kelowna, the District of Lake Country, the Okanagan Indian Band, and the Regional District of North Okanagan. Friends of Okanagan Rail Trail raises money and runs the trail ambassador program. Okanagan Rail Trail · Photo: Let's Go Biking Splatsin te Secwépemc / Shuswap North Okanagan Rail Trail. The Splatsin and two regional districts are building it, and it now runs 40 km from Sicamous to just south of Enderby. More than 26,000 people used the Sicamous–Mara Lake section this year. The free ferry that takes riders around the Bruhn Bridge work set a record of more than 800 trail users in one day. Donations for building and maintaining the trail go through the Shuswap Community Foundation . Grey Canal Trail, Vernon. The Regional District of North Okanagan runs it. Ribbons of Green has championed it and other Vernon-area trails for 25 years. Mission Creek Greenway, Kelowna. The Regional District of Central Okanagan runs it. The Friends of Mission Creek raised the money to buy land for the greenway. Kootenay Rockies Slocan Valley Rail Trail. The Slocan Valley Rail Trail Society looks after all 50 km under an agreement with the Province, and finished this year's fall brushing in early October. When Trans Canada Trail recognized their treasurer as one of 10 volunteers across Canada, the award paid for a pizza night for the trail's volunteers. There are donation boxes at every trailhead. Nakusp to Summit Lake rail trail. The Nakusp and Area Community Trails Society looks after the Nakusp end, where all-terrain vehicles are allowed. The Rosebery Bonanza Summit Trail Alliance looks after the non-motorized section east of Island View Road. New Denver, BC · Photo: Kari Medig Grand Forks. Grand Forks Community Trails develops and maintains the trails around town, including 17 km of crushed gravel and singletrack on the Kettle River Heritage Trail. Boundary Country rail trails, Eholt to McCulloch. Since 2015, the Trails to the Boundary Society has looked after 155 km of the Kettle Valley and Columbia & Western rail trails under an agreement with the Province. Its volunteer directors come from seven small communities along the way, including Greenwood, Midway, Rock Creek, and Beaverdell. Expect to share parts of it with ATVs. Railgrade, Rossland to Warfield. Kootenay Columbia Trails keeps it clear with a seasonal trail crew. It's rough; wider tires recommended. Skattebo Reach, Castlegar. Castlegar Parks and Trails finished upgrading this section of the Trans Canada Trail last fall to make it more bike-friendly. Coal Creek Heritage Trail, Fernie. The Coal Creek Heritage Society , Fernie Trails Alliance , and Tourism Fernie opened a new suspension bridge on the trail in June. Markin-MacPhail Westside Legacy Trail, Invermere to Fairmont. Columbia Valley Greenways led the more than $9 million project to build this 25 km paved trail, then handed it to the Regional District of East Kootenay. A local couple bought the land for one loop and donated it. It's closed for the season now and reopens May 1. NorthStar, Cranbrook to Kimberley. The two cities maintain it. The community spent five years putting a gazebo above Marysville, and volunteers wheeled the donated picnic tables up to it. Kimberley, BC · Photo: Kari Medig Northern BC Cycle 16, Smithers and Telkwa. The Regional District of Bulkley-Nechako owns and maintains it. The Cycle 16 Trail Society has raised $2.3 million toward the $7 million trail. The first section opened in 2023, and construction of the remaining sections is underway, including a planned underpass beneath Highway 16. Rec sites along our trails and resource roads # For bikepackers, the people behind the trails aren't the only ones to thank. Many of BC's simple, inexpensive places to camp depend on volunteers, too. Some of these campground operators aren't who you'd expect. The Back Country Horsemen of BC, for example, look after a handful of campgrounds as well as putting work into the Log Train Trail. A volunteer fire department runs one near 100 Mile House. The Four Wheel Drive Association of BC looks after 27, most with a few campsites by a lake or river. Some groups look after a whole string of lakes. The Lakes Outdoor Recreation Society keeps 25 campgrounds around Burns Lake. Just outside town, the local bike club, Ride Burns, runs the Kager Lake campground at Boer Mountain. Around Clearwater, a community services society looks after 17 lakeside campgrounds, and its job program lists rec site maintenance as paid work for adults with developmental disabilities. Burns Lake, BC · Photo: 6ix Sigma Productions And nearly 300 rec sites with camping and road access are "user maintained." If you stayed at one, you were the maintenance crew. Thank you. To find out who runs a site you stayed at, look it up on sitesandtrailsbc.ca . Each site's page names its operator under Contact. Ways to say thanks (no pie required) # Write a thank-you note. Two sentences is plenty. Trail volunteers usually hear about a trail when something's broken…. tell them about your good day instead :) Feed the trailhead box. The Slocan Valley Rail Trail has a donation box at every trailhead. We're all carrying less change in our saddlebags these days, so they take e-transfers and PayPal too . Join for less than the price of a pie. Island Pathways membership is $10 for life. Kootenay Columbia Trails is $10 a year. Buy a metre of trail. It costs about $160 to surface one metre of the Shuswap North Okanagan Rail Trail . Every bit helps, and gifts over $20 get a tax receipt. Trade a Sunday ride for a Sunday rake. Gabriola's trail volunteers meet twice a month on Sunday afternoons. Email them to get on the list . Be the trail's eyes. Spot a fallen tree or a washout? Tell the group that looks after it, with a photo and a specific location when you can. Leave the trailside better than you found it. Pack out what you brought, plus some litter. Tell your council you love your trail. Regional districts and cities own many of these trails, and they fund what people ask for. Riding singletrack? Mountain Biking BC's Support the Trails page will point you to local clubs – they need your support too! Know a group we missed? # The groups above are on our Trail Organizations page , with links to donate or get involved. If we missed a group that looks after a trail you love, tell us and we'll add them. Happy Thanksgiving!

title: Where can I camp this fall?
desc: Most BC campgrounds close by the end of October. Here's when they close, region by region, and where you can still pitch a tent this fall and winter.
body: Home / Field Notes / Where can I camp this fall? Where can I camp this fall? October 7, 2026 Vancouver Island, BC · Photo: Rob Wilson October can be some of the best riding of the year in BC. The roads are quieter, the leaves are turning, and in much of the province it's still dry. But – can you still camp? We checked the official pages of about 1,300 campgrounds and here's what we learned. When do campgrounds close? # This map shows every campground we could pin down, coloured by when it closes. The lighter the dot, the earlier in the fall it closes. The darkest dots are campgrounds that say they're open all year. Campground closures cluster around a few dates each year: The end of September is the big cluster. About 90 campgrounds close on September 30 or October 1; by October 1st about 220 of the campgrounds have closed. Thanksgiving Monday (October 12 this year) is the second wave of closing dates: about 70 more close by then. Mid-October and Halloween are the closure dates for most of the rest. So where should I camp in October? # It depends a lot on where you are. Here's the share of campgrounds on our map, including year-round ones, that are still open after Thanksgiving: In Northern BC, most campgrounds close early. Only about a third of the ones open on Labour Day are still open on October 1st. After Thanksgiving, about a quarter of the North's campgrounds are open. Campgrounds on the coast stay open much later. More than three-quarters of campgrounds in Vancouver, Coast and Mountains and on Vancouver Island are still open after Thanksgiving. The southern Interior sits in the middle, with about half its campgrounds open after Thanksgiving and fewer by the end of October. Campground closures roughly follow the frost. Here's each region side by side: how many campgrounds on our map are still open after Thanksgiving and on November 1st, next to a normal October from Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1991 to 2020 averages. Region Campgrounds on the map Open after Thanksgiving Open November 1 October overnight low Days with rain or snow Nights below freezing Average first fall frost Vancouver Island 178 135 (76%) 94 6 to 8°C 14 to 20 about 1 or fewer Nov 4 Vancouver, Coast and Mountains 144 119 (83%) 78 7°C 15 about 1 Nov 10 Thompson Okanagan 162 86 (53%) 39 4°C 10 6 to 7 Oct 8 to 12 Kootenay Rockies 108 48 (44%) 18 0 to 4°C 10 to 15 4 to 16 Sep 23 Cariboo Chilcotin Coast 55 26 (47%) 7 -1°C 13 18 Sep 14 Northern British Columbia 83 23 (28%) 16 -1 to 0°C 16 to 17 15 to 17 Sep 7 to 17 Weather towns: Victoria and Cape Beale on the west coast (Vancouver Island), Vancouver, Kamloops and Penticton, Nelson and Cranbrook (the frost date is Cranbrook), Williams Lake, Prince George, and Smithers. "Days with rain or snow" counts any day with at least 0.2 mm. What's the weather like? In October in BC you're mostly choosing between rain and frost. On the coast the nights stay mild, around 6 to 8°C, but expect rain on about half your days, and a lot more than that on the west coast of the mainland or the Island. In the Okanagan and around Kamloops, October is dry (about 10 wet days, and about a fifth of Vancouver's rainfall), the days are just as warm as the coast, and the nights drop to around 4°C with a frost about one night in five. In the Cariboo, the North, and around Cranbrook, about half of October nights go below freezing. Early October can be lovely in the dry Interior, provided you're equipped for freezing nights. Later in the month, you'll find more open campgrounds and milder nights on the coast. Nelson, BC · Photo: Kari Medig What about after Thanksgiving, or winter? # About 230 campgrounds on our map say they're open year-round, though "open year-round" can mean very different things. Some parks offer hot showers; others are unplowed, with little more than a pit toilet. Some private parks that stay open all winter take only RVs or monthly stays in the off-season. So we looked for ones that explicitly allow tents. We found 16 places that say on their own page that they take tents in winter: Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands Fillongley, on Denman Island Goldstream, near Victoria Jordan River (a Capital Regional District park) Narvaez Bay and Shingle Bay, in Gulf Islands National Park Reserve. Open in winter but not maintained, so you're on your own. North Park at Horne Lake (gravel road) Pedder Bay RV Park, Metchosin, near the Galloping Goose. Winter tent sites from about $48. Quinsam, at Elk Falls near Campbell River. About $11 a night, cash. Rathtrevor Beach, Parksville Sproat Lake, near Port Alberni Upper Campbell Reservoir (BC Hydro). Free, first-come, first-served. Snow is possible. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains Willingdon Beach, Powell River. In town, right on the beach, with a winter tent rate of about $27. Of everything we checked, it had the clearest winter tent policy. Shelter Point, on Texada Island (the gate is locked at night) Grace Lake (gravel forest road) Lone Duck One, in Manning Park. This is snow camping, at about 1,200 m. Thompson Okanagan Moon Shadows RV Park, Merritt, which keeps 19 tent sites open all year Services get thin in winter. Water may be shut off and the flush toilets closed, even where the campground is open. Call ahead about water so you are prepared. Vancouver Island, BC · Photo: Ben Giesbrecht Wait, that one closes when? # A few campgrounds close for reasons that have nothing to do with the weather, and one is open only in winter. Gwe Da Ts’ih , in Ts’ilʔos Park in the Chilcotin, closes in September and October for spawning salmon. It's open the rest of the year, November through August. Taylor Meadows , in Garibaldi Park, also closes in September and October, for bears. Cambie Creek , near Manning Park, is open only in winter, from early December to late March. Chute Lake Lodge , above Naramata on the Kettle Valley Rail Trail, says it closes in March and April. Can I still camp after a campground “closes” for the season? # Surprisingly, it is hard to know! We found some season information for 858 campgrounds, including ones too uncertain to map. Only 239 of them (28%) said anything about what happens after closing. Of those, 90 let you camp without services, 89 keep some services going, and 60 say no camping at all. Some leave the gate open and the taps off, but others lock them. You’re taking your chances. What's not on the map? # Lots of campgrounds aren't on the map because we couldn't find a clear season for them. Many of these are Recreation Sites and Trails BC sites. Most Rec Sites don't post a season at all. They're unstaffed, and you can use them while the road is open and there's no snow, which in practice can mean well into fall. About 430 campgrounds in the directory have no posted season, and most of them are Rec Sites. We also left off about 90 places where the information we found was weak or contradictory. Tent calling? # Check the campground's own website before you go, especially if you're travelling after Thanksgiving. And if you find a closure date we've got wrong, let us know so we can improve the directory for the next rider. You can find campgrounds along your route in the BC Bike Stops directory . Information checked in October 2026.

title: BC gifts for people who ride (and where they're really made)
desc: Gifts for people who ride, from under $5 to $300, each one labelled with where it's really made.
body: Home / Field Notes / BC gifts for people who ride (and where they're really made) BC gifts for people who ride (and where they're really made) November 27, 2026 A few of this year's picks · Photos: the makers and sellers This month I went looking for BC-made gifts for people who ride bikes. Here are about 30 fun ones, including a tee with a Sasquatch on a bike, a bear spray holder made by one person in Fernie, and coffee from a Victoria roaster that delivers by bike. Most of the bike gear that's truly made in BC comes from tiny shops, often just one or two people. Every pick says where it's made. "Made in BC" means the thing itself is built here. "Printed in BC" and "Roasted in BC" mean that step happens here. Where the maker doesn't say, I say that too. Prices are in Canadian dollars, as listed on November 20. Last chance: Two Wheel Gear , Vancouver. The company behind the pannier that turns into a backpack is closing on December 31, after more than 20 years. The panniers still in stock are $179.99 to $199.99 in the closing sale. BC company, made-in not stated. Under $10 # Myra-Bellevue Park sticker , BC Parks Foundation, $6. A park scene with an enthusiastic cyclist in it. Myra Canyon is where the Kettle Valley Railway (KVR) trestles are, so give it to anyone who rode them this summer. All the profits go to BC's parks. Made in Canada. Myra-Bellevue Park keychain , BC Parks Foundation, $8.99. The same park scene as the sticker, on a metal keychain. All the profits go to BC's parks. Made-in not stated. Bike World sticker , Kindred Coast, Vancouver Island, $6. A small vinyl sticker from an Island studio. Printed in Canada. "Bike Van Isle" sticker , Bough & Antler, Campbell River, $5. A waterproof sticker for the bottle or the frame of anyone who has toured Vancouver Island, or plans to. Made in Canada. Tandem Bike Party card , Porchlight Press, Vancouver, $6.50. A letterpress card, blank inside, for the person you ride with. Made in BC. Instant coffee pouch , Lark Coffee Roasters, Creston, $3.50. One cup of coffee that weighs four grams, which matters when you're carrying everything you own up a hill. Four pouches are $13. Roasted in BC, freeze-dried in Alberta. $10 to $25 # Let's Go Biking! guidebooks , $19.95 to $24.95 in paperback, $14.95 as ebooks. Colleen MacDonald's three guidebooks cover rides around Vancouver , on the Islands and Sunshine Coast , and from Hope to Cranbrook. That last one, Okanagan and Beyond , has more than 140 routes. There's a $15 neckwarmer too, and a portion of every sale goes to BC trail advocacy groups. I should tell you that Colleen is a director of the BC Cycle Tourism Society, which publishes this site. Written in BC. Eleven Speed Coffee , Victoria, $24.75 for a 340 g bag of the Podium espresso roast . A roaster run by bike people. They deliver by bike and host group rides. Roasted in BC. Freeze-dried meals , West Coast Kitchen, Cowichan Valley, $17.95 to $21.95. Camp dinners from a family farm, like butter chicken with rice . They're 15% off until December 3. Made in BC. South Away: The Pacific Coast on Two Wheels , by Meaghan Marie Hackinen, $20.95. A touring memoir that starts in Terrace and heads down the coast to Baja. It's the only gift on this list with a link to northern BC. I couldn't find a single bike gear maker up north. Written in BC, published in Alberta. Cycling the Islands , by John Crouch, Rocky Mountain Books, Victoria, $25. The updated edition, with more than 30 rides on 11 islands, including Salt Spring, Pender, Mayne, Galiano, Gabriola, Denman, and Hornby. Published in BC. Fading Light socks , 7mesh, Squamish, $20. Some colours are on sale from $12. 7mesh is open about sewing its clothing overseas, but this sock's page doesn't say where. BC brand, made-in not stated. "I Stop For Slugs" bumper sticker , Owl & Bear Studio, $11. Not strictly a bike gift, but it's funny. The maker suggests your bumper, your water bottle, or your bike. I found it at Bough & Antler in Campbell River. Made-in not stated. $25 to $50 # BIKE eco tee , Kindred Coast, Vancouver Island, $49.50. The bike on the front is drawn full of mountains, waves, trees, and a tent. The fabric is knit, cut, sewn, and screen-printed in Canada. Made in Canada. Speedy Bike tee , Ole Originals, Vancouver, $39. Printed by hand, one at a time, on a manual press in a small Vancouver studio. It comes in women's sizes too. Printed in BC. Biking Squatch tee , Westcoastees, Cowichan Valley, $35. A Sasquatch on a bike, letting the breeze through his fur. There's a kids' version for $27. Printed in BC. Merino cycling socks , Samsara Cycle, Vancouver, $35. From a company that designs cycling clothes for women, in Vancouver. They're on sale for $29. BC brand, made-in not stated. Classic Saddle Roll , Farsik Supply, Victoria, $28. A small roll for a tube and tools, in eight colours, handmade in the Victoria area. Made in BC. Bear spray holder , Ghostrider Equipment, Fernie, $50. It holds bear spray on your bike where you can reach it. One person designs, prototypes, and builds these in the Kootenays. If someone you love tours in bear country, this is the one. Made in BC. OSnack variety pack , Hornby Organic, Comox, $26.98. Twelve small organic bars from a family company that started on Hornby Island. They're an official supplier to Cycling Canada. Made in BC. McCulloch's Wonder , by Barrie Sanford, $27.95. The story of how the Kettle Valley Railway got built, for anyone who has ridden the trail and wondered who thought a railway there was a good idea. A BC story. Cycling Vancouver Island , by John Crouch, Rocky Mountain Books, Victoria, $30. More than 40 routes. This is the 2022 edition. An updated one was due this year and has slipped to April 2027. Published in BC. $50 to $100 # Top-tube pack, mini , Shaka Packs, Kelowna, $90. A little bag for snacks and a phone, from the only bike bag maker I found in the Okanagan. Each one is built to order, so order early. Made in BC. Cargo Cage , Wildwood Cycles, Nanaimo, $55. A cage for strapping a dry bag or a big bottle to your fork, from a solo builder who has been making frames since 2013. Made in BC. Hippie hip pack , Northern Ultralight, Nelson, $80. Designed and made in a small workshop in Nelson. Made in BC. XL Cargo Cage , Fauna Components, Vancouver, $79 or $85. A stainless steel cage, new this fall, from a woman-owned company. It's $79 in silver and $85 in black. Made in BC, with some imported parts. $100 to $300 # Candy Pack , HMPL Design, Vancouver, $105. Sewn to order in a one-person Chinatown studio, in 16 fabrics and colours. Made in BC. Little Basket , Threefold Objects, Vancouver, $105. A stainless steel front basket that's fabricated in Abbotsford, then welded and finished in Vancouver. Made in BC, with some imported parts. Bar Bag Pro , Farsik Supply, Victoria, $125. The big sibling of the saddle roll above. Made in BC. GR1 front light , Full On Lighting, Victoria, $149. I didn't find another bike-light company in BC. This one says the light is designed and tested in coastal BC. It doesn't say where it's made, so I can't either. Designed in BC, made-in not stated. Gift cards # If you'd rather let them choose: WZRD Bikes on Vancouver Island ($25 to $300), HMPL Design ($25 to $500), Hornby Organic ($25 to $100), and Eleven Speed Coffee ($20 to $100). For the rider who has everything # And for the rider who has everything? It's hard to go wrong with a donation in their name. Our Community Bikes in Vancouver gives refurbished bikes and free repairs to people facing financial barriers. $280 covers a refurbished kids' bike. $160 covers a year of repairs for one person. You can give in someone's honour, and they'll get an e-card. Gifts made now are being matched. Your own town may have a community bike shop doing the same kind of work. Or give to the groups that look after the trails they ride. GivingTuesday is December 1. That same $160 pays to surface one metre of the Shuswap North Okanagan Rail Trail. A lifetime membership in Island Pathways is $10. Our Trail Organizations page lists the groups that look after BC's touring trails, with links to donate, and Who to thank for our BC trails goes through them trail by trail. Happy holidays, and happy riding. Prices and stock checked November 20, 2026. No affiliate links, no paid placements.

title: HOW TO: Put your bike on a BC Transit or TransLink bus bike rack
desc: Almost every city bus in BC has a bike rack on the front. Here's how to load your bike, with BC Transit's short video and the rules for e-bikes, big tires, and kids' bikes.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Put your bike on a BC Transit or TransLink bus bike rack HOW TO: Put your bike on a BC Transit or TransLink bus bike rack November 27, 2026 Almost every city bus in BC has a bike rack on the front. It holds two bikes, and you load your own. It looks harder than it is. BC Transit made a short video that shows the whole thing: Watch BC Transit's video on YouTube → The video is from BC Transit, but TransLink's racks in Metro Vancouver work the same way. The short version # 1. Before the bus pulls up, take off your bags, water bottles, pump, and anything else loose. 2. Tell the driver you're loading a bike. 3. Pull the handle to fold the rack down. If the rack is empty, use the slot closest to the bus. 4. Lift your bike in so the wheels sit in the trays. Pull the support arm up and over the front tire so it holds the bike in place. 5. Get on and sit near the front where you can see your bike. When you get off, tell the driver, go out the front door, lift your bike off, and fold the rack back up if it's empty. In Metro Vancouver you can practise first. TransLink has 11 practice racks, including at Bridgeport, Main Street–Science World, Surrey Central, Lonsdale Quay, and UBC. The full list is on TransLink's bikes page. Good to know # Space isn't guaranteed. If both spots are taken, wait for the next bus. Tire size. TransLink's newer silver metal racks take tires up to 29" tall and 2.6" wide. The older racks with black plastic trays take up to 2.2" wide. Many BC Transit buses take tires up to 3" (75 mm), and the rest take 2" (51 mm). Have a big tire? Let 10 PSI or less out of the front tire and use the slot closest to the bus. That slot fits bigger tires. Weight. TransLink's racks take bikes under 25 kg (55 lb). BC Transit sets the same limit for e-bikes. E-bikes. They're allowed on the rack if they weigh under 25 kg and have a lithium battery. Take the battery off and carry it onto the bus. E-bikes with other kinds of batteries, and moped-style or scooter-style e-bikes, aren't allowed on the rack or on the bus. Small buses at night. On smaller buses, a bike on the rack blocks the headlights. BC Transit's community buses only allow bikes on the rack in daylight. TransLink's Community Shuttles have you bring your bike inside after dark. Kids' bikes. On TransLink, bikes with wheels 14" or smaller ride inside the bus, space permitting, and an adult holds on to them. Bigger kids' bikes go on the rack. Rack bikes need wheels at least 16" (40 cm) across. Trailers, tandems, and cargo bikes. TransLink doesn't allow bike trailers on any of its vehicles. Tandems and most cargo bikes won't fit on the rack, and most are over the weight limit. If you ride a handcycle, call the transit system first to ask what works. Full rules and who to ask # BC Transit (everywhere outside Metro Vancouver): Bikes and scooters . To reach your local system, start at BC Transit's Contact page . Head office: 250-385-2551, weekdays 8 am to 4 pm. TransLink (Metro Vancouver): Bikes on Transit , which also covers SkyTrain, SeaBus, and West Coast Express. Customer Information: 604-953-3333, or other ways to reach them . Information checked in November 2026. Sources: TransLink, Bikes on Transit ; BC Transit, Bikes and scooters ; BC Transit, "How To Use Bike Racks #BusReady" . Photo: Akusiroyo, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons.

title: HOW TO: Know when to replace your helmet
desc: When to replace your bike helmet, how to tell how old it is, and what to do with the old one.
body: Home / Field Notes / HOW TO: Know when to replace your helmet HOW TO: Know when to replace your helmet November 27, 2026 Felix Wong's helmet after crashes on the 2008 Tour Divide · Photo: Felix Wong, CC BY 4.0 Wondering when you should replace your helmet? If it's damaged, or, yup, just getting old: Replace it now if # You crashed in it, even if it looks fine. The foam inside is built to crush once, and the damage can be invisible. You dropped it hard enough to crack the foam, or the shell is cracked. Check around the vents. Small cracks and faded plastic there mean sun damage. The straps are frayed or the buckle doesn't click shut, or it doesn't fit anymore. There's no safety sticker inside. BC's helmet law accepts CSA, Snell, ASTM, and ANSI standards. Many helmets also carry the US CPSC sticker. It's past the maker's age limit. Most helmet makers say you should change out a helmet after 5 years, but a few say three years. Check your helmet's manual or the maker's website. How to tell how old your helmet is # 1. Look for the sticker inside. Helmets made for the US market must show the month and year they were made, in plain numbers. Many helmets sold in Canada carry the same sticker. It's often under the pads, so peel them back. 2. Check your email or your online order history. Search your inbox for the brand name or "helmet" to find the order confirmation. 3. Search your photos. Scroll back to the first ride photo with that helmet in it. If none of those work and you can't remember buying it? It's probably time. What to do with the old one # We couldn't find a helmet recycling program in BC. The City of Vancouver's Waste Wizard says a used helmet goes in the garbage. Don't give it away or sell it: nobody can tell whether it's been in a crash, and many consignment shops won't take used bike helmets for that reason. Health Canada also says not to buy a used helmet if you don't know its history. We do have a creative idea for you though. The Bicycle Helmet Safety Institute suggests turning your old helmet into a hanging planter. Tell us if you do 🙂 Screenshot: Bicycle Helmet Safety Institute Information checked in November 2026. Sources: Health Canada, Helmet safety ; Bicycle Helmet Safety Institute, When to replace and Recycling ; Trek, Bike helmet safety ; US Consumer Product Safety Commission, helmet labels ; BC Bicycle Safety Helmet Standards Regulation ; City of Vancouver Waste Wizard ; Kids Fair, items not accepted . Photos: Felix Wong , CC BY 4.0 ; Bicycle Helmet Safety Institute .

title: Ride BC indoors this winter
desc: Three BC rides to pedal along to on YouTube, free on any indoor bike, and the 45 BC rides on Rouvy, with what you need and what it costs.
body: Home / Field Notes / Ride BC indoors this winter Ride BC indoors this winter November 27, 2026 Riding the Stanley Park loop on Rouvy · Screenshot: Rouvy In the past year I've pedalled more than 90 hours indoors, keeping up my exercise habit when the cold or wet have made it otherwise unappealing to ride outside. Luckily, I've spent very little of that time looking at the wall: I was riding around Stanley Park, down the Okanagan Rail Trail, and through the Rockies to Emerald Lake. It isn't the same as being there, but it has been a fun way to get a sneak peek of bits of BC I haven't been to yet. The free way: YouTube # All you need is a phone or tablet propped on the handlebars, or a TV in front of the bike. Go to YouTube, find a ride someone filmed from the saddle, press play, and pedal along. It works on any stationary bike, including the spin bikes at the gym. Three BC rides to start with: The Myra Canyon trestles above Kelowna, 37 minutes, from Hiking British Columbia. Around Stanley Park on the seawall , 37 minutes, from Vancouver POV. The Westside Legacy Trail from Invermere to Fairmont Hot Springs , 24 minutes, from Don Barnett. We've mapped 432 more rider's-view YouTube rides around BC. They're all on our BC rides on YouTube page! If you want more: Rouvy # Looking for something more immersive than YouTube? I've had a Rouvy subscription for a year, and it has been a lot of fun riding in BC and all around the world. Rouvy plays video of a real road, filmed from a bike or car, and the video moves as fast as you pedal. With a smart trainer, the pedalling resistance gets harder on the climbs and easier on the way down. You can choose whether to see yourself on the road as a little avatar, and whether to see other riders too. You don't have to race anyone. Go your own pace. Coasting downhill in Yoho National Park, with speed, grade, and the hills ahead along the bottom · Screenshot: Rouvy The ride settings, where you choose how many ghost riders you see and whether to hide other users · Screenshot: Rouvy If you've heard of Zwift, it's kind of like that, but this is the real world instead of the animated fictional world in Zwift. Also Zwift is known for racing, but Rouvy is really just for riding around at your own pace. (Zwift actually bought Rouvy in April 2026, but the two still run separately.) Rouvy runs on laptops, phones, and Apple TV. I run it on my laptop and it works great. What you need # Unlike YouTube, Rouvy isn't just a video, so for it to "play" it has to get a signal from your bike. This means your indoor bike needs either a "smart" trainer or a speed sensor, not just the spin bike at the gym unfortunately. Here are options that work: A basic indoor bike trainer and an additional speed sensor, about $200 if you find the trainer used or on sale. A basic trainer is the simple stand your back wheel sits in, with no electronics. You may already have one in the basement. Rouvy calls it a "classic trainer." Add a Bluetooth speed sensor, like Garmin's Speed Sensor 2 ($55 to $100), and Rouvy can follow along, but the hills won't get harder. Bought new at full price, a basic trainer and a sensor cost about as much as a smart trainer. A smart trainer your back wheel sits in, $400 to $600 new, like the Garmin Tacx Flow Smart or Wahoo KICKR SNAP. The resistance you feel changes based on the Rouvy route. These are getting hard to find new. A smart trainer you mount your bike on, with the back wheel off, $800 to $900, like the Wahoo KICKR CORE 2 or JetBlack Victory. You need a cassette that matches your bike's gears, or the single-cog version that does virtual shifting. I have an older version of this that I use with my 25-year-old "inside" bike. An indoor smart bike, $2,100 to $3,800, like the Zwift Ride or Wahoo KICKR BIKE SHIFT. It's the full bike setup, so you don't attach a bike to these. Long hours on a trainer can make your bum more sore than the same hours on the road. A good saddle helps, and so does a spongy mat or tennis balls under the trainer's feet. What Rouvy costs # There's a 7-day free trial. After that: Single: $24.99 CAD a month or $224.99 a year. Duo: $39.99 a month or $349.99 a year. You invite the second person with a link, and they don't have to live with you. Even larger discounts with a bigger group, or after having a membership for more than a year. If you cancel, you keep a free version with 20 km a month. You can pause your subscription for up to 180 days once a year, which is handy if you ride outside all summer. See the prices on Rouvy's pricing page , and check out places like Reddit's r/rouvy for groups that form for discounts. The BC rides on Rouvy # So how many of Rouvy's rides are in BC? 45! Together they cover 1,005 km of road and trail. Rouvy filmed 26 of them, and riders contributed the other 19 as community rides. Blue rides were filmed by Rouvy and orange ones by riders. Open our map to zoom in and click each ride. A few to look for: Along the Skeena River near Prince Rupert (36 km, flat), the most-ridden BC route on Rouvy. Through Pacific Rim National Park Reserve to Tofino (24 km), new in August. The Stanley Park loop (9 km). From Stanley Park over the Lions Gate Bridge to Howe Sound (21 km). Up to Rogers Pass on Highway 1 (36 km, 756 m up). The Okanagan Rail Trail from Coldstream to Lake Country (26 km, gravel), filmed by a rider. Along the Skeena River on Highway 16 · Screenshot: Rouvy The full list of all 45, with links and a map, is on our BC rides on Rouvy page. Rouvy's own rides have public pages. The rider-filmed ones need a Rouvy account to open. Want to say hi? If you're on Rouvy, add me as a friend . I'm @heather_bccycletourism. I've also started a community there for riding BC routes, called Bike Beautiful British Columbia . Come join us, maybe we'll set up some group rides? What Rouvy leaves out # Every one of Rouvy's official BC rides is on a paved road, and most are highways. Through Pacific Rim, for example, Rouvy filmed the highway, not ʔapsčiik t̓ašii (pronounced ups-cheek ta-shee), the paved path beside it which is a bit of a miss. Also, there's nothing at all in the Cariboo, the Fraser Valley, the Sunshine Coast, or the Gulf Islands yet. Riders have filled some of the gaps. Two rail trails on Rouvy, Myra Canyon and the Okanagan Rail Trail, were both filmed by a rider this spring. The Okanagan Rail Trail, filmed by a rider · Screenshot: Rouvy If you have a GoPro with GPS, you can film and upload a route yourself for others to ride. Finally, another miss: if you ride " Ride to Emerald Lake ," it ends just before you get to see the lake!?!? I guess for some rewards we have to do the rides for real :) My husband and me on the ride from Golden to Lake Louise, which goes through Yoho National Park. PS I often listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks (free from the library via the Libby app) while looking at the pretty virtual scenery... if you've got biking-related recommendations for those, drop me a line :) Information checked in November 2026. Sources: Rouvy, pricing ; Rouvy, FAQ ; Rouvy, compatibility guide ; Rouvy, how to record a route ; Rouvy, Zwift acquisition ; Wahoo, drivetrain compatibility ; Parks Canada, ʔapsčiik t̓ašii pathway . Route list pulled from Rouvy's rider map, November 21, 2026. Screenshots are from the Rouvy app.

title: Dispatch October 2026
desc: Hot news and deep dives for BC cycle tourism, October 2026
body: Home / Field Notes / October 2026 Dispatch BC Cycle Tourism Society The Field Notes Dispatch October 2026 Issue #5 · Monthly newsletter on cycle tourism in British Columbia This issue is coming to you a little earlier in the month than usual, so you could get it before Thanksgiving. In that spirit, read about the trail organizations that make our trails possible , and drop one of them a thank-you this long weekend. Then check out when BC campgrounds close for the season , in case you want one more trip. At the end of the month, Colleen MacDonald and I are presenting at the Active Transportation Summit in Victoria. Come say hi! Details are under Talks and appearances. Lots of people have been out riding and writing about it, so this issue has plenty of trip reports. Also in this issue: how to keep your food away from wildlife when you're camping without a car , and a poll about who you've accidentally shared a meal with. Enjoy! The Feature Where can I camp this fall? # October 7, 2026 Vancouver Island, BC · Photo: Rob Wilson October can be some of the best riding of the year in BC. The roads are quieter, the leaves are turning, and in much of the province it's still dry. But – can you still camp? We checked the official pages of about 1,300 campgrounds and here's what we learned. When do campgrounds close? # This map shows every campground we could pin down, coloured by when it closes. The lighter the dot, the earlier in the fall it closes. The darkest dots are campgrounds that say they're open all year. Campground closures cluster around a few dates each year: The end of September is the big cluster. About 90 campgrounds close on September 30 or October 1; by October 1st about 220 of the campgrounds have closed.
