Thanksgiving Monday (October 12 this year) is the second wave of closing dates: about 70 more close by then. Mid-October and Halloween are the closure dates for most of the rest. So where should I camp in October? # It depends a lot on where you are. Here's the share of campgrounds on our map, including year-round ones, that are still open after Thanksgiving: In Northern BC, most campgrounds close early. Only about a third of the ones open on Labour Day are still open on October 1st. After Thanksgiving, about a quarter of the North's campgrounds are open. Campgrounds on the coast stay open much later. More than three-quarters of campgrounds in Vancouver, Coast and Mountains and on Vancouver Island are still open after Thanksgiving. The southern Interior sits in the middle, with about half its campgrounds open after Thanksgiving and fewer by the end of October. Campground closures roughly follow the frost. Here's each region side by side: how many campgrounds on our map are still open after Thanksgiving and on November 1st, next to a normal October from Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1991 to 2020 averages. Region Campgrounds on the map Open after Thanksgiving Open November 1 October overnight low Days with rain or snow Nights below freezing Average first fall frost Vancouver Island 178 135 (76%) 94 6 to 8°C 14 to 20 about 1 or fewer Nov 4 Vancouver, Coast and Mountains 144 119 (83%) 78 7°C 15 about 1 Nov 10 Thompson Okanagan 162 86 (53%) 39 4°C 10 6 to 7 Oct 8 to 12 Kootenay Rockies 108 48 (44%) 18 0 to 4°C 10 to 15 4 to 16 Sep 23 Cariboo Chilcotin Coast 55 26 (47%) 7 -1°C 13 18 Sep 14 Northern British Columbia 83 23 (28%) 16 -1 to 0°C 16 to 17 15 to 17 Sep 7 to 17 Weather towns: Victoria and Cape Beale on the west coast (Vancouver Island), Vancouver, Kamloops and Penticton, Nelson and Cranbrook (the frost date is Cranbrook), Williams Lake, Prince George, and Smithers. "Days with rain or snow" counts any day with at least 0.2 mm. What's the weather like? In October in BC you're mostly choosing between rain and frost. On the coast the nights stay mild, around 6 to 8°C, but expect rain on about half your days, and a lot more than that on the west coast of the mainland or the Island. In the Okanagan and around Kamloops, October is dry (about 10 wet days, and about a fifth of Vancouver's rainfall), the days are just as warm as the coast, and the nights drop to around 4°C with a frost about one night in five. In the Cariboo, the North, and around Cranbrook, about half of October nights go below freezing. Early October can be lovely in the dry Interior, provided you're equipped for freezing nights. Later in the month, you'll find more open campgrounds and milder nights on the coast. Nelson, BC · Photo: Kari Medig What about after Thanksgiving, or winter? # About 230 campgrounds on our map say they're open year-round, though "open year-round" can mean very different things. Some parks offer hot showers; others are unplowed, with little more than a pit toilet. Some private parks that stay open all winter take only RVs or monthly stays in the off-season. So we looked for ones that explicitly allow tents. We found 16 places that say on their own page that they take tents in winter: Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands Fillongley, on Denman Island Goldstream, near Victoria Jordan River (a Capital Regional District park) Narvaez Bay and Shingle Bay, in Gulf Islands National Park Reserve. Open in winter but not maintained, so you're on your own. North Park at Horne Lake (gravel road) Pedder Bay RV Park, Metchosin, near the Galloping Goose. Winter tent sites from about $48. Quinsam, at Elk Falls near Campbell River. About $11 a night, cash. Rathtrevor Beach, Parksville Sproat Lake, near Port Alberni Upper Campbell Reservoir (BC Hydro). Free, first-come, first-served. Snow is possible. Vancouver, Coast and Mountains Willingdon Beach, Powell River. In town, right on the beach, with a winter tent rate of about $27. Of everything we checked, it had the clearest winter tent policy. Shelter Point, on Texada Island (the gate is locked at night) Grace Lake (gravel forest road) Lone Duck One, in Manning Park. This is snow camping, at about 1,200 m. Thompson Okanagan Moon Shadows RV Park, Merritt, which keeps 19 tent sites open all year Services get thin in winter. Water may be shut off and the flush toilets closed, even where the campground is open. Call ahead about water so you are prepared. Vancouver Island, BC · Photo: Ben Giesbrecht Wait, that one closes when? # A few campgrounds close for reasons that have nothing to do with the weather, and one is open only in winter. Gwe Da Ts’ih , in Ts’ilʔos Park in the Chilcotin, closes in September and October for spawning salmon. It's open the rest of the year, November through August. Taylor Meadows , in Garibaldi Park, also closes in September and October, for bears. Cambie Creek , near Manning Park, is open only in winter, from early December to late March. Chute Lake Lodge , above Naramata on the Kettle Valley Rail Trail, says it closes in March and April. Can I still camp after a campground “closes” for the season? # Surprisingly, it is hard to know! We found some season information for 858 campgrounds, including ones too uncertain to map. Only 239 of them (28%) said anything about what happens after closing. Of those, 90 let you camp without services, 89 keep some services going, and 60 say no camping at all. Some leave the gate open and the taps off, but others lock them. You’re taking your chances. What's not on the map? # Lots of campgrounds aren't on the map because we couldn't find a clear season for them. Many of these are Recreation Sites and Trails BC sites. Most Rec Sites don't post a season at all. They're unstaffed, and you can use them while the road is open and there's no snow, which in practice can mean well into fall. About 430 campgrounds in the directory have no posted season, and most of them are Rec Sites. We also left off about 90 places where the information we found was weak or contradictory. Tent calling? # Check the campground's own website before you go, especially if you're travelling after Thanksgiving. And if you find a closure date we've got wrong, let us know so we can improve the directory for the next rider. You can find campgrounds along your route in the BC Bike Stops directory . Information checked in October 2026. Read on the web → Talks and appearances Oct 29, 4:10 pm Making Connections for Cycle Tourism in BC Directors Heather Piwowar and Colleen MacDonald are presenting at the BC Cycling Coalition's Active Transportation Summit: Thursday, October 29, 4:10 to 5:00 pm, in the Oak Bay Room at the Victoria Conference Centre, 720 Douglas St. The summit runs October 28 to 30, and you need to register to attend. Come to the talk, or find us in the hall and say hi. Program → Summit → Jan 19 Attending in January The Vancouver, Coast & Mountains Industry Forum, Destination BC's yearly gathering for tourism businesses in the region, has moved from October 15 to January 19. Heather Piwowar will be there. Reach out so we can find each other at a coffee break. Also in this issue Who to thank for our BC trails Find out who looks after the BC trails and rec sites you rode this summer, and easy ways to say thanks this Thanksgiving. READ THE DEEP DIVE → HOW TO: Store your food when you're camping by bike No car to lock your food in at night? Here's what works at BC campgrounds, from bear canisters to the bear-proof garbage bin. READ THE HOW-TO → Quick poll In September we asked when your touring season ends. Half of you ride until the campgrounds close, and the other half own fenders and keep going. If you're in the first group, this month's feature shows when campgrounds close across BC. Weigh in on this month's question: Loading... News from the field Oct 7 Still time to join the Active Transportation Summit Registration is still open for the BC Cycling Coalition's Active Transportation Summit in Victoria, October 28 to 30. Bursaries are still available and take 50% off registration for all three days. If cost is a factor, you're eligible. When you register, you can also ask to be matched with others to carpool, share a taxi, or cycle in together. Day 1 is half-day workshops, $59 each, on topics like walking and biking to school and the Motor Vehicle Act, and they're filling up fast. BC Cycle Tourism Society (Colleen and Heather) are presenting on Thursday afternoon. Bursary → Workshops → Register → Sep 30 More room for bikes on the Vancouver–Seattle train Amtrak Cascades has started running its new Airo trains. Each one has racks for 18 bikes, some of them in the passenger cars, so you can keep your bike near you rather than only in the baggage car. Two Airo trains are running so far: one arrives in Vancouver from Seattle at 12:30 pm, and one leaves Vancouver for Seattle at 4:45 pm. The rest of the fleet switches over by early 2027. You still need a bike reservation, and Amtrak's booking system may cap them at six per train until it catches up. E-bikes are allowed under 50 lb, with tires no wider than 2". Amtrak → Oct 2 Free bikepacking gear in Nelson Building Momentum Bikepacking runs a free gear library for women and gender-diverse riders: bikepacking bikes, bags, tents, and other camping gear, borrowed for up to a week (two with a renewal) and picked up in Nelson. Since it opened in late July, 35 people have borrowed 67 items. Gear library → Oct 6 Adventure Cycling's new members-only chats Adventure Cycling Association (ACA) is a US non-profit, but a few of its routes run through BC, including the Vancouver Crossing Loop, the start of its Pacific Coast Route, and part of the Great Divide Route. (This month it also launched an Eastern Canada Route, 1,500 km from Toronto to Québec City, roughly two-thirds car-free, swoon!) ACA members get Adventure Cyclist, a beautiful touring magazine, in print or digital. New this year are Campfire Chats, small monthly online conversations for members. October's is about eating on tour (Oct 21, 4 pm Pacific). Campfire Chats → BC Trip Reports People keep writing about riding BC. A few recent favourites. Sep 9 Gravel riding and a bike hotel in Clinton Not a trip report exactly, but a lovely ten minutes of riding in the South Cariboo. Kelly Servinski and Erin Yeo sold everything to open the Tutti Gravel Inn in Clinton, which they call Canada's first gravel bike hotel. The film follows them and a few riders out on the gravel roads around town. It was made with support from the region's tourism association and two bike brands, it's a polished look at what a stay built around bikes can be like. Since filming, wildfires have hit the area hard, with an evacuation order and homes and businesses lost. The inn came through fine, but the community has a hard road ahead. It's a great time to consider making the trip and supporting local businesses along the way. Video on YouTube → Oct 2 Around the Little Slocan Nine riders from Building Momentum Bikepacking rode from Winlaw along the Slocan Valley Rail Trail to lunch in Slocan, then climbed to camp at the Little Slocan Lake rec site. They hung their food in a tree. Ride report on Substack → Sep 28 Babines to Terrace A northern BC rider linked the Babines loop to Telkwa Pass: 205 km over three and a half days, including 30 km of purpose-built alpine singletrack. Cronin Pass still had snow in mid-July. Their tip: if you time it right, you can take VIA Rail from Terrace back to Smithers. Trip report on Reddit → Sep 11 Victoria to Sombrio Beach and back Eden Sun's second bikepacking trip: 400 km over four days, along the Juan de Fuca coast to Sombrio Beach and back through Lake Cowichan. Three crashes and two falls along the way, and a bus to get past a stretch closed to bikes. Trip report at the UBC Varsity Outdoor Club → Sep 22 Up the Koch Creek road in the Valhallas A photo trip into the Valhallas near McKean Lakes, then down to Burton on a recently decommissioned ATV road. No bears, though lots of bear scat. Trip report on Reddit → Sep 18 A week of hub-and-spoke riding from Penticton Twenty-four Cross Canada Cycle Tour Society riders based themselves in Penticton for a week of hub-and-spoke riding: Summerland backroads past the Trout Creek Trestle, Oliver and Okanagan Falls, and a last ride through the Little Tunnel to Naramata, just after the Bald Range fire. Trip report in the CCCTS Newsbrief → Aug 12 Victoria to Elk Pass Kate Bradley rode about 2,190 km of the Great Northern Bikepacking Route in 43 days, through Nelson and Fernie. Her rear hub failed at Elk Pass, on the Alberta border, and that ended the trip. Trip summary on Substack → Ride along with us The next Dispatch lands in November. Subscribe to receive it. Subscribe → Issue #5 · October 2026 · BC Cycle Tourism Society Web version · Past issues & Field Notes archive

title: Dispatch September 2026
desc: Hot news and deep dives for BC cycle tourism, September 2026
body: Home / Field Notes / September 2026 Dispatch BC Cycle Tourism Society The Field Notes Dispatch September 2026 Issue #4 · Monthly newsletter on cycle tourism in British Columbia It's the end of September in BC. The mornings are crisp, the campgrounds are quieter, and some of us are wondering when to call it a season (tell us in this month's poll). This issue lands on September 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. Our feature, Riding through Indigenous BC , is a guide to Indigenous-owned places to stay, eat and learn along BC's bike routes. October is a busy month for us, and we'd love to meet you. See where we'll be under Talks and appearances. Come say hi! Also in this issue: the transcript of my conversation on the BC Cycling Coalition's Bike Sense podcast , how to eat enough on a bike tour (a banana and three Oreos, anyone?), and how to stock up on vegan snacks for the road . Enjoy! The Feature Riding through Indigenous BC # September 30, 2026 Hazelton, BC · Photo: Mattias Fredriksson September 30 is the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It's a day to remember the children who were sent to residential schools, and the ones who never came home. It's also a good day to think about whose land we ride on, and where our money goes when we travel. A bike gives you time for both. You move slowly, you stop in small places, and you spend your money close to where you sleep. Indigenous Tourism BC suggests choosing the Indigenous-owned lodge over the chain hotel, or a meal with an Indigenous host over a fast-food stop. Most of us are curious, too: the Conference Board of Canada found 88% of people in Canada are interested in Indigenous cultural activities. A night in a lodge isn't reconciliation. But it's a start to know whose territory you're riding through, and to spend some of your trip with the people who live there. Bike paths with Indigenous art and signs # Many paths you probably already ride have new art and signs made by local First Nations. Chilliwack, BC · Photo: Viranlly Liemena Vancouver. Next time you ride the Seawall, stop at Brockton Point in Stanley Park for the poles and Susan Point's three carved gateways. In Port Moody, five Coast Salish house posts went up along the Shoreline Trail between 2025 and this spring, one from each of five host Nations. Ride the paved path. Some posts sit on the gravel trail or the Pigeon Cove boardwalk, where you walk your bike. Nearby, the Traboulay PoCo Trail follows the Coquitlam River past "Continuum," panels made with the Kwikwetlem First Nation. Chilliwack. On the Vedder Rotary Trail, Peach Park has the Lhewá:mel Welcome Portal and Gathering Place , led by the Ts'elxwéyeqw Tribe. Victoria. Around the Inner Harbour, seven bronze spindle whorls by Songhees carver Butch Dick mark places the Lekwungen people named. A spindle whorl is the carved wooden disc Coast Salish weavers use to spin wool. Start at Songhees Point . The walkway there is for people on foot, so walk your bike from one whorl to the next. The E&N Rail Trail itself was built with the Songhees and Esquimalt Nations as partners. Okanagan. On the Okanagan Rail Trail, the gateway at Km 0 by Kalamalka Lake has panels on Syilx people, language and culture, written in n̓syilxcən. The Okanagan Indian Band's fluent speakers set the spelling, and the words are written without capital letters, as a sign of equality. The Km 0 page has audio for the pronunciations. Riding out of Kelowna, turn off at Pelmewash Parkway in Lake Country, where three sculptures by Syilx artists Clint George and Les Louis stand a short distance from the trail. Duncan, BC · Photo: Rob Wilson Cowichan. Duncan calls itself the City of Totems. Its self-guided tour follows yellow footprints painted on the streets past 43 poles. It's a walking tour, so lock your bike downtown. Look for Coast Salish artist Charlene Johnny's mural, Nanum'IyusTth'ele (A Meeting of Happy Hearts). A few things to know: some poles are meant to weather and return to the earth, so a leaning or mossy pole isn't a neglected one. Mortuary and memorial poles honour the dead. At burial grounds, like the one in Alert Bay, view from the road. And if a sign says a road or an area is closed or local traffic only, that includes you on a bike. Indigenous cultural stops in five regions # Tofino and Ucluelet ʔapsčiik t̓ašii and the Tofino multi-use path. Tofino, BC · Photo: Jordan Dyck ʔapsčiik t̓ašii is the 25 km paved path between Tofino and Ucluelet through Pacific Rim National Park Reserve. An Elders' working group from the Tla-o-qui-aht and Ucluelet First Nations named it when it opened in 2022. The name means "going the right way on the path," and it also carries the teaching to speak the truth. It's pronounced "ups-cheek ta-shee," and Parks Canada has a recording of Tla-o-qui-aht Elder Kaamatḥ, Levi Martin, saying it. Indigenous-led cycling businesses are still rare. T̓iick̓in E-bikes is one, a family business with deep roots in the Ucluelet First Nation. They rent e-bikes at the Tofino–Ucluelet junction, right where the path starts. Their hours change with the season, so call ahead (250-266-3482). You can also pick up their bikes at Tin Wis. Sleep at the Tla-o-qui-aht Nation's Tin Wis Resort , an 85-room hotel on tinwis Beach about 400 m from the Tofino path, or at the Ucluelet First Nation's Wya Point , with oceanside tent sites and hot showers on 600 acres of old growth, 1.4 km off the path. In downtown Tofino, Himwitsa Lodge shares a building with the House of Himwitsa gallery and its smoked fish store. Roy Henry Vickers' gallery , which he built in 1986, is 300 m from the path. South Okanagan The Kettle Valley Rail Trail and the South Okanagan–Similkameen bike network. The Osoyoos Indian Band's sx̌ʷəx̌ʷnitkʷ campground at Okanagan Falls is about 100 m from the Kettle Valley Rail Trail, beside the river's little falls. Ride south on the bike network to Osoyoos, where the band runs the Nk'Mip Desert Cultural Centre , a campground on Osoyoos Lake, Canada's warmest, and Nk'Mip Cellars , which calls itself the first Indigenous-owned winery in North America. All three are within about a kilometre of each other, a good argument for a two-night stop in Osoyoos. The band's sẃiẃs (Haynes Point) campground is on the same network. (The Penticton Indian Band's section between Summerland and Kaleden is closed, so you can't ride the trail down from Penticton.) Up the valley in Westbank, the Sncewips Heritage Museum and Kekuli Cafe are both worth a stop. Victoria to Port Renfrew The Port Renfrew–Cowichan loop. The route heads into old-growth country on BC's southwest coast, and Port Renfrew, where the San Juan River meets the sea, has been Pacheedaht territory for thousands of years. Their campground sits right on the route: beachfront, riverside and forest sites between two rivers, open year-round. Start the ride at Ship Point on the Inner Harbour, where Songhees Tours leaves for canoe and walking tours with Lək̓ʷəŋən hosts. North Island by ferry The Island touring route north from Courtenay, with ferries to Quadra and Alert Bay. Alert Bay, BC · Photo: Jordan Dyck From Campbell River, a short ferry reaches Quadra Island, where the We Wai Kai campground borders Rebecca Spit, and the Nuyumbalees Cultural Centre at Cape Mudge holds part of the potlatch collection that came home in 1979. Call ahead for hours. Farther north, take the ferry from Port McNeill to Alert Bay for the U'mista Cultural Centre , which holds regalia the government took after a 1921 potlatch and that has since come home. If you stay the night, the 'Namgis First Nation has fourteen cabins with kitchens. At the top of the Island, the Kwa'lilas Hotel in Port Hardy is right on the last few kilometres of the route. Kwa'lilas means "a place to sleep" in Kwak̓wala. Gwa'sala-'Nakwaxda'xw Elders chose the art and design inside, and there's a pub and restaurant downstairs. Highway 16 and Haida Gwaii Highway 16 along the Bulkley and Skeena rivers, then the ferry and the Haida Gwaii route. Near Hazelton, 'Ksan Historical Village sits on Gitxsan land where the Skeena and Bulkley meet, with a museum, longhouses and a campground, 2 km off the route. At Witset, the Widzin Kwah Canyon House Museum overlooks the canyon where Witsuwit'en people still fish. Between Terrace and Prince Rupert, Kitsumkalum's Kasiks is right on the highway with hot showers and a restaurant on site, so there's no dinner to carry. Skidegate, BC · Photo: Shayd Johnson Haida Gwaii, BC · Photo: Shayd Johnson The ferry from Prince Rupert takes you to Haida Gwaii, an archipelago the Haida have called home for at least 13,000 years. Old-growth cedar runs to the edge of the sea, the towns are small, and the art is everywhere. The Haida Heritage Centre at Ḵay Llnagaay in Skidegate has the Haida Gwaii Museum, carving sheds and a restaurant, 100 m off the route. Near North Beach, the Old Massett Village Council's longhouse cabins at Hiellen have wood fireplaces, with tent sites beside them. A few more places worth a stop These don't belong to a single route, but each is worth planning a day around. Whistler. The Squamish Lil'wat Cultural Centre in the Upper Village is under a kilometre from the Sea to Sky Trail. Kamloops. The Secwépemc Museum & Heritage Park is run by Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc. Its programs include the history of the former Kamloops Indian Residential School, which stands next to the park. North Shore. Takaya Tours takes you out from Cates Park in 35-foot ocean-going canoes, with Tsleil-Waututh guides. The North Shore bike routes get you there easily. Lillooet. On the Great Northern Bikepacking Route north of town, Xwísten Experience Tours brings you to the Bridge River fishing rocks, a salmon fishery thousands of years old, with a grill on site. Vancouver. Among the big institutional museums, the University of British Columbia's Museum of Anthropology (MOA) is the one to see. It holds a major collection of Northwest Coast art, admission is free for Indigenous visitors, and their own directions warn that the ride up to campus is hilly. Victoria. The Royal BC Museum closed its First Peoples galleries in 2022. Jonathan Hunt House and Our Living Languages have since reopened, but Totem Hall is still closed. Indigenous-owned places to stay # This is just a selection of Indigenous-owned accommodations, those near a trail. For more Indigenous businesses across BC, see Indigenous Tourism BC . Fraser Valley Fraser River Lodge , Cheam First Nation, near Agassiz. A kilometre off the Canyon to Coast Trail loop, with dining on site, Mount Cheam out the window and a resident bison herd. Vancouver Island Pacheedaht Campground , Port Renfrew. On the Port Renfrew–Cowichan loop; beach, river and forest sites, open year-round. Snaw-naw-as Campground , Nanoose Bay. Right on the Island touring route. Qualicum First Nation Campground , where the Big Qualicum River meets the sea. On Highway 19A, first-come tent sites, May to September. Puntledge RV Park and Campground , K'ómoks First Nation, Courtenay. Under a kilometre from the Courtenay Riverway and a short walk from downtown; showers and laundry. We Wai Kai Campground , Quadra Island. Beside Rebecca Spit, a paved ride from the ferry, tent sites. The Cabins at Alert Bay , 'Namgis First Nation. Fourteen cabins with kitchens, a short ride from the ferry. Kwa'lilas Hotel , Port Hardy. On the touring route's last kilometres; pub and restaurant downstairs. Tin Wis Resort , Tla-o-qui-aht Nation, Tofino. 85 rooms on tinwis Beach, breakfast included, 400 m from the Tofino path. Tsawaak RV Resort , Tla-o-qui-aht Nation, Tofino. 300 m from the path, only five tent sites, so book early. Himwitsa Lodge , downtown Tofino. Gallery and smoked fish store in the same building. Wya Point , Ucluelet First Nation. Oceanside tent sites and hot showers on 600 acres of old growth, 1.4 km off ʔapsčiik t̓ašii; reserve online, no walk-ups. Lillooet and the Fraser Canyon (bikepacking routes) Retasket Lodge , T'it'q'et community, Lillooet. A 20-room motel on a hilltop above town, right on the Great Northern. Lil'tem' Mountain Hotel , Tsal'alh Band, Seton Portage. Hotel and cabins between Anderson and Seton lakes, on the Great Northern and The Big Griz. Spapium Farm , Nlaka'pamux heritage farm near Lytton, farmed since 1882. Ten campsites on the Coast Mountains Bikepacking route. Tuckkwiowhum Campground , Boston Bar First Nation. 400 m off Highway 1, with showers and a heritage village on site. South Okanagan sx̌ʷəx̌ʷnitkʷ (Okanagan Falls) Campground , run by the Osoyoos Indian Band. 100 m from the Kettle Valley Rail Trail. sẃiẃs (Haynes Point) Campground , Osoyoos, run by the band. On the South Okanagan–Similkameen bike network. Nk'Mip Campground , Osoyoos Lake. Beach and indoor pool, a kilometre from the network; priced for RVs more than tents. Kootenays Ainsworth Hot Springs Resort , owned by the Lower Kootenay Band (Yaqan Nukiy) of the Ktunaxa Nation since 2015, right on the Kaslo–Slocan loop above Kootenay Lake. The hot pools include a 150-foot horseshoe cave the Ktunaxa have used for healing since time immemorial. Nearby, the Slocan Valley Rail Trail has panels at Slocan Narrows and Vallican about more than 3,000 years of Indigenous settlement. Highway 16 and Haida Gwaii Key-oh Lodge , Burns Lake. A 42-room hotel right on Highway 16. Witset Campground , beside the Bulkley. Showers, laundry and charging; the canyon museum is a short walk. Kasiks , Kitsumkalum, between Terrace and Prince Rupert. Right on the highway, hot showers and a restaurant on site. Crest Hotel , Prince Rupert. Gitxaała-owned since 2023. Haida House at Tllaal , Tlell. Lodge rooms, cabins and a dining room on the river, on the Haida Gwaii route. Gwaii Naay Island House , Masset. The first Haida-owned hotel in town, six rooms in a former Red Cross hospital. Hiellen Longhouse Village , North Beach, run by the Old Massett Village Council. Cedar longhouse cabins with wood fireplaces, and tent sites. More resources # The BC Bike Stops directory has an "Indigenous tourism" filter in the sidebar with three boxes: Owned, Operated, and Culture & heritage. Tick any of them and the map shows only those places, in every category from campgrounds to cafes. That link opens it with all three ticked. Zoom in on your route to see what's along the way. Indigenous Tourism BC has a free app , too. And read their Travel Responsibly page before a trip; it's short and good. Accurate as of September 2026. Read on the web → Talks and appearances Oct 1 Attending the BEST event Better Environmentally Sound Transportation (BEST) is marking 35 years with an evening panel, "Building Streets for Life: How to Create a City for All Ages," at Creekside Community Centre in Vancouver. Event → Oct 28–30 Presenting at the Active Transportation Summit Directors Heather Piwowar and Colleen MacDonald are presenting on cycle tourism in BC at the BC Cycling Coalition's summit in Victoria. title: Dispatch August 2026
desc: Hot news and deep dives for BC cycle tourism, August 2026
body: Home / Field Notes / August 2026 Dispatch BC Cycle Tourism Society The Field Notes Dispatch August 2026 Issue #3 · Monthly newsletter on cycle tourism in British Columbia It's late August in BC: the blackberries are ripe, the days are still warm, and we're all checking the smoke forecast before we roll out. We are right there with you in this issue of the newsletter. This summer we launched Plan Your To and Fro , a new tool on the site: pick any two BC communities to see which buses, trains, and ferries will get you there with your bike. It's useful if you already have a destination in mind, and just plain fun+interesting if you poke around... read our feature to learn more :) Also in this issue: a cyclist's guide to berry snacking in BC, how to plan around wildfire smoke (with links to useful BC resources!), how to get a bike mechanic to come to you, a fresh crop of trip reports, and a poll about what we're all really fantasizing about as we cycle through a hot afternoon. Enjoy! The Feature Plan Your To and Fro: which buses, trains, and ferries take your bike # August 30, 2026 How do you bike somewhere that is too far away to get to by bike? Drive? But then you have to find a place to park your car for a while, and it doesn't solve getting home from a point-to-point ride, and is awkward for those of us without a car. What about transit? Is there transit? Buses, trains, ferries, and floatplanes can be a lovely way to see the province. It hasn't been easy to figure out how practical it is to travel that way between two communities, let alone with your bike in tow. But now it is :) Doesn't Google Maps already do this? # Surprisingly, no. Ask Google Maps for transit from Castlegar to Kamloops and it says, "Sorry, we could not calculate transit directions," then offers to route you there by car. The buses exist; most of BC's intercity carriers just never make it into the big trip planners. Our page for that pair shows what actually runs: a weekly Kootenay coach that does the long haul, and the one direct bus chain that breaks because its Kelowna leg ( Silver City Stagelines ), alas, won't take your bike. Sites like Rome2Rio come closer, and they were part of our inspiration. But none of them will tell you whether the bus takes bikes, whether yours needs to be boxed, what it costs, or whether an e-bike is welcome. That gap is why we built Plan Your To and Fro . How it works # Go to Plan Your To and Fro , then pick two BC places from the dropdowns. You get a page listing every way we know to move yourself and your bike between them, step by step: buses, trains, ferries, water taxis, floatplanes, carpools, even a one-way rental car where that's genuinely the only link. There are 115 places to choose from. Seattle and Calgary are in the dropdowns too, as honorary BC cities: if you live there, we'd love to make it easy to come ride here. What we don't have, at least for now, is schedules or prices on the page. We know the map, not the timetable, so each option links to the operator for times and fares so you can look those up before your trip. We do try to list whether you need to box or bag your bike, if e-bikes are ok, if reservations are required. And if you know more than we've got listed, let us know so we can add it to the tool. When you'd reach for it # Riding point to point. You've ridden Castlegar to Kamloops; now you and the bike need to get home . Riding a loop somewhere else. The riding is in the Kootenays but your front door isn't. Get there, ride the loop, come home. Changing plans late. A smoked-out forecast, or plain whim. The pages show which buses and ferries can move the whole trip to a clearer corner of the province; our wildfire smoke how-to covers that move in detail. Things we learned building it # BC Transit holds the province together. It shows up in the answers for more than 8 of every 10 pairings: front rack, no fee, all over BC. Obviously BC Transit isn't perfect, but it is a workhorse: thanks, bus driver. The intercity spines are alive and take bikes. Ebus and Rider Express cover the interior corridors, Mountain Man Mike's links Vancouver to the Kootenays all the way to Fernie, BC Bus North covers the highways out of Prince George, and VIA Rail checks bikes through the mountains. You can take your bike on a floatplane. Harbour Air will carry it with the front wheel off for $20 plus the weight fee of the bike, on all of their routes. Just don't book a Twin Otter on the Vancouver to Victoria route. Alas, some key carriers don't take bikes. Island Link, we are looking at you, and a few others, making some connections much more challenging. We will advocate for better bike connections in these corridors, but in the meantime the tool shows these options while showing plainly that you cannot take your bike on these carriers. Carpools and one-way car rentals fill gaps. Do you know about Poparide , the carpool platform? Poparide drivers who take bikes mark it with a bicycle icon, super easy! Where no bus or boat crosses a gap, we list one-way rental car options too. It's not just BC Ferries on the water. Hullo crosses the Strait, inland ferries are free and fun, the SeaBus views are fantastic, and water taxis let you get far from town. (Our ferry directory lists many more boats, including the international runs to Port Angeles and Seattle.) Every carrier has its own packaging rules. Ebus wants bikes bagged in cloth, not plastic. Rider Express charges $50, non-refundable. VIA Rail checks bikes as baggage, but only at staffed stations. The pages spell out each carrier's quirks so you find out at home, not at the curb. E-bikes are a patchwork. Roll onto BC Ferries freely, but Hullo says no, most airlines say no, and BC Transit takes them only under 25 kilograms with the battery carried on board. If you ride electric, read the bike facts on your option before you commit. The network goes further than we expected. The longest pair with a real answer runs from Haida Gwaii to Sparwood, the Elk Valley coal town in BC's far southeastern corner that keeps the world's biggest truck parked by the highway: 1,244 kilometres as the crow flies, chaining a BC Ferries sailing, a VIA Rail train, two Ebus legs, and Mountain Man Mike's to finish. The page for Haida Gwaii to Sparwood: 1,244 kilometres, one itinerary Haida Gwaii to Sparwood: one sailing, one train, three buses Missing info? # Behind every option is a listing in our directory with the operator's bike policy and where we found it. Things change: routes get cut, policies get rewritten, ferries go on refit. Every page has a tell-us link, and we mean it. If you find something wrong or out of date, that report fixes the page for the next rider too. Reading this from the USA? Come ride in BC! # For the sake of making it easy for you to figure out how to get here, we've included Seattle WA as an honorary BC town in To and Fro . Check out all the great ways to get here: you can take a ferry up to Victoria, a train to Vancouver, or heck even a floatplane. Come north, bring your bike, and stay awhile! Try it # Start with the trip you've been putting off because getting there seemed like the hard part: Plan Your To and Fro . We'd love to hear what you think. Accurate as of August 2026. Place counts are from the August 2026 build of the To and Fro pages. Read on the web → Also in this issue The Trailside Buffet: a cyclist's guide to BC's wild berries Late August is huckleberry and blackberry season. What to look for, where and when to find it, and where picking is actually allowed. READ THE DEEP DIVE → HOW TO: Plan around wildfire smoke in BC Fire season is part of BC riding now. The forecasting tools are genuinely good, BC is enormous, and a bit of planning usually means changing your trip, not losing it. READ THE HOW-TO → HOW TO: Get a bike mechanic to come to you Awkward to get your bike to a bike shop? In BC, sometimes the bike shop can come to you. Mobile repair vans don't do roadside assistance, but they can still save a touring trip. READ THE HOW-TO → Quick poll In July we asked whether BC's three summer long weekends are prime touring time. The people have spoken, all five of them: "good luck finding a campsite or room" takes it, with "just another day in biking paradise" close behind. Two optimists do plan their touring around the long weekends. Labour Day here we come! Weigh in on our question for this month: Loading... News from the field Aug 5 Two more pieces of the Okanagan Rail Trail Two new sections opened August 5: a paved stretch along Airport Way at Kelowna International Airport, and 3.2 km of gravel from Old Vernon Road to Beaver Lake Road that closes a gap riders used to bridge on the Highway 97 shoulder. Only 2.6 km remains before the trail runs unbroken from Kelowna to Coldstream, pending a land transfer involving the Okanagan Indian Band. And Vernon received $3 million to strengthen the connections between East Hill and the rail trail. Castanet → Aug 11 The Kettle Valley Rail Trail makes another bucket list BCBusiness named the Kettle Valley Rail Trail (KVR) to its bucket list of five BC bike trails, alongside the Cowichan Valley Trail and the Slocan Valley rail trail. Travel writers keep discovering Coalmont, too, a tiny ex-mining town right on the trail near Princeton with trailside camping and swim spots. August's fire near Trout Creek burned close to the trail, so check current conditions before you ride. Bucket list → Aug 17 Nanaimo extends the E&N Trail The City of Nanaimo and the Island Corridor Foundation are adding about 900 metres to the Esquimalt and Nanaimo (E&N) Trail's south end, from Junction Avenue to Extension Road, with $550,000 approved by council. Short, but it's another piece of the corridor Island riders hope to one day follow end to end. Island Corridor Foundation → Applications close Sept 10 One more overnighter before the season turns Building Momentum Bikepacking, the Nelson crew whose gear library we covered in July, is running a year-end overnighter in the Kootenays: 80 km, applications close September 10. Apply → Oct 28–30 Come say hi at the Active Transportation Summit The BC Cycling Coalition brings its Active Transportation Summit to Victoria October 28 to 30: three days, 30 sessions, and more than 80 speakers on making it easier to get around BC by bike and on foot. Heather will be one of them. Registration is open. Summit → BC Trip Reports People keep writing about riding BC. A few favourites from the past month. Aug 6 Vernon to Fernie, the whole story Last month we pointed at Rick McCharles's 11-day, 750 km ride across BC's rail-trail spine. The rest of the series is worth your time too: the pre-trip gear list, Myra Canyon's trestles on video, the first flat tire of his riding life, and the snapped rear rack that ended the trip in Fernie. BestHike → Aug 7 Three days on the Cowichan Valley 8 Anna Dong wrote up the Cowichan Valley 8 for BIKEPACKING.com's Friday Debrief: a 20-person group ride from Seattle friends, 210 km over three days of trestles, lakes, and gravel, rolling into Victoria. Friday Debrief → and the route → August The filmmaker in the group Yeti Adventure Films is a small BC YouTube channel making proper bikepacking documentaries: five friends riding gravel from Kamloops toward Abbotsford, until a washed-out climb forced a rethink partway in. Their earlier films circle Shuswap Lake. Watch → Ride along with us The next Dispatch lands in September, with a new BC cycling podcast worth a listen (you may recognize one of the voices). Subscribe to receive it. Subscribe → Issue #3 · August 2026 · BC Cycle Tourism Society Web version · Past issues & Field Notes archive

title: Dispatch July 2026
desc: Hot news and deep dives for BC cycle tourism, July 2026
body: Home / Field Notes / July 2026 Dispatch BC Cycle Tourism Society The Field Notes Dispatch July 2026 Issue #2 · Monthly newsletter on cycle tourism in British Columbia It's the heart of BC riding season, and this issue is a full one. May and June took us on the road. At the Canadian Trail Summit in Winnipeg, I (Heather Piwowar) presented on cycle tourism in the tourism breakout. A few weeks earlier, the Outdoor Recreation Council of BC's 50th anniversary conference in Kamloops had me and Colleen MacDonald on a panel about sustainable tourism. Two rooms, one message: trails are economic infrastructure, and BC's are worth investing in. Closer to home, the BC Cycle Tourism Society just had its first board meeting. A small step on paper, a big one for us. In this issue: 145 places across BC have earned their place on BC Bike Stops, we're looking at the law behind every road you ride, and we've rounded up the latest cycling news, trip reports, and ways to get involved. The Feature 145 places in BC that want you to visit with your bike # July 30, 2026 Smithers, BC · Photo: Andrew Strain We hit a milestone this month: the first 145 accredited places went live on BC Bike Stops. These aren't paid placements or self-nominations we took on faith. Each one earned it the same way: by showing us, in their own words, how they welcome cyclists. Red Beard Cafe in Kamloops was one of the first to be accredited. "Red Beard is just off the Rivers Trail on the flat North Shore of Kamloops. We have many bike racks, and locks if you forget yours." Locks if you forget yours. That's exactly the kind of detail we were hoping to find. Red Beard Cafe, Kamloops, BC · Photo: Red Beard Cafe In Vancouver, Our Community Bikes has been fixing bikes and teaching people to fix their own since long before we showed up. "We strive to create an environment where all people feel safe, included and respected." Our Community Bikes, Vancouver, BC · Photo: Our Community Bikes And Accent Inns has made bike-friendliness a chain-wide promise across five BC locations. "Love your bike? Bring it to your room." There's also a wash station and a 37-piece tool kit. It's not just cafes, shops, and hotels. At The Butchart Gardens , "it is always a pleasure for us to welcome bikers." And Kelowna's Okanagan Heritage Museum encourages visitors to arrive by bike. The full directory now covers more than 18,000 places across BC, from water refills to welcoming beds. New to BC Bike Stops? We introduced the program in our launch announcement . The accredited ones are where someone has gone further and put it in writing, on their website or to us directly. Know a business that belongs on the list? Send them to bccycletourism.ca/apply . — Heather Read on the web → Also in this issue BC road rules are being rewritten BC is consulting on changes to the Motor Vehicle Act. Most of the attention goes to city streets. Here are five proposed changes that matter most when you're touring. READ THE DEEP DIVE → HOW TO: Take your bike in a taxi or rideshare No bike rack required. With a little prep, a bagged bike rides fine in a cab, an Uber, or a Coastal Rides car. READ THE HOW-TO → HOW TO: Keep your drivetrain happy on a multi-day ride Mat from Trip Longer cleans his chain every night on tour, and it takes five minutes. Here's his routine. READ THE HOW-TO → Quick poll In May's poll we asked what you look for in a Junuary cycling raincoat. A rigorous scientific sample of four riders settled it: armpit vents win, with a strong showing for anything neon green. Our audience has grown since then, so this month's results might even reach double digits. Everybody's gotta start somewhere. :) Loading... News from the field July 13–15 Sea to Sky corridor stays in public hands Transportation Minister Mike Farnworth confirmed the province will keep the former BC Rail corridor, Squamish to Prince George, in public hands. Two days later we met with MLA Jeremy Valeriote to talk about how cycling could fit into the corridor's future. Ministerial statement → July A bikepacking gear library opens in Nelson Building Momentum Bikepacking, a Nelson group creating space for women, non-binary and gender non-conforming riders, launched a free gear library: bikes, bags, and camping gear on 7 to 14-day loans, donations welcome, and borrowing open to everyone. An Okanagan group is already asking how to copy the model. Gear library → July Two ways to speak up for backcountry access The Outdoor Recreation Council of BC wants to know which resource roads matter for your riding, and has a new guide for weighing in on the forest landscape plans now underway around the province. Resource road survey → and Forest planning guide → July 3–17 New 14 km on the Shuswap North Okanagan Rail Trail A new 14 km section between Rosemond Lake Bridge and Grindrod is open, celebrated with a July 17 ribbon cutting at Mara Trailhead alongside development partner Splatsin te Secwépemc. About 32 km of the Sicamous to Armstrong corridor is now rideable, across three separate segments. Castanet → June 18 Kettle Valley Rail Trail: the door reopens a crack The province stepped partway back from decommissioning the damaged Kettle Valley Rail Trail sections near Princeton. Repairs to three priority segments are now on the table, pending federal disaster-assistance funding and a long-term maintenance commitment from the regional district, whose board decides by the end of 2026. The hardest-hit 17 km near Coquihalla Lakes is still being decommissioned this summer, though the railbed stays, and the province says it is open to reroute proposals from Trans Canada Trail. Progress, not a rescue. Province's announcement → All summer Before you head out Wildfire smoke, road closures, and heat are part of BC summer riding. Our Be Prepared page gathers the checks worth doing before you roll out. Be Prepared → BC Trip Reports People keep writing about riding BC. A few favourites from the past month. July 29 An overnighter to Sooke Potholes The Gravel Buddies crew rode out of Victoria through fields, wildflowers, and oak meadows to camp at Sooke Potholes, lunch spot overlooking Matheson Lake included, and posted it as a ready-made plan for the long weekend. Trip report on Instagram → July 27 11 days from Vernon to Fernie Rick McCharles logged about 750 km across the province's rail-trail spine: the Okanagan Rail Trail, Myra Canyon, the Kettle Valley, and the Columbia & Western. Trip report on BestHike → July 25 20 days across BC A self-supported Reddit trip report, Banff to Vancouver, taking in Paleface Pass and the Kettle Valley Rail Trail through Myra Canyon, with a lively question thread. Trip report on Reddit → July 16 Four days of small-town stops around the Cowichan Valley Leigh McAdam's Victoria loop for Trans Canada Trail, out the Galloping Goose and home by the Lochside, is also a stop-by-stop case for how bike travellers spread their spending through small communities. Read at Trans Canada Trail → July 10 Spiraling on the Tree to Sea Loop A long read on the 1,000 km gravel loop from Comox around northern Vancouver Island. Read on BIKEPACKING.com → July 9 The best campsite is 90 minutes away A reflective photo essay on a close-to-home BC overnight, riverside camping and all. Read on BIKEPACKING.com → Ride along with us The next Dispatch lands in your inbox in August. Subscribe to receive it. title: Dispatch May/June 2026
desc: Hot news and deep dives for BC cycle tourism, May/June 2026
body: Home / Field Notes / May/June 2026 Dispatch BC Cycle Tourism Society The Field Notes Dispatch May/June 2026 Issue #1 · Monthly newsletter on cycle tourism in British Columbia Welcome to the inaugural issue of The Field Notes Dispatch . The BC Cycle Tourism Society wants to make British Columbia an easier, safer, and more welcoming place to explore by bike. We're starting with building out practical information for riders, communities, and businesses — and we're starting by listening. A great bike trip is made of two pieces, right? A beautiful, interesting place — we have that covered, BC is incredible. The other piece is the people we meet along the way. So we're starting with an invitation: we'd love to hear from you. Read the full hello → The Feature Every BC bike trip starts with the same questions. Not anymore. # May 27, 2026 Whistler, BC When I planned my ride on the Sea to Sky Trail with my family, I had questions I couldn't fully answer from my desk. Would the hostels have somewhere to store our bikes inside overnight? Would the buses take three bikes? The Squamish Connector said two maximum. SkyLynx would take three but only bagged… what kind of bag, exactly? We found out, eventually. The Whistler hostel had a ski room. The Squamish hostel had locked cargo containers. The bus took all three bikes despite what the website said. I overnighted a bike bag from Amazon and packed my bike in a parking lot. Every answer required a phone call, an email, or a calculated guess. Every touring cyclist in BC is doing the same detective work. That's the problem BC Bike Stops is designed to fix. What we built, and why # Quebec figured this out a long time ago. Their Bienvenue cyclistes! program has been running for decades, and 31% of overnight cycle tourists in Quebec adapt their itinerary based on Bienvenue cyclistes! certification. Ontario By Bike has done the same since 2007 and now has over 1,600 certified businesses. BC has had pieces of this, GoByBike BC's directory among them, but nothing built for touring. Until now. BC Bike Stops is the BC Cycle Tourism Society's accreditation for businesses that serve bikepackers and cycle tourists well. Seven categories, criteria written for what each one needs. The part I care about: every listing tells you what you're getting before you arrive. Squamish Adventure Inn, Squamish, BC For accommodations, secure indoor overnight storage is required. Not a bike rack out front. The arrangement gets described in the listing, so you know whether it's a locked room, a garage, or bikes-in-rooms before you book. (Whistler hostel: would have passed.) Campgrounds commit to always having space for self-contained cyclists arriving by bike. Not "we'll try." A real commitment, for groups up to six, for one night. Restaurants have to give you somewhere to park where you can keep an eye on your loaded bike. Anyone who's parked a fully loaded bike at a rack 2 blocks away while trying to enjoy lunch knows why. Squamish, BC And transportation — buses, ferries, shuttles, luggage transfer — is its own category in our criteria, with the listing telling you about bagging requirements, advance booking, and bike fees. (SkyLynx: would have told me about the bag.) How it works # Apply through our website. We review applications ourselves. You'll hear from us. Approved businesses appear in the directory, filterable by category, region, and the amenities that matter to a touring cyclist. If you run a business that's great for cyclists, Apply for accreditation → . If you know one, send them our way. If you're planning a trip, search the directory → . We built these criteria for cyclists like the three of us, sorting out bike bags in a Whistler bus loop ... and cyclists like you. If we missed something, tell us: contact us → . — Heather ** Bikes on BC buses and ferries is its own saga! More in a future issue. ** Sources: Bienvenue cyclistes! attestation program , Vélo Québec; Ontario By Bike business directory , Ontario By Bike. Read on the web → Also in this issue HOW TO: Take your bike on a coach bus Coach buses are one of BC's most underrated tools for cycle tourists: economical, low-carbon, and they usually accept bikes. Here's how to pack and ride along. READ THE HOW-TO → Quick poll Loading... News from the field June 5–7 Revelstoke Bikepacking Weekend Revelstoke Cycling Association and Revy Outdoors are hosting a beginner-friendly bikepacking weekend, with an in-town social Friday and an overnight campout Saturday–Sunday. Register → June 2–7 National Bike Count / Pedal Poll Vélo Canada Bikes is running Pedal Poll / Sondo Vélo — a national bike and micromobility count to help build the case for safer cycling infrastructure across Canada. Pedal Poll → June 1–19 Okanagan Rail Trail closure A section of the Okanagan Rail Trail between Kick Willie Road and Kekuli Bay Provincial Park will be closed for erosion-prevention work. RDNO notice → May 30–June 5 Go by Bike Week Go by Bike Week runs May 30–June 5. Log rides, win prizes, and find a Celebration Station near you. GoByBike BC → and HUB Cycling → May 15 CN Rail Sea to Sky corridor Province confirmed in Hansard that it will not sell or dismantle the CN Rail Sea to Sky corridor. Farnworth's Hansard commitments → May 10 KVR / The Narwhal The Narwhal reports that KVR decommissioning would create the first permanent break in the Trans Canada Trail, placing it in the broader context of BC Parks' maintenance backlog. Read the piece → May 2 Port Alberni rail-with-trail Alberni Pacific Railway extended service along Port Alberni's Quay-to-Quay Railside corridor, with renewed participation from Tseshaht and Hupacasath First Nations. Read here → Ride along with us The next Dispatch lands in your inbox in June. Subscribe to receive it. body: Dave Heath Kaslo, BC Support The people who keep BC rideable Home / Trail Organizations Most BC trails are a team effort. A city, a regional district, or the Province usually owns the trail. A volunteer society fought for it, raises money for it, or comes out each spring to clear it. Here are 50 of those societies, in six regions, picked for the paths, rail trails, and gravel that touring riders love. Back the ones whose trails you ride. Want the stories behind them? Read Who to thank for our BC trails , our Thanksgiving Field Note. Donations go directly to each organization, not to the BC Cycle Tourism Society. Where you see “tax receipt,” the organization is a registered charity. Donations to the BC Cycle Tourism Society are also welcome, contact us for details. Most of their work is grooming the Cornish Mountain and Meadows ski trails, and they welcome bikes and boots too. Membership is twenty dollars a year, and it goes straight to trail upkeep.
