title: About
desc: About the BC Cycle Tourism Society — a nonprofit organization supporting cycle tourism and bikepacking across British Columbia.
body: Home / About About the BC Cycle Tourism Society British Columbia has some of the world's most spectacular cycling terrain: rail trails through mountain valleys, coastal routes along the Pacific, wine country roads, rainforest paths, and gravel that goes on forever. What it has been missing is a provincial organization to help turn these remarkable cycling assets into a coherent, connected, and world-class visitor experience. That's what the BC Cycle Tourism Society is building. The whole story on one page: read the backgrounder → We incorporated in spring 2026 as a new nonprofit provincial cycle tourism organization working to build the marketing, standards, partnerships, and policy environment that can help cycle tourism and bikepacking thrive across British Columbia. Our goal is to grow cycle tourism as a meaningful economic opportunity for rural communities, tourism organizations, local businesses, and BC as a whole. BC Cycle Tourism Society grew out of several organizations already working to make cycling, trails, and active transportation stronger in British Columbia: The BC Cycling Coalition, Trails BC, and Let's Go Biking. The Society is building an Advisory Council with regional knowledge and sector experience. We're a regional organization member of the Outdoor Recreation Council of BC (ORCBC), and a sector association member of the Tourism Industry Association of BC (TIABC). We work alongside the BC Cycling Coalition and Trails BC on advocacy and active tourism, and we help Bike Across Canada with mapping and web development for their cross-country route network. We look to places like New Zealand and Québec as models: jurisdictions that invested in coordinated route networks, destination development, and visitor information, and built cycle tourism into a recognized economic driver. Our team Heather Piwowar | Founding Director (full-time volunteer) Heather Piwowar is a Vancouver-based cyclist with 25 years of touring experience. She is an Adventure Cycling Association tour leader and the planner behind all the family bike trips. She joined the cross-organization cycle tourism working group in 2025 as a Director of Trails BC and proposed the business model that became the Society. All that touring comes with opinions: see her favourite gear , especially the bike sandals. Before founding the BC Cycle Tourism Society, Heather co-founded OurResearch, a nonprofit that builds open research infrastructure. Unpaywall and OpenAlex, two of its core tools, are used by millions of people across research, journalism, and public-interest communities. Heather holds a BS and MEng from MIT and a PhD in Biomedical Informatics. Board of Directors The Society is governed by a volunteer Board of Directors, which oversees the organization's direction and finances. Colleen MacDonald | Board Director Colleen MacDonald is the author of the Let's Go Biking website and three BC cycling guidebooks: Vancouver , Okanagan , and Vancouver Island . A Board Director with the BC Cycling Coalition, she is passionate about promoting cycle tourism across British Columbia. She loves exploring and discovering great places to ride, walk and roll — in BC and around the world. Colin Stein | Board Director Colin has been working in active transportation advocacy on and off since 2013, including previous staff, consulting, and Board roles with the BC Cycling Coalition, GoByBike BC, BEST, and HUB Cycling. A Vancouver resident since 1995, Colin began his career in communications, marketing, and operations in the private sector and public sectors, including economic development, health education, insurance, software, and sports. Since 2022, Colin has been working in BC’s gulf islands as a communications and engagement consultant and project manager for Rural Islands Economic Partnership , a Salt Spring Island-based NGO. In 2022, he also self-published an oral history of bicycle advocacy and activism on the south coast, Vanbikes : Vancouver’s Bicycle People and the Fight for Transportation Change, 1986-2011. Talks and appearances BEST 35th anniversary: “Building Streets for Life: How to Create a City for All Ages” (October 1, 2026): Heather will be attending. BC Active Transportation Summit (Victoria, October 2026): Heather and Colleen will be presenting on cycle tourism in BC. Come say hi! Vancouver, Coast & Mountains Industry Forum (January 19, 2027): Heather will be attending. Parksfest 2026 (Metro Vancouver Regional Parks Foundation, Burnaby Lake, September 2026): Heather attended. BikeSense podcast (BC Cycling Coalition, 2026): “Can BC Become the Next New Zealand for Cycle Tourism?” Heather on the coordination BC has been missing and the tools that fix it. Canadian Trail Summit (Winnipeg, June 2026): Heather was a panelist on the summit's trail tourism panel, speaking on welcoming infrastructure and provincial coordination (then as a director of Trails BC). ORCBC conference (May 2026): Heather and Colleen presented on cycle tourism in BC (Heather then with Trails BC). BC Bike Show (Vancouver, February 2026): Heather, Colleen, Colin, and others from the working group that became the Society hosted a booth on cycle touring in BC. We use AI BC Cycle Tourism Society uses AI tools — particularly Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) — to synthesize information, refine ideas, and compose text. It has enabled us to accomplish a lot quickly with a very small team. We bring our deep cycling, bikepacking, tourism, nonprofit, and local expertise to every interaction. We credit creators Route makers BIKEPACKING.com, the Adventure Cycling Association, and Let's Go Biking share their official route descriptions and photos with us directly; we republish them with permission and credit. We credit photographers on photos wherever we can, and we name the people and organizations who have helped us on our thanks page . We value Open BC Cycle Tourism Society benefits every day from open resources, including for example: Vancouver's open data portal, OpenStreetMap, publicly shared Ride with GPS routes, Creative Commons–licensed photography, and the publicly filed bylaws and constitutions of fellow BC societies. We're grateful to those communities, and to the contributors, advisors, partners, and volunteers who have shared their time and expertise with us directly. We believe in giving back, both to build trust and to help others learn from and build on what we've done. If something would help you that you don't see here, please reach out. If you are a cycle tourism coordination organization, or are interested in getting something like BC Cycle Tourism Society running in your province/state/country, say hello , let's share tips! We are on Indigenous land The cycling routes and communities featured on this website are located throughout what is now British Columbia, on many First Nations territories, including unceded and treaty lands. We acknowledge the enduring relationships, rights, laws, cultures, and stewardship responsibilities of First Nations in these places. Read our full land acknowledgement → We want to hear from you BC Cycle Tourism Society is incorporated as a BC nonprofit society. We're looking to connect with communities, tourism organizations, cycling advocates, route stewards, Indigenous partners, businesses, and others who see the potential for cycle tourism and bikepacking in BC. If you want to be part of this, we'd love to hear from you. hello@bccycletourism.ca

title: Advocacy
desc: What BC Cycle Tourism Society advocates for: getting there with a bike, e-bikes, safe roads between communities, protecting rail corridors and resource road access, measuring the cycle tourism economy, and tourism that respects place. Includes our Sea-to-Sky rail corridor reports and the Kettle Valley Rail Trail.
body: Home / Advocacy Advocacy Cycle touring depends on a lot of decisions that happen in meeting rooms: whether an old rail corridor is kept in one piece, whether a washed-out trail gets repair money, whether a bus takes bikes. Those decisions often get made without anyone in the room who travels by bike. Our goal is to change that, so the benefits and interests of cycle tourism in BC are considered. We come at this as a tourism economic development organization, and it shapes how we advocate. We do the research first, publish it openly, and offer it to the people making the decision. We are a young organization, so some of what follows is what we do today, and more of it is what we plan to do as we grow. The datasets and reports behind the work we have already done are on our Research and Data page. Here is what we care about, in three groups: the journey itself, the corridors and trails it runs on, and growing cycle tourism well. The journey # Getting there with a bike. A trip only works if the bike can reach the start and get home from the finish. We publish what every ferry, bus, train, and airline in BC actually does with bikes, so riders and operators are working from the same information. As we grow, we plan to work with carriers on capacity, packaging rules, and reservable bike spaces. E-bikes. E-bike touring is the fastest-growing part of cycle tourism, and most of BC's rules were written before it existed. We make the case for charging along multi-day routes, for carriage policies on buses and ferries that fit e-bikes as they actually are, and for consistent access rules across parks and Crown land. Safe roads between communities. Most touring routes include stretches of highway between trail sections, and a narrow shoulder can be the reason an otherwise great route does not work. We support paved shoulders and comfortable connections on the roads that link trails and communities. Those few kilometres often decide whether a whole route is rideable. Signage and wayfinding. We would love to see a provincial standard for route markers and distance posts, so a rider can follow a route across regional boundaries without the signage changing dialect at every border. Campgrounds that expect cyclists. A lower rate for arriving without a car, always room for someone who rode in, and no two-night minimums for a traveller who is, by definition, passing through. Corridors and trails # Rail corridors. BC's retired rail lines are the closest thing the province has to ready-made long-distance cycling routes: gentle grades, communities every few hours, and scenery that sells itself. Some corridor sections have already been lost to decommissioning, and a few more decisions like that are being made right now. Once a corridor is broken up, reassembling it is close to impossible, so the useful moment to speak up is before the decision, not after. We make the case for holding corridors intact while their future is being worked out, and for trail conversion when the trains stop. Trail designation. Surface quality is what makes a trail work for touring, and shared motorized use changes that surface quickly. Long stretches of BC rail trail that were once rideable on a loaded touring bike no longer are. We plan to bring the touring rider's needs into designation decisions, which rarely hear from anyone who rides a loaded bike 80 km a day. Resource roads. Much of BC's best bikepacking runs on resource roads, and access can disappear with a locked gate or an unrepaired washout. No government agency is responsible for keeping resource roads open for recreation. The Outdoor Recreation Council of BC (ORCBC) is building a provincial inventory of the resource roads that matter for recreation through its Resource Road Access Survey , and we encourage riders and cycling organizations to put their routes on that map. Motorized recreation groups are well represented at that table. Cyclists should be too. Climate resilience funding. Floods, fires, and washouts damage BC trails every year, and repair money is rarely part of the original build budget, so a closure can outlast the damage by years. We make the case for repair funding as a standing budget line, and we can help estimate what a closed section costs the businesses along it. A cycle tourism infrastructure fund. New Zealand built its Great Rides network through a dedicated national fund, started as a jobs program during a recession, and those trails are now a cornerstone of rural tourism economies there. BC's own Trails Strategy called for sustained trail investment more than a decade ago. We support a dedicated provincial fund for cycle tourism infrastructure, so building and repairing routes stops depending on one-off decisions. Growing this well # Measuring the cycle tourism economy. When a cycling sector measures its economic impact, investment follows. Mountain Bike BC has shown how this works: economic impact studies in six BC communities helped unlock provincial trail funding and a standing place in destination marketing. That evidence base does not exist yet for cycle touring in BC, so we are building it, starting with the Sea-to-Sky reports below. Good numbers also give Destination British Columbia what it needs to market BC as a cycle touring destination to the world. Tourism that respects place. BC does not need more visitors everywhere. It needs the right visitors in the right places, at a pace those places choose. We try to be deliberate about how and when we direct riders toward small communities and wild places, and we hold that Indigenous communities decide how and whether visitors are invited onto their lands. Part of directing people well is preparing them, so we are building responsible travel into what we publish: Leave No Trace, AdventureSmart trip planning, wildfire awareness, and stopping the spread of invasive species. A few specific topics # Advocacy is slow work, and ours is just getting going. Here are a few topics where it has already started. Sea-to-Sky rail corridor # The former BC Rail line runs about 350 km from North Vancouver through Squamish, Whistler, and the Pemberton Valley to Lillooet and on to 100 Mile House. It is one of the most scenic rail corridors in Canada. Canadian National Railway (CN) has said it intends to end its lease on the line, which put the corridor's future into play through 2026. The province has since said it intends to keep the corridor in public hands. The conversation about the corridor's future has been mostly about freight and passenger rail. Provincial statements do not mention cycling, and regionally, trails have surfaced as one of the things people do not yet agree on. A bikeway running alongside the tracks has been raised publicly by a planner working on corridor feasibility, but as a secondary idea, without numbers attached to it. We think rail and trail are complementary rather than competing, and there is a fair amount of published evidence for that. Around the world, a trail beside a working railway feeds the railway passengers, and the railway extends the trail's reach. The two do better together than either does alone. Our position is that a corridor that stops carrying trains should become a trail, and one that keeps carrying trains should get a bikeway alongside it wherever the terrain allows. Through the spring of 2026 we wrote to the elected officials, planners, local governments, and study teams working on the corridor, and offered to supply that evidence. One of the feasibility study teams took us up on it, with a specific question: how much traffic could cycle tourism actually generate for a passenger service? These two reports are our answer, prepared as input to that work in April 2026. In July 2026 we met with MLA Jeremy Valeriote and members of his staff. He is the Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) for West Vancouver–Sea to Sky, and his office convenes a regional roundtable on the corridor's future. We walked through the economics and talked about where cycling fits. Rail and Trail as Complementary Infrastructure (PDF). Global evidence that rail and trail are mutually reinforcing rather than competing, with case studies from North America, Europe, Australasia, and East Asia. Squamish–D'Arcy Bikeway: Cycle Tourism Economic Research (PDF). The economic case for a bikeway on the corridor: comparable-trail benchmarks, visitor spending evidence, First Nations connections, emergency access, and extension scenarios. There are companion appendices (PDF) with operational recommendations and full references. All three reports are CC BY 4.0 . Share them, quote them, build on them, including commercially, with credit to BC Cycle Tourism Society. Kettle Valley Rail Trail # The Kettle Valley Rail Trail (KVR) is BC's most famous rail trail and the spine of the Trans Canada Trail through the southern Interior, running from Hope through the Okanagan toward the Kootenays. At its best it is world class: the trestles of Myra Canyon alone draw about 75,000 visitors a year. Parts of it are in trouble. The floods of November 2021 destroyed the 67 km between Brookmere and Princeton, and in February 2026 the province announced it intends to decommission that section permanently rather than repair it. In June 2026, after months of local pushback, the province partially reopened that door: it agreed to explore repairs to three segments near Princeton, while decommissioning goes ahead on the westernmost 17 km. Whether those repairs happen depends on long-term maintenance commitments and federal funding, with decisions expected around the end of 2026. Another 67 km of the connected Columbia and Western Rail Trail lost its recreation designation in 2020. We think decommissioning is the wrong economics. The repair has been estimated at $60 million and the decommissioning at $20 million, which means spending $20 million to permanently lose a $60 million asset, along with the visitor spending it brings to communities like Princeton and Merritt. New Zealand faced a similar choice during a recession and chose to build cycle trails as a jobs program, and those trails now anchor rural economies across that country. Reporting on the Brookmere to Princeton decision has called it the first permanent break in the Trans Canada Trail anywhere in Canada. Local governments, trail organizations, and the Trans Canada Trail are at the table working on alternatives, including locally led maintenance plans that answer the question of who looks after the trail once it is repaired. We maintain a section-by-section status assessment of the full corridor and the economic case for repair as rural economic development, and we offer both to anyone working on the corridor's future. This work is early. If you are involved and want to compare notes, we would like to hear from you. Campgrounds and no turn-away # A campground that promises to find room for someone arriving by bike, even when every site is booked, costs almost nothing and changes what is possible on a multi-day trip. In January 2026, seven cycling and outdoor recreation organizations asked Metro Vancouver Regional Parks to adopt that policy, with letters of support from four more, including Destination British Columbia and Trans Canada Trail. The letter was written by our founder, Heather Piwowar, while she was on the board of Trails BC. The full letter, its five asks, and the places the policy already works are on our no turn-away camping page. More coming # Several other pieces of advocacy work are underway. We write them up in Field Notes as they land, and the monthly Dispatch collects them. Subscribe here . Working on something related, or want to compare notes? I would like to hear from you: heather@bccycletourism.ca

title: No turn-away camping
desc: Campgrounds that always find room for someone arriving by bike. The January 2026 letter from seven cycling and outdoor recreation organizations to Metro Vancouver Regional Parks, with the evidence behind it.
body: Home / Advocacy / No turn-away camping No turn-away camping Photo: Heather Piwowar The single most useful thing a campground can do for cycle tourism costs almost nothing: promise that someone who arrives by bike will always be found somewhere to sleep, even when every site is booked. In January 2026, seven cycling and outdoor recreation organizations asked Metro Vancouver Regional Parks to adopt exactly that, as part of its Regional Parks Camping Opportunities Study. Four more organizations sent letters of support, including Destination British Columbia and Trans Canada Trail. Why cyclists need it # A cyclist cannot camp the way a driver can. Weather, fatigue, injury, and mechanical trouble make it hard to commit to a date months ahead, which is what a reservation system asks for. Arriving early to claim a first-come, first-served site is hard when you spend the day riding. And if the campground is full at the end of a long day, riding another 40 km is not a small adjustment. There are practical differences too. A cyclist has no car trunk to keep food away from animals. Distance is the constraint that shapes everything, so sites in many parks matter more than lots of sites in one park. None of this is unusual or extreme. It is what self-contained cycle touring is normally like. The 2025 Metro Vancouver camping study did not consider it at all. What the letter asks for # 1. Adopt a no turn-away policy. Anyone arriving by active transportation gets a place for the night, even when the campground is full, in a communal overflow space or small scattered areas. 2. Add hiker, biker, paddler, and transit sites inside existing campgrounds. Small tent sites, or a shared non-vehicle area, within campgrounds that already exist. 3. Add camping to parks and greenways that have no campground at all. Alongside trails, group campgrounds, or day-use areas. 4. Install what makes it work. Food storage lockers to deter bears and raccoons, safe bike access to and within the campground, and basics like potable water and washrooms. Cyclists can manage on very little, but food storage is the one that matters. 5. Market it. Metro Vancouver already sits on several long-distance routes, including the Trans Canada Trail, Experience the Fraser, the Great Blue Heron Way, and the Pacific Coast route. Word travels fast among cyclists. Of the five, the letter is explicit about which matters most: a no turn-away policy is the single most impactful change. It already works elsewhere # This is a proven policy, not an experiment. Quebec. 103 campgrounds certified under Bienvenue cyclistes!, including 17 provincial and Sépaq parks. Washington State. All 30 state park campgrounds, under a policy adopted in 2000. State parks in ten more American states have since followed. British Columbia. The Capital Regional District includes tent sites for cyclists at the Sooke Potholes Regional Park campground, and BC Parks operates 19 walk-in campgrounds. Alberta. Hiker and biker areas added in 2021 at Spray West Campground, Buller Mountain and Sawmill day-use areas, and Pocaterra overflow campground. The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal towpath. More than 30 primitive hiker and biker sites, one every 10 to 15 km along the trail. The Pacific Coast bike route. A continuous corridor of hiker and biker sites through Washington, Oregon, and California that riders plan multi-week trips around. Who signed it # The letter was signed by Trails BC, the BC Cycling Coalition, HUB Cycling, the Outdoor Recreation Council of BC, the UBC Varsity Outdoor Club, Let's Go Biking, and Our Community Bikes. Letters of support came from Destination British Columbia, Trans Canada Trail, the Federation of Mountain Clubs of BC, and BC Marine Trails. The Metro Vancouver Regional Parks Foundation and CTS Youth Society also expressed support. The support letters make a point worth repeating: this is not only about cyclists. Hikers, paddlers, and people arriving by transit all need the same thing, which is a way to camp that does not assume a car. BC Marine Trails added one caveat we think is right, that a no turn-away policy should cover individuals and small groups, not commercial tour groups. Read the letter # Strengthening Cycle Tourism in Metro Vancouver: Regional Park Campgrounds (PDF, 10 pages). The full letter as submitted on January 2, 2026, with all four letters of support attached. Republished with permission from Trails BC , where it first appeared. The letter was written by Heather Piwowar while she was on the Trails BC board, and submitted by Trails BC on behalf of all the signatories. Where this goes next # No turn-away is one of the things BC Cycle Tourism Society advocates for province-wide, and a commitment we hope campgrounds will make on their own. If you run a campground and want to talk it through, or you have been turned away and want to tell us about it: heather@bccycletourism.ca

title: Research and Data
desc: Preliminary datasets and reports from BC Cycle Tourism Society: an interactive character map of BC's roads and trails, Sea-to-Sky rail corridor reports, and a global cycling route database.
body: Home / Research and Data Research and Data BC Cycle Tourism Society builds its programs on evidence. Along the way we produce datasets and reports that may be useful to trail organizations, researchers, tourism planners, and advocates. Everything on this page is preliminary. It is working material — shared early because it may be useful, not because it is finished. Figures and classifications are subject to revision. The research is led by Heather Piwowar ( Google Scholar · ORCID · LinkedIn ). Working on something related, or want to be kept in the loop as we release new reports and datasets? I'd love to hear from you: heather@bccycletourism.ca Using this data # The datasets on this page, except for the ones derived from OpenStreetMap data (see below), are released under CC0 1.0 Universal , a public domain dedication. We have waived our copyright worldwide. Use them, change them, redistribute them, build a product on them. No permission needed and no conditions attached. Attribution is not legally required under CC0, but often requested as a community norm. A citation facilitates transparency and discovery, so thanks in advance! Every download carries a suggested citation, on the cover sheet of the spreadsheet and at the top of the plain-text column guide. Many of our datasets include measurements built from OpenStreetMap data. Those datasets stay CC0 — just add this attribution too: contains information from OpenStreetMap, © OpenStreetMap contributors. Two datasets are different: the BC Bike Stops directory and the road and path character scores are built directly from OpenStreetMap's own records, so they carry OpenStreetMap's own licence, the Open Database Licence , instead of CC0. The written reports on this page — the Sea-to-Sky reports and the methodology PDFs — are prose rather than data, so they go out under CC BY 4.0 instead: share them and build on them, including commercially, as long as you credit us. The code that produces these files is not packaged for release yet. We hope to release it soon. In the meantime, if you want to know exactly how a number was computed, ask and we will walk you through it. Global cycling route database # A comparative database of 693 multi-day cycling routes worldwide, built to understand what makes routes succeed and how British Columbia compares. Route inventory (Excel) — 693 routes with length, surface, terrain, country, and parent network. Research bibliography (Excel) — 619 studies, reports, and articles about these routes: economic impact studies, visitor surveys, and planning documents, with links. We compiled the routes by hand from route networks' own pages, guidebooks, and tourism inventories. The bibliography is the research we could find about those routes, not everything written about cycle tourism. Neither file is complete, lengths and surfaces are as each route's publisher states them, and a blank cell means we don't know, not that there is nothing to know. Both files are CC0 . BC route metrics # Every published cycling route we list for British Columbia, with the measurements behind its difficulty tier and its descriptive labels: surface, ruggedness, traffic comfort, steepness, remoteness, and how much of the route we could measure at all. The routes are published by route makers across the province. What we add is one consistent description of all of them. Route metrics (Excel) — one row per route, with a column guide and notes on what the numbers do and don't tell you. Also available as CSV with a separate plain-text column guide . A blank cell means we could not measure that thing, not that it is zero. If you want the rider's version of what the labels mean, that lives on how we describe routes . These files are CC0 . The measurements are derived from OpenStreetMap: contains information from OpenStreetMap, © OpenStreetMap contributors. How we rate routes: methods and limitations (PDF) — the full methodology behind the dataset and the labels on our route pages: data sources, matching, every rule table and threshold, validation against HUB Cycling's Metro Vancouver labels, and an unsoftened list of limitations. The character of BC's roads and trails # We are working on ways to characterize routes and bike touring options around British Columbia. Not just how hard a ride is, but what it feels like. Nearly every road and path in the province carries scores for traffic comfort, grade, surface, and remoteness, computed from OpenStreetMap along with public land cover and elevation data. Three more, flow, quiet, and scenic, are computed on 100 metre slices rather than whole roads. Character map — an interactive map rather than a download. Seven ways of reading the same road. Click any road to see why it scored the way it did. Comfort between communities — an interactive map rather than a download. Every BC community routed to its five nearest neighbours on our comfort ratings, each trip coloured by how much traffic you share, with the pairs where the only road is the highway. Two views: public roads and trails only, or forest roads and bare trails allowed. Experimental, and not for navigation. Road and path scores (CSV, about 96 MB, or gzipped at about 20 MB) — one row per road or path, 528,742 of them: the four whole-road scores, the name where OpenStreetMap has one, and a point on it so you can find it. Comes with a plain-text column guide . These three files are served from our asset host, so those links leave this page. The file is too big for Excel and is meant for pandas, R, or a database. How we read the terrain: methods and limitations (PDF) — every rule, threshold, and diagram behind the seven scores, and an unsoftened account of what they do not tell you. One naming note: in the report, surface appears under its model name, ruggedness, and quiet as peaceful. Two things to know before you use the file. The assumed speed and traffic columns are modelling inputs assigned from a road's classification, not measurements taken on it. On a separated path they are meaningless, which is why the map does not show them. And a blank cell means we could not measure that thing, not that it is zero: traffic comfort is blank on about a quarter of the rows, on paths where the classifier declines to guess. These scores are computed, not ridden. We have calibrated them most carefully in Metro Vancouver, so expect rougher edges elsewhere in the province. Flow, quiet, and scenic are not in the file yet. They live on 100 metre slices, and rolling them up to a whole road needs a choice we are not ready to defend. Ask if you want them. The scores are derived from OpenStreetMap, so they carry OpenStreetMap's own licence, the Open Database Licence (ODbL) 1.0 , with the attribution © OpenStreetMap contributors. The methodology report, as prose, is CC BY 4.0 . British Columbia transit routes and bicycle policies # Which buses, ferries, water taxis, trains, and flights connect British Columbia's communities, and what each carrier does with a bicycle. Transit network map — an interactive map rather than a download. Every bus, train, ferry, and water taxi that takes bikes, drawn as hops between neighbouring places. Click any line to see who runs it and how often. A side list names the places hardest to reach without a car. Routes and stops — 348 scheduled services and their 1,091 ordered stops, in two files: routes (Excel, also CSV and column guide ), and stops (Excel, also CSV and column guide ). Carriers and bicycle policies (Excel) — 72 operators: whether they carry bicycles, under what conditions, where the answer came from, and when a person last checked. Also as CSV with a plain-text column guide . Journeys (Excel) — every way of getting between two communities, 99,348 of them, in the order we rank them. Also as CSV (21 MB) with a plain-text column guide . Community connections (Excel) — 18,628 community pairs, with both a neutral summary of what runs and the journey we would suggest. Also as CSV with a plain-text column guide . These five files are CC0 . They are our own compilation from operator sources, with no OpenStreetMap records in them. How we map transit and bicycle policies (PDF) — where the data comes from, how a carrier's bicycle answer is reached, how the connections are computed, and what the whole thing does not tell you. Places in British Columbia that a cyclist might want # Our whole BC Bike Stops directory as data: 18,513 cafes, grocery stores, campgrounds, places to stay, bike shops, attractions, and transport connections, with where they are and what we know about how they treat an arriving cyclist. Three files that join on one column. Places (Excel) — one row per place: category, community, coordinates, tier, ownership, and its OpenStreetMap identifier. Also as CSV (12 MB) with a plain-text column guide . Amenities (Excel) — 54,909 rows, one per place and amenity, with the source and the date we recorded it. Long rather than wide, so it pivots. Also as CSV with a plain-text column guide . Sources (Excel) — where every field of every place came from: OpenStreetMap, our own enrichment, a language model, or a person. Also as CSV with a plain-text column guide . Everything, in one file (JSON Lines, gzipped, 6 MB) — the same places, whole: every field we hold, nested, including the amenity detail and the scores. This is the file our own trip planner reads. If something is missing from it, our planner cannot use it either. These three are licensed under the Open Database Licence (ODbL) 1.0 , with the attribution © OpenStreetMap contributors. Most of the listings began as OpenStreetMap records, which makes this a derivative database and share-alike, unlike our other datasets. How we build the stops directory (PDF) — where the listings come from, what earns each of the four tiers, how the categories and amenities are assigned, and what the directory does not cover. When British Columbia campgrounds open and close # When each campground in our directory opens and closes for the season, which ones stay open all year, and whether you can camp outside the season. We read it from BC Parks data, Recreation Sites and Trails BC data, and campgrounds' own websites between September 30 and October 2, 2026. Campground seasons map — an interactive map rather than a download. Every campground, coloured by when it closes. Pick a night to see what's still open. Campground seasons (Excel, also CSV and column guide ) — one row per campground, 1,395 of them. 858 have a season: 418 with high confidence, 298 medium, and 142 low. The rest are in the file too, each with the reason we have no season for it. How we found campground seasons (PDF) — where the dates come from, how an AI model read them, how we checked its quotes, and what the file does not tell you. Most of these seasons were read by an AI model. Low confidence means the evidence was thin: an indirect hint, a listing site rather than the campground's own page, or a web search result we couldn't confirm on the page it linked to. The date may still be right. Check before you go. For a narrative walk through, region by region, see our Field Note Where can I camp this fall? This file is built on our directory, so it carries the same licence as the stops files: the Open Database Licence (ODbL) 1.0 , with the attribution © OpenStreetMap contributors. The methods report, as prose, is CC BY 4.0 . Sea-to-Sky rail corridor # Two reports prepared as input to a Sea-to-Sky rail feasibility study, April 2026. Rail and Trail as Complementary Infrastructure (PDF) — Global evidence that rail and trail are mutually reinforcing: the trail generates rail passengers, and rail service amplifies the trail's economic output. Case studies from North America, Europe, Australasia, and East Asia. Squamish–D'Arcy Bikeway: Cycle Tourism Economic Research (PDF) — The economic case for a bikeway on the corridor: comparable-trail benchmarks, visitor spending evidence, First Nations connections, emergency access, and extension scenarios. Companion appendices (PDF) with operational recommendations and full references. These three reports are CC BY 4.0 : share them and build on them, including commercially, with credit to BC Cycle Tourism Society. BC rides on Rouvy # Rouvy is an indoor cycling app that plays video of real roads. This is every British Columbia ride on it that we could find: 26 filmed by Rouvy and 19 filmed by riders, with distance, climbing, where each one runs, and a link. Map of BC rides on Rouvy — an interactive map rather than a download. Every ride as a dot at its start, coloured by who filmed it. BC rides on Rouvy (Excel, also CSV and column guide ) — one row per ride, 45 of them. We read the list from Rouvy's rider map on November 21, 2026. Distances and climbing are Rouvy's figures. "Where it runs" is our own reading of each ride's start and end points. This file is CC0 . It is our own compilation, with no OpenStreetMap records in it. BC bike rides on YouTube # BC bike rides on YouTube — 579 rides in British Columbia filmed from the rider's view, on a map and in a list you can sort by place, views, length, date, or creator. Free to pedal along to on any indoor bike. Cycling gear # Not everything we test has a spreadsheet. Cycle touring gear favourites : field-tested over tens of thousands of kilometres, sample size of one. The research here uses AI assistance (Claude models, Anthropic) for data collection, analysis, and writing. Feel free to ask for more details if you are interested.

Road and path scores (CSV, about 96 MB, or gzipped at about 20 MB) — one row per road or path, 528,742 of them: the four whole-road scores, the name where OpenStreetMap has one, and a point on it so you can find it. Comes with a plain-text column guide . These three files are served from our asset host, so those links leave this page. The file is too big for Excel and is meant for pandas, R, or a database. How we read the terrain: methods and limitations (PDF) — every rule, threshold, and diagram behind the seven scores, and an unsoftened account of what they do not tell you. One naming note: in the report, surface appears under its model name, ruggedness, and quiet as peaceful. Two things to know before you use the file. The assumed speed and traffic columns are modelling inputs assigned from a road's classification, not measurements taken on it. On a separated path they are meaningless, which is why the map does not show them. And a blank cell means we could not measure that thing, not that it is zero: traffic comfort is blank on about a quarter of the rows, on paths where the classifier declines to guess. These scores are computed, not ridden. We have calibrated them most carefully in Metro Vancouver, so expect rougher edges elsewhere in the province. Flow, quiet, and scenic are not in the file yet. They live on 100 metre slices, and rolling them up to a whole road needs a choice we are not ready to defend. Ask if you want them. The scores are derived from OpenStreetMap, so they carry OpenStreetMap's own licence, the Open Database Licence (ODbL) 1.0 , with the attribution © OpenStreetMap contributors. The methodology report, as prose, is CC BY 4.0 .

title: British Columbia transit routes and bicycle policies (Research and Data)
body: Which buses, ferries, water taxis, trains, and flights connect British Columbia's communities, and what each carrier does with a bicycle. Transit network map — an interactive map rather than a download. Every bus, train, ferry, and water taxi that takes bikes, drawn as hops between neighbouring places. Click any line to see who runs it and how often. A side list names the places hardest to reach without a car. Routes and stops — 348 scheduled services and their 1,091 ordered stops, in two files: routes (Excel, also CSV and column guide ), and stops (Excel, also CSV and column guide ). Carriers and bicycle policies (Excel) — 72 operators: whether they carry bicycles, under what conditions, where the answer came from, and when a person last checked. Also as CSV with a plain-text column guide . Journeys (Excel) — every way of getting between two communities, 99,348 of them, in the order we rank them. Also as CSV (21 MB) with a plain-text column guide . Community connections (Excel) — 18,628 community pairs, with both a neutral summary of what runs and the journey we would suggest. Also as CSV with a plain-text column guide . These five files are CC0 . They are our own compilation from operator sources, with no OpenStreetMap records in them. How we map transit and bicycle policies (PDF) — where the data comes from, how a carrier's bicycle answer is reached, how the connections are computed, and what the whole thing does not tell you.

title: Places in British Columbia that a cyclist might want (Research and Data)
body: Our whole BC Bike Stops directory as data: 18,513 cafes, grocery stores, campgrounds, places to stay, bike shops, attractions, and transport connections, with where they are and what we know about how they treat an arriving cyclist. Three files that join on one column. Places (Excel) — one row per place: category, community, coordinates, tier, ownership, and its OpenStreetMap identifier. Also as CSV (12 MB) with a plain-text column guide . Amenities (Excel) — 54,909 rows, one per place and amenity, with the source and the date we recorded it. Long rather than wide, so it pivots. Also as CSV with a plain-text column guide . Sources (Excel) — where every field of every place came from: OpenStreetMap, our own enrichment, a language model, or a person. Also as CSV with a plain-text column guide . Everything, in one file (JSON Lines, gzipped, 6 MB) — the same places, whole: every field we hold, nested, including the amenity detail and the scores. This is the file our own trip planner reads. If something is missing from it, our planner cannot use it either. These three are licensed under the Open Database Licence (ODbL) 1.0 , with the attribution © OpenStreetMap contributors. Most of the listings began as OpenStreetMap records, which makes this a derivative database and share-alike, unlike our other datasets. How we build the stops directory (PDF) — where the listings come from, what earns each of the four tiers, how the categories and amenities are assigned, and what the directory does not cover.

title: When British Columbia campgrounds open and close (Research and Data)
body: When each campground in our directory opens and closes for the season, which ones stay open all year, and whether you can camp outside the season. We read it from BC Parks data, Recreation Sites and Trails BC data, and campgrounds' own websites between September 30 and October 2, 2026. Campground seasons map — an interactive map rather than a download. Every campground, coloured by when it closes. Pick a night to see what's still open. Campground seasons (Excel, also CSV and column guide ) — one row per campground, 1,395 of them. 858 have a season: 418 with high confidence, 298 medium, and 142 low. The rest are in the file too, each with the reason we have no season for it. How we found campground seasons (PDF) — where the dates come from, how an AI model read them, how we checked its quotes, and what the file does not tell you. Most of these seasons were read by an AI model. Low confidence means the evidence was thin: an indirect hint, a listing site rather than the campground's own page, or a web search result we couldn't confirm on the page it linked to. The date may still be right. Check before you go. For a narrative walk through, region by region, see our Field Note Where can I camp this fall? This file is built on our directory, so it carries the same licence as the stops files: the Open Database Licence (ODbL) 1.0 , with the attribution © OpenStreetMap contributors. The methods report, as prose, is CC BY 4.0 .

title: Sea-to-Sky rail corridor (Research and Data)
body: Two reports prepared as input to a Sea-to-Sky rail feasibility study, April 2026. Rail and Trail as Complementary Infrastructure (PDF) — Global evidence that rail and trail are mutually reinforcing: the trail generates rail passengers, and rail service amplifies the trail's economic output. Case studies from North America, Europe, Australasia, and East Asia. Squamish–D'Arcy Bikeway: Cycle Tourism Economic Research (PDF) — The economic case for a bikeway on the corridor: comparable-trail benchmarks, visitor spending evidence, First Nations connections, emergency access, and extension scenarios. Companion appendices (PDF) with operational recommendations and full references. These three reports are CC BY 4.0 : share them and build on them, including commercially, with credit to BC Cycle Tourism Society.

title: The character map — every BC road, seven ways
desc: An interactive map scoring nearly every road and path in British Columbia seven ways: scenic, peaceful, flow, comfort, ruggedness, remoteness, and grade. Click any road to see why it scored what it did.
body: Home / Research and Data / Character map The character map What is it actually like to ride there? Nearly every road and path in BC, scored seven ways from open data. Pick a lens, zoom in, and click any road to see why it scored what it did. Traffic comfort Grade Surface Flow Quiet Remoteness Scenic show 0.00 to 1.00 C1 : separated paths, or slow streets with few cars C2 : sharing light traffic, or bike lanes on calm roads C3 : sharing busier traffic, or bike lanes on busy roads C4 : fast or heavy traffic, a painted line at most C5 : highway-speed traffic (60+ km/h), a painted line at most C6 : fast highway traffic (70+ km/h), a painted line at most FORBIDDEN : cycling not permitted BACKCOUNTRY : bare track, beyond traffic data R0 Paved: any bike R1 Champagne gravel: almost pavement R2 Standard gravel: gravel bike R3 Chunky gravel: wider tires R4 Extreme gravel: borders mountain biking Try: All of BC Stanley Park seawall Galloping Goose, Victoria Salt Spring Island Myra Canyon (KVR) Kamloops Fernie Slocan Valley Loading the map… the first view can take 15 to 20 seconds What you're looking at # Nearly every road, street, and path in British Columbia, scored seven ways from open data. We built these scores to help characterize routes and bike touring options around BC, and they seemed too useful to keep to ourselves. Four of the lenses are preferences. More is not better, you just pick the level that suits the ride you want: Traffic comfort classifies how much motor traffic you share the road with, from separated paths through quiet streets to fast highways. Grade measures climbing in the harder direction: steady ascent per kilometre plus the steepest short pitch. Surface rates how rough it is underfoot, from R0 (paved) to R4 (extreme gravel, borders mountain biking). Remoteness measures how far you are from the next place to buy food, using the stores in our BC Bike Stops directory. The other three are qualities, where more is better: Flow counts what makes you stop: traffic signals, stop signs, and crossings over the next kilometre of riding. Quiet is about noise. It measures distance from busy roads, rail lines, industrial land, and dense street networks. A road can be gorgeous and loud at the same time. Scenic reads the 100 metres around the road: water, forest, natural grass, farmland, cliffs, waterfalls, viewpoints, and how built-up it is. Scenic, quiet, and flow are computed on roughly 100 metre slices of every road, so you can see a street turn from loud to calm as it leaves an arterial. The other four are computed per road segment. The honest limits # These scores are computed, not reviewed ride by ride. So far, we've calibrated them most carefully in Metro Vancouver, so expect rougher edges elsewhere in the province. Everything is derived from OpenStreetMap and public land cover and elevation data, so where those sources have gaps, we have gaps too. Remoteness is measured in straight lines, which understates real riding distance and is plain wrong across water. All of it is preliminary and will keep changing as we improve the models. The traffic comfort ladder is adapted from HUB Cycling's bikeway classification, and we thank them for publishing it. The C1 to C6 labels are our own: HUB's map of Metro Vancouver is checked street by street in a way our computed province-wide estimates are not, so our classes carry our own names. If a road you know well scores strangely, we would genuinely like to hear about it: heather@bccycletourism.ca . Methods and licence # The full write-up of how these scores are computed, with every rule and threshold and an unsoftened list of limitations, is in the methodology report: How we read the terrain (PDF). More datasets and reports live on our Research and Data page. Two naming notes for anyone cross-reading: in the dataset and the methodology PDF, quiet appears under its model name, peaceful, and surface as ruggedness. None of this would exist without open data. The datasets this map is built from are credited in full on our thank-you page . This map contains information from OpenStreetMap, © OpenStreetMap contributors , available under the Open Database Licence . Basemap cartography © OpenMapTiles . The research here uses AI assistance (Claude models, Anthropic) for data collection, analysis, and writing. Feel free to ask for more details if you are interested.

title: Comfort between communities
desc: Every community in British Columbia routed to its five nearest neighbours by bike on our ride comfort ratings, traffic and surface combined, with the share of each trip on roads very few people enjoy.
body: Home / Research and Data / Comfort between communities Comfort between communities For every BC community and its five nearest neighbours, the most comfortable bike route we can find, and how much of it is on roads very few people enjoy. Hover a line for the trip. Click a town for all its trips. THIS IS EXPERIMENTAL WORK. FEEDBACK WELCOME. DO NOT RELY ON IT FOR NAVIGATION OR DECISION MAKING. Public roads and trails Plus forest roads and bare trails Routes use only maintained public roads, designated cycling trails, open Trans Canada Trail sections, and paved town paths. Forest roads and bare trails are left out. 475 of 486 pairs routed. Across the province, 36.9% of the routed kilometres are C1 or C2, and 48.6% are C4 to C6. Go to: Vancouver Victoria Island Sunshine Coast Sea to Sky Fraser Valley Okanagan Kootenays Thompson Cariboo North Peace All BC Loading the map… Ride comfort (traffic and surface combined) # CR1 most riders CR2 some CR3 few CR4 very few CR5 experienced only CR6 risk backcountry (bare track) not rated ferry (not counted) Solid is pavement. Short dashes are gravel or unknown surface. Long dashes are the Trans Canada Trail. Grey dots are a section tctrail.ca listed as closed in July 2026. Trans Canada Trail Whole comfort network underneath Community # Least comfortable links # Share of the route on C4 to C6 roads. What you're looking at # Every community in our Plan Your To and Fro list, plus a few cycling towns it misses, joined to its five nearest neighbours by straight line: 153 places and 486 pairs. For each pair we route a bike trip on our own ride comfort ratings and colour every piece of it by its class. Ride comfort combines traffic and surface. The traffic classes are the ones behind the character map , C1 for most riders through C6 for risk. Where OpenStreetMap says the surface is chunky or worse, a loose pebble rail trail or a sandy climb, the piece moves up the ladder: a chunky surface makes it at least CR3, a rugged one at least CR4. Smooth and ordinary gravel change nothing, so a gravel rail trail stays CR1. The route is the most comfortable one the model can find, not the shortest. Each metre costs its length times a multiplier for its comfort class, so a quiet road is cheap and a highway shoulder is expensive. Both directions are routed and the more comfortable one is kept, because one-way streets and where a start point snaps can make them differ. What the shares say # Across the province, with public roads and trails only, 36.9% of the routed kilometres are on CR1 or CR2 riding and 48.6% are on CR4 to CR6. With forest roads and bare trails allowed, the figures are 46.3% and 32.1%. The second set looks better because the model trades a highway for a forest road. Whether that is better depends on your bike and your appetite. The list beside the map names the pairs with the largest share of CR4 to CR6 riding. Most are places where the only maintained road between two towns is the highway. That is the finding, not a bug in the map. What the two views count as a road # Public roads and trails: a road is in if the BC Digital Road Atlas calls it a public road, from highway through to lane, or if OpenStreetMap marks it as a cycleway, a designated bike route, or an open Trans Canada Trail section, or if it is a paved town path. Forest service roads, bare tracks, unsigned trails, and roads of unknown status are left out on purpose. The cost is honesty. Between many pairs in the north and the Kootenays, the only route left is the highway. Plus forest roads and bare trails: everything rideable goes back in. Forest roads and roads of unknown status are priced as experienced-only riding, so the model still prefers a public road when one exists. Overgrown and decommissioned roads stay out in both views. The limits # Nobody has ridden these routes. The comfort classes are computed from OpenStreetMap, and the character map page explains their limits. Check conditions and closures before you go. 11 of 486 pairs have no route in the public roads view, and 3 in the other. Nine involve Tofino or Ucluelet: our road data predates the Kennedy Hill highway rebuild, so neither town connects. Comox and Courtenay share a centre point. Mayne and Saturna have no ferry in OpenStreetMap. We checked 30 gravel pieces from the public roads routes against satellite imagery. 28 were public gravel roads, rail trails, or dykes. Two were forest roads let in because a Trans Canada Trail route relation runs along them. The fix is queued. Trips run town centre to town centre, and each place is paired only with its five nearest by straight line. A pair you expect may not be drawn. Shares are over rated, non-ferry kilometres. Ferry kilometres are reported separately. Not rated is the few metres of footway or service road a route touches at its ends. The surface lift only works where someone has tagged the surface in OpenStreetMap. Most BC trails carry a surface tag but almost none carry a condition tag, so a rail trail torn up by motorized use can still show as CR1 until it is tagged. We treat untagged forest tracks as unknown rather than rough. Only the Trans Canada Trail sections tctrail.ca listed as closed in July 2026 are avoided. Other closures are not yet. Where the direct road is a CR6 highway, the model sometimes takes a very long paved detour instead. Golden to Revelstoke, at 604 km, is the extreme. The multipliers will be retuned. A neighbourhood street with no speed limit in OpenStreetMap lands at CR2 even when it is a signed bikeway. Streets posted 30 km/h climb to CR1. If a route you know well looks wrong, we would genuinely like to hear about it: heather@bccycletourism.ca . Methods and licence # The traffic comfort classes are the character map's, and its methodology report, How we read the terrain (PDF), explains them. The surface side uses the same ruggedness scale as the character map's surface view, R0 paved to R4 extreme, and lifts a piece to CR3 at R3 and CR4 at R4. The routing itself, the multipliers, and the road rules are not written up for release yet. Ask and we will walk you through them. On this page backcountry is drawn magenta rather than the character map's purple, because purple and CR6 are hard to tell apart on a thin line. Trail alignment from the Trans Canada Trail (tctrail.ca, retrieved July 2026). Road classes from the BC Digital Road Atlas . title: Where can I camp in BC?
desc: Pick a date and see which BC campgrounds are open that night, with their seasons, how sure we are, and which take tents in winter.
body: Home / Research and Data / Campground seasons Where can I camp in BC? Pick a date and see every campground in our directory that's open that night. Hover over a dot for its season, or click or tap it for the details and a link to the campground. 858 campgrounds with a known season 278 are open all year 510 stay open past Thanksgiving Loading the map… Open on # Today After Labour Day After Thanksgiving Nov 1 Jan 15 Ignore the date, show every campground Posted seasons, checked in October 2026. Find # Map key and filters Colour: when it closes # Closes by Labour Day 21 Closes later in September 218 Closes Oct 1 to Thanksgiving 75 Closes later in October 215 Closes in November or later 17 Open all year 278 Season runs through winter 5 No season found 547 How sure we are # Low-confidence dates 141 Hollow dots are low confidence. Check those before you rely on them. What you're looking at # The slider starts on today. Drag it, or tap one of the dates under it, and the map and the list below show only the campgrounds open that night. Tick "Ignore the date" to see every campground, coloured by when it closes. The darker the green, the later it stays open. Grey dots are campgrounds with no posted season. Most are Recreation Sites, which are usually open whenever the road is clear of snow. In winter, that's a big if. Untick "No season found" to hide them. Open all year doesn't always mean tents. Some campgrounds take only RVs in winter, so we leave them off the map in the months they say no tents. Where we've checked that a campground takes tents in winter, or BC Parks posts winter camping there, it says so. For hike-in and boat-in camps, the question is getting there, so check winter access. Everywhere else, call ahead. How sure we are # We found a season for 858 of the 1,395 campgrounds: 418 with high confidence, 298 medium, and 142 low. Hollow dots are the low-confidence ones. They are on the map because the season may well be right, but treat them as a lead and check before you go. Patterns across a region hold up well. A single campground's date can be wrong. The map shows 1,376 of them. The rest have no location yet, or turned out to be closed or not a campground. We collected these dates between September 30 and October 2, 2026. Campgrounds change their dates every year, and some had only last year's posted when we looked. The operator's own page is the answer that counts. More # For riders, our Field Note Where can I camp this fall? walks through it region by region, with the campgrounds that take tents in winter. The data behind this map, and how we built it, are on our Research and Data page. title: Cycle touring gear favourites
desc: A few favourite (in some cases quirky) pieces of cycle touring gear: helmet mirror, visibility gear, locks, tires, and camping comforts.
body: Home / Cycle touring gear favourites Cycle touring gear favourites The gear you’ll want to take on your trip depends on the time of year, whether you’ll be camping, how remote you’ll be, and many other factors. There are many great resources on the web that recommend packing lists and review gear options for cycle touring and bikepacking, so this won’t be a comprehensive list, at all. Instead, here are a few pieces of gear — some of them quirky — that this author (hi!) has found delightful and you might too: See and be seen # 🪞 Helmet mirror The biggest improvement in my cycle touring gear has been the addition of this helmet mirror . See this write-up for info on why bike mirrors are so great , and worth the dorkiness. The EVT Helmet Mirror is the one I love. 💡 Helmet with lights Wearing a helmet with built-in lights has been a game changer: my lights are always available to turn on, including in heavy traffic, and they are easy to charge in the tent at night from a battery. Brand: Lumos 🔺 Reflective triangle Adventure Cycling requires all riders on its tours to wear helmets, and also display a reflective triangle on the back of their panniers or around their waist. Strongly recommended. The Joglite brand has a strap that fits around a pannier or your waist. 🦺 Visible I want to be visible on roads, or even on trails in hunting season. The Women’s Tour Cycling Jacket (sleeves zip off to become a vest) is a comfortable solution for road riding, or something simple like the Jogalite Cycling Vest . I wear something this bright almost every day on tour. On the bike # 🔒 Lock It’s hard to decide what lock to bring touring, because you need something heavy-duty in the cities, but don’t want the weight otherwise. The one I bring is the LITELOK GO FLEXI-U . It weighs 650g (1.4lb) which is about half as much as a heavy-duty D-locks but still has a Sold Secure Silver rating. 🩴 SPD bike sandals SPD bike sandals are cool in the summer, warm in the winter (with wool socks), dry quickly in the rain, comfortable walking around a store, look incredibly stylish (well ok you can’t have everything), and a great touring choice. Seriously they are the only bike shoes I’ve used for the last 20 years. Shimano brand: SH-SD501 🛞 Tires I’ve never gotten a flat with Schwalbe Marathon tires , after tens of thousands of kilometers touring. 📱 Phone holder If you are using a phone for navigation, get a phone holder for your handlebars. 🔋 Rechargeable batteries I have two 10,000 mAh rechargeable batteries and I’ve found that enough to charge my phone, helmet, GPS watch, and Garmin Inreach overnight (and sometimes during rides) if I’m able to charge them up at campgrounds or coffeeshops every day or two. 🚲 Kickstand Life was better when my touring bike had a kickstand . The Pletscher Twin-Legger Kickstand is center-mounted and my favourite, however unfortunately it won’t fit on many bikes. A Click-Stand is a fairly useful work-around if your bike wont fit any other touring-capable kickstand. 💨 Tire pump The Topeak Road Morph G Pump with gauge tire pump is reliable, easy to pump up (it can rest on the ground with little fold-out legs), and has a gauge. 👜 Handlebar bag I love having a quick-release handlebar bag that I can easily take into stores or bathrooms. It contains all my valuables, as well as things I want in easy reach. I never leave my valuables (wallet, keys, etc) unattended on my bike. I use one from Jandd but it has been discontinued alas. Around camp # 🧺 Laundry line This clever laundry line is small and easy to use. Don’t forget to wring out your clothes first in your towel; it makes a world of difference. Also, always pack up your clothesline whenever you take off your last piece of laundry so you don’t forget it! Sea to Summit brand 🪣 Collapsible bucket A collapsible bucket helps make daily laundry at camp less of a chore. Sea To Summit brand 🧎 Seat/kneeling pad A seat/kneeling pad can be a relief when everywhere is rocky or wet 🔨 Tent stake mallet To take all the frustration out of pitching my tent, I bring a lightweight tent stake mallet as a comfort item. Brand: Coghlan’s. 🪑 Camping chair Lots of bike campers love a lightweight camping chair ⛺ Big vestibules Your mileage may vary, but I love big vestibules in my tent . I use the North Face Stormbreak 2 when camping solo. A bit heavy, but inexpensive and it makes me happy. Finally, don’t forget a first-aid kit and a repair kit!

title: Backgrounder
desc: The BC Cycle Tourism Society on one page: the opportunity, the gap, what we do, what's already live, and how to get involved.
body: Home / About / Backgrounder Backgrounder · September 2026 BC Cycle Tourism Society We're building the provincial organization that makes British Columbia a world-class cycle touring destination : the marketing, standards, partnerships, and advocacy that turn great riding into a rural tourism economy. 3× longer stays than the average visitor (3.7 vs 1.4 nights) $400 vs $220 cycle tourist spend per trip vs other visitors $1B /yr what New Zealand's cycle trails earn each year The gap # BC has world-class cycle touring and bikepacking routes, but no organization pulling them together: no shared story, no quality standards, no data on what cycle tourists spend. Québec and New Zealand built this layer decades ago. The province has set a goal of doubling visitor spending by 2036, and cycle tourists deliver exactly the growth it's asking for: high-value visitors, in shoulder seasons, in rural communities. Over half of BC's tourism organizations actively promote mountain biking. Only about 1 in 5 actively promote cycle touring, and almost none offer a digital route file a rider could actually follow. BC tourism runs on sector organizations: craft beer, paddling, mountain biking. Cycle touring doesn't have one yet. What we do # Tell BC's story One coherent cycle touring story for the world: routes on regional websites, a provincial trip planner, and the platforms riders use, kept current. Improve the experience Difficulty ratings riders can trust, bike-friendly business accreditation, new route development, and education for operators. Build the evidence Annual data on cycle tourism demand and gaps: numbers regions can take to their boards, funders, and hotel-tax reports. Already live # ✓ 300+ published routes Explore BC's published cycle touring and bikepacking routes in one place. ✓ Transit with your bike Plan how to get to and from your ride, including ferries, buses, and trains that take bikes. ✓ BC Bike Stops A province-wide directory of bike-friendly businesses. Free for any operator. Who we are # An independent nonprofit society, grown out of organizations already working to make cycling and trails stronger in British Columbia: the BC Cycling Coalition, Trails BC, and Let's Go Biking. We're a regional organization member of the Outdoor Recreation Council of BC and a sector association member of the Tourism Industry Association of BC. Hear the story: “Can BC Become the Next New Zealand for Cycle Tourism?” on the BC Cycling Coalition's BikeSense podcast ( bccycling.ca/podcast ). Get involved # Tourism organizations Partner with us to develop and showcase your region's cycle tourism. Businesses Join the BC Bike Stops directory. Free for cafés, motels, campgrounds, and shops. Riders & supporters Explore routes and sign up for the newsletter. bccycletourism.ca hello@bccycletourism.ca

title: Apply for Accreditation
desc: Apply to the BC Bike Stops accreditation program. Free for hotels, campgrounds, restaurants, bike shops, and other businesses across BC that welcome touring cyclists.
body: Home / Apply for accreditation Join BC Bike Stops BC's cycle tourism accreditation program. Free to join. Cycle tourists plan their trips around businesses that genuinely welcome them. In Quebec, where the Bienvenue cyclistes! program has run for decades, 31% of overnight cycle tourists adapt their itinerary based on certification (47% stayed at a certified establishment, and two-thirds of those said certification influenced their choice). The Accredited badge is how we signal that to BC's growing cycle tourism market. What Accreditation brings Full and customized listing in our BC Bike Stops directory with the teal Accredited badge Highlighted placement in route-planning tools Features in our newsletter and social channels A digital "BC Bike Stops" badge for your website, if you would like that The form takes about 10 minutes. We review applications ourselves and aim to respond within two weeks. Accreditation lasts two years — we check in then to confirm your listing is still accurate. Your business Business name * Address Phone Website Email for cyclist enquiries An email cyclists can use to ask about bike storage, availability, etc. This will be visible on your listing. Describe your business in a few sentences This will appear in your listing. What would you want a cyclist to know? Category * Attractions — visitor centres, museums, libraries, rec centres, hot springs, markets Accommodation — hotels, motels, hostels, guesthouses, B&Bs, inns Camping — campgrounds, RV parks, group campsites, backcountry sites Food & Drink — restaurants, cafés, pubs, food trucks, bakeries, wineries, breweries Supplies — grocery stores, general stores, convenience stores, farm stands Bike Services — bike shops, repair, gear shops, rentals, guides, tour operators Transport — buses, shuttles, ferries, taxis, luggage transfer, bike transport Don't fit neatly into a category? Email us and we'll figure it out together. Required criteria for Accreditation — please confirm Each category has specific requirements. Please confirm your business meets all of these. Optional amenities — check what you offer These appear as tags on your listing so cyclists know what to expect. Details about your amenities Anything a visiting cyclist should know about the amenities you checked — where to find them, when they're available, any conditions. These show up as notes on your listing that cyclists read before they arrive — extra information here is very helpful and makes your business even more welcoming. Anything else about your listing? General notes — seasonal closures, things that are changing, anything we should know that doesn't fit above Your local knowledge BC Bike Stops Local Knowledge Sheet A short card your staff can keep at the front desk for cyclists who ask "where can I get my bike fixed?" or "is there a grocery store nearby?" We can look up trail maps and hospital phone numbers — what we can't look up is the local knowledge that makes a cyclist's trip easier. Fill in what you know and we'll email you a printable sheet to review, edit, and keep behind the desk. Partial answers are fine, we'll help fill gaps. See an example → Nearest bike repair Where would you send a cyclist with a flat tire or a broken spoke? Nearest food and groceries Closest options for a hungry cyclist — include distance if it's not obvious Getting out with a bike If a cyclist needed to leave the area with their bike — what are the options? Public bus, local taxi with a van, a neighbour who does runs to town, a shuttle service? Insider knowledge — hazards, access, seasonal quirks Things a visiting cyclist wouldn't know but should. Trail closures, wildlife, road conditions, water sources, cell coverage, great pie, anything. Your contact info Contact name * Contact email * Contact role I confirm that our business meets all required criteria for our category, and I agree to be contacted in two years to confirm our listing is still accurate. Submit application That didn't send. Please email hello@bccycletourism.ca and we'll sort it out.

body: Home / Privacy Privacy Policy Last updated: April 29, 2026 This Privacy Policy describes how we collect, use, and protect your information when you visit this website. 1. Information We Collect We may collect the following information: Contact information : such as your name and email address when you fill out a contact form Usage data : information about how you use this website (pages visited, time spent, etc.) Technical data : such as browser type, device, and IP address 2. How We Use Your Information We use your information to: Respond to inquiries submitted through our contact form Improve our website and user experience Analyze website traffic and usage patterns 3. These tools may collect information such as pages visited, time on site, and general location (not precise). 4. Data Security We take reasonable steps to protect your information from unauthorized access, use, or disclosure. 6. Third-Party Services Our website may use third-party services (such as form providers or analytics tools) that collect and process data on our behalf. 7. Your Rights Under applicable privacy laws (including PIPEDA), you may have the right to: Request access to your personal data Request correction of inaccurate data Withdraw consent where applicable To make a request, contact us at hello@bccycletourism.ca .

title: Land Acknowledgement
desc: Land Acknowledgement for the BC Cycle Tourism Society website.
body: Home / Land acknowledgement Land Acknowledgement The cycling routes and communities featured on this website are located throughout what is now British Columbia, on many First Nations territories, including unceded and treaty lands. We acknowledge the enduring relationships, rights, laws, cultures, and stewardship responsibilities of First Nations in these places. As this network grows, we are committed to listening and building respectful relationships with Indigenous communities whose territories and priorities are connected to cycle tourism in BC. We're also committed to deepening our understanding of the history and present-day stories of the peoples whose lands we ride through, and we encourage our readers to do the same. Tools such as Native Land and Whose Land can be useful starting points.

title: With Thanks
desc: The open data, open source software, generous programs, and people this site is built on, with our thanks.
body: Home / With thanks With Thanks This site runs on generosity. Much of what you see here, the trails, the maps, the data, the hosting, exists because people and organizations chose to share their work openly, so others could build on it. The people on the ground # Every trail on this site exists because someone builds and maintains it, usually a volunteer trail society working with hand tools and small budgets. If you ride these trails, support the trail organizations . The routes we feature were designed by real people who scouted, mapped, and documented them. Meet the route makers . Riding in BC keeps getting better because bike advocacy organizations have spent decades building bike-friendly culture, laws, and infrastructure. Thank you to the BC Cycling Coalition , HUB Cycling , GoByBike BC , and the many local groups doing this work in their own communities. Data contributors # Some of the best facts in our directory come from people who told us what's really there: where the water refill is, whether the washroom is open to you, which places will charge your phone while you eat. Thank you to: Dimitri Adamopoulos (Ithaka Greek Restaurant, Victoria) Want to join this list? Suggest a stop or a fix and check the credit box. OpenStreetMap # The foundation of this site. Our maps, our directory of bike stops, and our route data all draw on OpenStreetMap , a world map built by volunteers. Thousands of mappers have surveyed British Columbia's roads, trails, campgrounds, and cafés so that anyone can use the results for free. We are grateful to every one of them. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License . Open data # The Province of British Columbia , through the BC Data Catalogue and GeoBC: tourism region, municipality, and regional district boundaries, the BC Geographical Names register, the Freshwater Atlas, and listings for BC Parks and Recreation Sites and Trails BC. Statistics Canada census data and NASA's Shuttle Radar Topography Mission elevation data, which powers our steepness data. The Commission for Environmental Cooperation's North American Land Change Monitoring System (NALCMS) land cover data, which helps us guess the surface of backcountry tracks nobody has mapped, and spot supply stops that are across water. BC Transit and TransLink open schedule data, and BC Ferries schedules, which power our travel planning pages. Indigenous Tourism BC (ITBC) , whose business listings help us identify Indigenous-owned and Indigenous-operated stops. HUB Cycling , whose comfort classification work informs how we describe cycling conditions, and CAN-BICS , the Canadian Bikeway Comfort and Safety Classification system, developed by Simon Fraser University's CHATR Lab with the Public Health Agency of Canada and now used by Statistics Canada to map cycling infrastructure nationally. Open source software # This site is built with free, open source software. MapLibre GL and the OpenMapTiles schema render the interactive maps. PostgreSQL with the PostGIS extension and Valhalla power the cycling route network we build behind the scenes, and the Python tools osmium and Shapely do much of the data work. Thank you to the maintainers and contributors, and to the many other projects we rely on. Generous programs # GitHub Pages hosts this site for free. Google Places offers a free tier that helps us check our facts, like whether a place is still open, against Google's fresher data. Destination BC's Content Hub provides much of the photography on this site. Individual photographers are credited on each image. Spotted something wrong? # Corrections are a contribution too. If a listing is out of date, a trail is misdescribed, or a map is wrong, suggest a fix . We read every one, and we're thankful for each. Last updated August 2026.

title: Slocan Valley Rail Trail
desc: 13 places to stay, eat, resupply, and find bike services along the Slocan Valley Rail Trail, Kootenay Rockies, for touring cyclists.

title: ʔapsčiik t̓ašii (Pacific Rim Multi-use Path)
desc: 125 places to stay, eat, resupply, and find bike services along the ʔapsčiik t̓ašii (Pacific Rim Multi-use Path), Vancouver Island, for touring cyclists.
body: Photo: Jordan Dyck Tofino, BC Vancouver Island ʔapsčiik t̓ašii (Pacific Rim Multi-use Path) Home / Trails / ʔapsčiik t̓ašii (Pacific Rim Multi-use Path) 54 km Vancouver Island 125 stops ʔapsčiik t̓ašii runs through Pacific Rim National Park Reserve between Tofino and Ucluelet, on the traditional territories of the Tla-o-qui-aht and Yuułuʔiłʔatḥ. The paved path winds through rainforest, with spur trails to the big beaches. Surf, sand, and cedar, all car-free.
